OpenSearch's BM25 implementation and parameters, matching the Lucene defaults.

t: Collaborative filtering: neighbourhoods, matrix factorisation (ALS and SGD) and implicit feedback
sum: Learning taste from behaviour alone: the user–item matrix and its sparsity, item-to-item neighbourhoods with cosine similarity, matrix factorisation trained by SGD and by alternating least squares (one ALS step worked on a 3×3 matrix), implicit feedback with confidence weights, negative sampling and BPR, and how the Netflix Prize and Hu, Koren and Volinsky's TV study shaped practice.
prereq: rec1
Candidate generation pulls a few thousand items from millions using item representations computed ahead of time; collaborative filtering is one of the oldest ways to build those representations.
ml4
Gradient descent nudges parameters against the gradient of a loss; the learning rate sets the step size, and stochastic gradient descent uses one example (or a small batch) per step.
ml3
L2 regularisation adds λ times the squared size of the parameters to the loss, pulling them towards zero so the model cannot fit noise with huge weights.
lm10
A dot product of two vectors is large when they point the same way; cosine similarity is the dot product of the vectors scaled to length 1.
why:
In the early days of online shopping, a bookshop had a problem the shop assistant used to solve by intuition. A customer buys a book on beginner rock climbing. What should the website suggest next? A content rule, "other books with 'climbing' in the title", produces a list of more climbing books, many redundant, and misses the things climbers actually buy next: a guide to knots, a first-aid manual, a book about a famous expedition. Nothing in the text of a rock-climbing book says "people who buy this also want wilderness first aid". But the order history says it, loudly, thousands of times.

That observation is the whole idea of collaborative filtering: let the behaviour of many people reveal what goes with what, and who is like whom, without needing to understand the items at all. It works for books, films, songs, products and posts, in any language, for items whose appeal no feature describes. It is why a recommender can learn that a particular indie band appeals to the same listeners as a particular podcast, a connection no metadata would suggest.

It also comes with problems that shape the whole field. The data is a gigantic table that is more than 99% empty. Most of what we observe is implicit, a click or a play rather than a rating, so we never see a clear "no". New items and new users have no history at all. And whatever is popular gets recommended, gets clicked and becomes more popular.

This lesson builds collaborative filtering from the ground up: the user–item matrix and why its empty cells are unknown rather than zero; neighbourhood methods, worked with cosine similarity; matrix factorisation, the idea that won the Netflix Prize, trained both by stochastic gradient descent and by alternating least squares, with one ALS step worked by hand on a 3×3 matrix; and the adjustments for implicit feedback, confidence weights, negative sampling and pairwise ranking. Its embeddings are the direct ancestors of the two-tower models in rec4.
primer:
Picture a giant spreadsheet. Each row is a person, each column is an item, and each cell records what that person did with that item: a star rating, a purchase, how many times they played a song. Almost every cell is blank, because each person has touched only a tiny part of the catalogue. Collaborative filtering is the job of guessing which blank cells would be high if the person encountered that item, and recommending those.

There are two ways to make the guess. The first is to look for neighbours. To guess whether Priya will like a film, find films similar to ones Priya liked, where "similar" means "liked by the same people"; or find people whose past ratings resemble Priya's and see what they thought. This is like asking friends with similar taste for advice. It is easy to explain, and with clever precomputation it scales well.

The second way is to find hidden factors. Suppose every film could be described by a few numbers, such as how much action it has, how much romance, how arty it is, and every person by how much they enjoy each of those. Then a person's interest in a film is roughly the sum of (their love of action × the film's action) + (their love of romance × the film's romance) + ..., a dot product. Matrix factorisation learns such numbers for every person and every film purely from the filled-in cells, without being told what the factors mean. Often the learned factors line up loosely with genres or with "mainstream versus niche", but they are whatever best explains the data.

The spreadsheet analogy breaks in an important place. A blank cell in a spreadsheet is just blank. In a recommender, blanks are not random: people rate what they chose to watch, and they chose because they expected to like it. And with implicit data, a blank might mean "never saw it" or "saw it and scrolled past". How you treat the blanks is the single most consequential modelling decision in collaborative filtering, and much of this lesson is about it.

Both approaches share one assumption worth saying out loud: the past predicts the future. If a thousand people who bought a tent also bought a stove, the next tent buyer probably wants a stove. That is usually true, which is why collaborative filtering works, and occasionally false in ways that matter: tastes change, seasons change (nobody needs the tent-and-stove pairing in January), and the system's own recommendations shape what people buy, so the "past" it learns from is partly its own doing. Keep that in the back of your mind; rec10 returns to it.

Two facts make the factor approach powerful. It compresses: 50 million users and 5 million items with 64 factors each is 3.5 billion numbers instead of 250 trillion cells. And it generalises: a user who rated only ten films still gets a sensible vector, because each of those films' vectors was learned from thousands of other people.
body:
1. The user–item matrix and the meaning of a blank

Formally we have m users, n items and a matrix R whose entry rui records user u's interaction with item i. Two kinds of data fill it. Explicit feedback is a stated preference: 1-5 stars, thumbs up or down. It is clean in meaning but scarce, because most people never rate. Implicit feedback is behaviour: purchases, clicks, plays, minutes watched, add-to-cart. It is plentiful, but its meaning is fuzzy: a play may be a mis-tap, a purchase may be a gift, and there is no explicit "no".

The matrix is extremely sparse. The Netflix Prize dataset had about 100 million ratings from roughly 480,000 users on 17,770 films: 100 million ÷ (480,000 × 17,770) ≈ 1.2% filled, and that was a dataset of active raters. A shop with 50 million customers, 5 million products and 4 billion interactions is 4 × 10⁹ ÷ 2.5 × 10¹⁴ = 0.0016% filled.

The key conceptual point is what a blank means. With explicit ratings, a blank is unknown, and it is missing not at random: people rate films they chose to watch, which they chose because they expected to like them, so observed ratings skew high, and unrated films skew towards ones people expected to dislike. A model that treated blanks as zero ratings would learn that everything unrated is terrible. So explicit-feedback models fit only observed entries. With implicit data, a blank is a weak, ambiguous negative: the item was either not wanted or never noticed. Implicit models therefore include blanks, but with low weight. Keep this distinction in mind; every method below takes one side or the other.

2. Neighbourhood methods: item-to-item similarity

The most direct collaborative method says: two items are similar if the same people engage with both. To make that a number, represent each item by its column in the matrix, a vector with one entry per user, and compare columns. For binary data (did the user engage or not), the standard measure is cosine similarity: the number of users who engaged with both items, divided by the square root of the product of the two items' user counts. Dividing by the counts matters: without it, a bestseller that everyone buys would be "similar" to everything.

A worked example with five customers of an outdoor shop and four items: A (tent), B (sleeping bag), C (camping stove), D (a novel).

CustomerBought
u1A, B, C
u2A, B
u3B, C
u4A, D
u5D

Item user counts: A 3 (u1, u2, u4), B 3 (u1, u2, u3), C 2 (u1, u3), D 2 (u4, u5). Co-purchases: A and B share u1, u2, so cos(A, B) = 2 / √(3 × 3) = 0.667. B and C share u1, u3: 2 / √(3 × 2) = 0.816. A and C share u1: 1 / √6 = 0.408. A and D share u4: 1 / √6 = 0.408. B and D, C and D share nobody: 0.

To score candidates for a user, sum each candidate's similarity to the items the user already has. Customer u2 has A and B. Candidate C scores cos(C, A) + cos(C, B) = 0.408 + 0.816 = 1.225. Candidate D scores 0.408 + 0 = 0.408. Recommend the stove, which matches intuition: tent-and-sleeping-bag buyers buy stoves. Production systems weight the user's items by recency and strength (a purchase over a view), keep only each item's top 50-200 neighbours, and normalise scores.

The user-based variant compares rows instead of columns: find users similar to u2, then recommend what they bought. It works, but at scale item-based usually wins, as Amazon's 2003 paper explained: item-to-item similarities are more stable (an item's audience changes slowly, while a user's similarity to others shifts with every purchase), they can be computed offline into a table of each item's top neighbours, and serving is then a few table lookups: for each of the user's recent items, fetch its neighbours, merge and score. The method also explains itself: "because you bought a tent".

The weaknesses are visible in the example. The novel D has only one co-purchase with anything; similarities from one or two shared users are noise. Real systems require a minimum co-occurrence count, shrink low-support similarities towards zero, and still find that neighbourhoods are thin for the long tail of rarely bought items. Matrix factorisation addresses exactly that.

3. Matrix factorisation: the model

Give each user u a vector xu of k numbers and each item i a vector yi of k numbers, where k (the number of latent factors) is small: 20 to 256. Predict the interaction as their dot product:

r̂(u, i) = x_u · y_i = x_u1·y_i1 + x_u2·y_i2 + ... + x_uk·y_ik

In matrix terms, the whole m × n matrix is approximated by X Yᵀ, where X is m × k (users' vectors as rows) and Y is n × k. That is a low-rank approximation: rank k, far below m or n. The model's claim is that taste has a few main directions, and both people and items can be located along them.

The training objective for explicit ratings fits only the observed entries, with L2 regularisation (ml3) to stop vectors growing to fit noise:

minimise   Σ over observed (u,i):  (r_ui − x_u · y_i)²   +   λ ( Σ_u |x_u|² + Σ_i |y_i|² )

Real models add bias terms: r̂ = μ + bu + bi + xu · yi, where μ is the global average rating, bu captures that some users rate everything high, and bi that some films are liked by everyone. Koren, Bell and Volinsky's 2009 article showed that biases alone explain a large share of rating variance, and the factors then model the interaction.

Why not use the singular value decomposition from linear algebra, which gives the best rank-k approximation of a matrix? Because SVD needs every entry, and here 99% are unknown. Filling them with zeros or averages biases the result badly. The Netflix Prize popularised the name "SVD" for the learned model above, but it is fitted to observed entries only, which needs an iterative algorithm. There are two standard ones.

4. Training with stochastic gradient descent

SGD loops over observed entries in random order. For each (u, i, r), compute the error e = r − xu · yi, then move both vectors a small step to reduce it, with η the learning rate:

x_u ← x_u + η ( e · y_i − λ · x_u )
y_i ← y_i + η ( e · x_u − λ · y_i )      (using the old x_u)

The intuition: if the prediction is too low (e > 0), move the user vector towards the item vector and the item vector towards the user vector, so their dot product grows; the λ terms shrink both slightly towards zero.

One update by hand, with k = 2, η = 0.05, λ = 0.1. User vector x = (1.0, 1.0), item vector y = (1.0, 0.2), observed rating r = 5. Prediction: 1.0 × 1.0 + 1.0 × 0.2 = 1.2. Error e = 3.8. New x = (1.0 + 0.05 × (3.8 × 1.0 − 0.1 × 1.0), 1.0 + 0.05 × (3.8 × 0.2 − 0.1 × 1.0)) = (1.185, 1.033). New y = (1.0 + 0.05 × (3.8 × 1.0 − 0.1 × 1.0), 0.2 + 0.05 × (3.8 × 1.0 − 0.1 × 0.2)) = (1.185, 0.389). New prediction: 1.185 × 1.185 + 1.033 × 0.389 = 1.404 + 0.402 = 1.81. The error shrank from 3.8 to 3.2 in one step; thousands of passes over millions of ratings do the rest.

SGD is simple, uses little memory, and accepts any differentiable loss, which is why it dominated the Netflix Prize and why variants with side features, time effects and pairwise losses are easy to write. Its drawbacks: a learning rate to tune, sequential updates that are awkward to parallelise (in practice, parallel workers update shared vectors without locks and tolerate occasional conflicts), and trouble with losses over all user–item pairs, which implicit data needs.

5. Training with alternating least squares

The objective is hard to minimise jointly, because the prediction multiplies two unknowns. But fix all item vectors, and the problem for each user becomes ordinary linear regression with an L2 penalty (ridge regression): the user's rated items' vectors are the inputs, the ratings are the targets, and xu is the weight vector. Ridge regression has an exact solution:

x_u = (Y_uᵀ Y_u + λI)⁻¹ Y_uᵀ r_u

where Yu stacks the vectors of the items user u rated and ru is the vector of those ratings. Solve that for every user (independently, so in parallel), then fix users and solve every item the same way, and repeat. Each half-step solves its subproblem exactly, so the loss never goes up. This is alternating least squares (ALS).

One ALS step on a 3×3 matrix, by hand. Three users, three items, k = 2, λ = 0.1. Observed ratings (· is unknown):

item 1item 2item 3
user 153·
user 24·1
user 3·15

Start with item vectors y1 = (1.0, 0.2), y2 = (0.6, 0.4), y3 = (0.2, 1.0), and all user vectors (1, 1). Squared error on the six observed entries at the start: 40.76.

Solve user 1. User 1 rated items 1 and 2. Build A = y1y1ᵀ + y2y2ᵀ + λI. The outer products are y1y1ᵀ = [[1.00, 0.20], [0.20, 0.04]] and y2y2ᵀ = [[0.36, 0.24], [0.24, 0.16]]. Sum plus 0.1 on the diagonal: A = [[1.46, 0.44], [0.44, 0.30]]. The right-hand side b = 5 × y1 + 3 × y2 = (5.0, 1.0) + (1.8, 1.2) = (6.8, 2.2).

Solve A x = b. The determinant is 1.46 × 0.30 − 0.44 × 0.44 = 0.438 − 0.1936 = 0.2444. The inverse of a 2×2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]] is (1/det) [[d, −b], [−c, a]], so x1 = (1/0.2444) × (0.30 × 6.8 − 0.44 × 2.2, −0.44 × 6.8 + 1.46 × 2.2) = (1/0.2444) × (2.040 − 0.968, −2.992 + 3.212) = (1.072, 0.220) / 0.2444 = (4.386, 0.900).

Check: x1 · y1 = 4.386 + 0.180 = 4.57 (target 5) and x1 · y2 = 2.632 + 0.360 = 2.99 (target 3). The regulariser keeps it from fitting exactly.

The other users, same procedure: user 2 (items 1 and 3) gets A = [[1.14, 0.40], [0.40, 1.14]], b = (4.2, 1.8), x2 = (3.570, 0.326). User 3 (items 2 and 3) gets A = [[0.50, 0.44], [0.44, 1.26]], b = (1.6, 5.4), x3 = (−0.825, 4.574). After this half-step the squared error on observed entries drops from 40.76 to 0.78 (the regularisation term rises to 5.71, because the vectors grew; the total objective falls from 41.62 to 6.49).

Then solve items with users fixed: y1 becomes (1.101, 0.173), y2 (0.613, 0.328), y3 (0.175, 1.120). The objective falls to 5.75, almost all of it regularisation; observed entries are now fitted to within 0.01. The predictions for the blanks: user 1, item 3: 1.77; user 2, item 2: 2.30; user 3, item 1: −0.12, which you would clip to the rating range. User 3 loves item 3 and dislikes item 2's neighbour item 1, and the factors have captured "users 1 and 2 like item 1's kind of thing; user 3 likes item 3's kind".

Cost. Building A for a user costs about k² operations per item they rated, and solving it costs about k³. With k = 64 that is 4,096 per interaction and 262,144 per user. For 50 million users with 80 interactions each, a user half-step is about 50 × 10⁶ × (80 × 4,096 + 262,144) ≈ 3 × 10¹³ operations: tens of seconds of compute on a large cluster, which is why ALS runs comfortably as a nightly batch job. Spark MLlib's ALS is a widely used implementation.

6. Implicit feedback: preference and confidence

With implicit data the explicit objective breaks. If you fit only observed entries, which are all positive, the model learns that everyone likes everything, a trivially perfect fit. You must include the blanks. But blanks are ambiguous, and observed counts mean "more evidence", not "likes more".

Hu, Koren and Volinsky's 2008 paper, written for a TV recommender built on viewing data from about 300,000 set-top boxes, separated two quantities. The preference pui is 1 if user u interacted with item i at all, else 0. The confidence cui is how much we trust that preference: cui = 1 + α · rui, where rui is the interaction strength (in their case, how much of a show was watched, summed over viewings). Unobserved pairs get preference 0 with confidence 1, a weak "probably not"; a show watched in full five times gets preference 1 with confidence 1 + 40 × 5 = 201, using their reported α = 40. The objective covers every user–item pair:

minimise   Σ over all (u,i):  c_ui (p_ui − x_u · y_i)²   +   λ ( Σ|x_u|² + Σ|y_i|² )

Every pair means m × n terms: 50 million × 5 million = 2.5 × 10¹⁴. Visiting them with SGD is impossible. ALS handles it with an algebraic trick. The user solve becomes xu = (YᵀCuY + λI)⁻¹ YᵀCupu, where Cu is a diagonal matrix of the user's confidences over all items. Write YᵀCuY = YᵀY + Yᵀ(Cu − I)Y. The first term, YᵀY, is the same for every user and is computed once per sweep. The second involves only items where Cu differs from 1, the user's observed items. So each user's solve costs about k² per observed item plus k³, linear in the data, despite fitting all pairs. This is why implicit ALS remains a workhorse.

The paper's results, on a test week following a four-week training window, used expected percentile rank: where, as a percentage of the ranked list, the shows people actually watched appeared (lower is better; random is 50%). Recommending by popularity gave 16.46%, an item-neighbourhood method 10.74%, and the factor model improved with more factors, reaching 8.35% at 200 factors. The paper also notes that predicting re-watching is much easier than predicting a first-time view, so it removed previously watched shows from the test, an evaluation choice that still matters today.

7. Implicit feedback with SGD: negative sampling and BPR

Many models cannot use the ALS trick: those with side features, nonlinear components or custom losses, trained by SGD. They need another way to include the blanks: negative sampling. For each observed (user, item) pair, a positive, sample a few unobserved items for the same user and treat them as negatives, label 0. Train with a binary cross-entropy loss on positives and sampled negatives.

Which unobserved items to sample matters a lot. Uniform sampling mostly picks obscure items the user never had a chance to see and that the model already scores low; the gradient from them is tiny and learning is slow. Sampling in proportion to popularity picks items the user plausibly encountered and passed over, which carry more information. A common compromise borrowed from word2vec samples in proportion to count raised to the 0.75 power, flattening the popularity curve. Hard negatives, items the current model scores high but the user did not engage with, teach the most but risk being false negatives: items the user would like but has not yet seen.

BPR (Bayesian personalised ranking, Rendle and colleagues, 2009) changes the question from "is this pair positive?" to "is this positive item ranked above this negative one?". For a triple (user u, observed item i, sampled unobserved item j), it maximises ln σ(sui − suj), where s is the model's score and σ the sigmoid. Only the difference matters, which suits ranking: we care about order, not calibrated probabilities. BPR with matrix factorisation scores is a standard strong baseline for implicit top-k recommendation. The same "positive versus sampled negatives" idea, scaled up to softmax over many negatives at once, is how two-tower retrieval models are trained in rec4.

8. Evaluating collaborative filtering

How you hold out data decides whether the evaluation means anything. A random split of interactions leaks the future: the model trains on a user's March purchases and is tested on their January ones. A temporal split, train on everything before a date and test on what happened after, matches deployment. Hu and colleagues trained on four weeks and tested on the following week. Within the test period, decide whether repeated interactions count: recommending a show someone already watches every week is easy and inflates scores, so for discovery surfaces, test only on new items per user.

Metrics should be ranking metrics on top-k lists, recall@k, nDCG@k, MRR (rec8), not RMSE on ratings. Compare against popularity: on many datasets, "recommend the most popular items" is a surprisingly strong baseline, and a personalised model that barely beats it is not earning its complexity. Report results by user activity bucket (users with 1-5 interactions versus 100+), because CF is strong for heavy users and weak for light ones, and an average hides that.

9. Serving collaborative filtering inside the funnel

In the multi-stage stack from rec1, collaborative filtering usually shows up in three places, and it is worth knowing which one an interviewer means.

As an item-to-item candidate source: a nightly (or hourly) job computes each item's top 100-200 neighbours and writes them to a key-value store. At request time, take the user's last 10-20 interactions, fetch each one's neighbour list (one batched read), merge the lists by summing similarities weighted by recency, drop items the user already has, and return the top few hundred. The cost is a handful of milliseconds and the source is very strong for "more like what you just did". The neighbour table for 5 million items × 200 neighbours × (8-byte ID + 4-byte score) is about 12 GB, comfortably held by a small key-value cluster or even in memory on each retrieval host.

As an embedding candidate source: item vectors from MF are loaded into an ANN index (lm10); the user vector is read from a store or folded in from recent interactions; the top few hundred items by inner product become candidates. This captures broad taste better than item-to-item lookups, which only explore around the user's recent items.

As ranking features: the MF dot product for this user and item, the item-to-item similarity between the candidate and the user's last item, the number of the user's recent items that list the candidate as a neighbour. These features are cheap and strong, and they let a ranker built on other signals benefit from collaborative structure.

Freshness differs by place. A neighbour table that is a day old is usually fine for established items. A user vector that is a day old misses everything the user did today, which is why folding in recent interactions at request time (the deep section shows how) or using the item-to-item source for the most recent behaviour is common.

10. What collaborative filtering cannot do

Three limits motivate much of the rest of this track. Cold start: an item nobody has touched has no column to learn from, and a user with no history has no row; CF alone cannot recommend them (rec11). Popularity bias: popular items have more data, more confident vectors and more co-occurrences, so they are recommended more and become more popular (rec10). No context and no content: plain MF knows nothing about time of day, device, the query, or what the item is about. Two-tower models (rec4) generalise MF by building user and item vectors from features, not just IDs, so new items can be placed from their content and context can shape the user vector.
deep:
Folding in new users without retraining

ALS gives a neat trick for users who arrived after the last training run. Hold item vectors fixed and solve the user's ridge regression from whatever interactions they have, x = (YuᵀYu + λI)⁻¹ Yuᵀ ru, at request time: with k = 64 and a dozen interactions this is microseconds. Some systems never store user vectors at all, computing them on the fly from the user's latest interactions, which also makes them perfectly fresh. The same idea, a user represented as a function of their items, is what the user tower of a two-tower model generalises.

Why the factors are not unique

If X and Y fit the data, so do XQ and YQ⁻ᵀ for any invertible k × k matrix Q, because XQ(YQ⁻ᵀ)ᵀ = XYᵀ. Regularisation narrows the choice but individual factors still have no fixed meaning, can rotate between training runs and can flip sign. Practical consequences: you cannot compare a factor across two training runs, embeddings from different runs live in different spaces (so a user vector from today's model must never be scored against item vectors from yesterday's), and "factor 3 is comedy" interpretations are fragile. Versioning user and item vectors together is a real production requirement.

Similarity measures beyond cosine

Cosine on binary columns is a reasonable default, but alternatives fix specific problems. Jaccard (shared users divided by users of either item) behaves similarly. Lift and pointwise mutual information compare co-occurrence with what independence would predict (count(A, B) × total ÷ (count(A) × count(B))), which removes popularity effects strongly but over-rewards rare pairs with tiny support. Conditional probability P(B | A) is asymmetric, useful for "people who bought A then bought B", where order matters (a phone then a case, rarely a case then a phone). Adding a shrinkage term, multiplying similarity by n/(n + β) where n is the number of shared users, pulls low-evidence similarities towards zero. Which works best is an empirical question per catalogue.

Matrix factorisation and neighbourhoods are closer than they look

An item-item model with learned similarity weights (rather than cosine) can be written as a factorisation in which a user's vector is the sum of the vectors of items they interacted with. Models such as SLIM and EASE learn a full item-item weight matrix with regularisation; EASE has a closed-form solution and, on several public benchmarks, is competitive with far more complex neural models. Conversely, the user tower of a two-tower model that averages the embeddings of recently watched items is a learned neighbourhood method. Knowing this lets you treat "neighbourhood or factorisation?" as a modelling choice along a spectrum rather than two different worlds.

Reproducibility and strong baselines

Recommender-systems research had a well-documented period in which many published neural models were compared against poorly tuned baselines. Dacrema, Cremonesi and Jannach's 2019 study tried to reproduce a set of neural recommendation papers from top conferences and found that most could not be reproduced with reasonable effort, and that of those that could, the majority were beaten by simple, well-tuned neighbourhood or factorisation methods. The lesson for practitioners: always run tuned item-kNN, implicit ALS or EASE, and popularity, on your own data, before believing a complex model is better.

Temporal dynamics

Taste and popularity move. Koren's work during the Netflix Prize added time-dependent biases (an item's popularity drifts; a user's rating scale shifts; a household's ratings on one day may come from a different person) and gained meaningful accuracy. In implicit settings the equivalent is weighting recent interactions more, either by decaying confidence with age or by training on a sliding window, which is what Hu and colleagues' choice of a four-week window did implicitly, since TV schedules change seasonally.

Scaling the item side

Serving MF for retrieval means finding, for a user vector, the items with the largest dot products: maximum inner product search. ANN indexes are usually built for cosine or Euclidean distance; inner product can be handled directly by some indexes, or converted by appending one extra coordinate to each item vector so that the largest inner product becomes the nearest neighbour. Vector norms matter here: in MF, popular items often get larger norms, so inner-product retrieval favours them, another route by which popularity bias enters. Normalising item vectors (cosine) reduces it at some cost in accuracy; it is a knob worth testing.
prod:
The public case: from the Netflix Prize to implicit feedback

Two public stories bracket the history of collaborative filtering in industry. The first is the Netflix Prize (2006-2009). Netflix released about 100 million anonymised star ratings and offered $1 million to the first team to beat its own system, Cinematch, by 10% on RMSE. Matrix factorisation with biases and temporal effects, trained by SGD, became the core technique of the leading teams, and the winning entry was a blend of over a hundred models. Netflix's 2012 engineering blog post "Netflix Recommendations: Beyond the 5 stars" described what happened next. Netflix took two components from an earlier progress-prize solution, matrix factorisation (0.8914 RMSE alone) and restricted Boltzmann machines (0.8990), blended them linearly to about 0.88, and put them into production. It evaluated the grand-prize methods offline but judged that "the additional accuracy gains that we measured did not seem to justify the engineering effort needed to bring them into a production environment". Meanwhile the business had moved to streaming, where what members play is a far richer signal than what they rate, and the objective moved from predicting stars to ranking titles.

The second story is the one this lesson's implicit section is built on. Hu, Koren and Volinsky's 2008 paper came from a TV recommender built on viewing data from about 300,000 set-top boxes, about 17,000 programmes over four weeks, with no ratings at all. Their preference-and-confidence model, with α = 40, and the ALS trick that makes fitting every pair affordable became the standard approach to implicit feedback and the "implicit" mode of Spark MLlib's ALS. The results (popularity 16.46%, neighbourhood 10.74%, 200-factor model 8.35% expected percentile rank) are a useful reminder of the ordering you should expect on your own data: popularity is a real baseline, neighbourhoods beat it, factor models beat them, and the gaps are modest.

How collaborative filtering fails in production

Popularity collapse. Recommendations drift towards the same few hundred items for everyone. Symptom: catalogue coverage (share of items ever recommended) and the number of distinct items shown per day falling. Causes: popularity-heavy negative sampling, inner-product retrieval with large popular-item norms, and the feedback loop of training on one's own recommendations. Fixes: normalise, re-rank for diversity, add exploration, and watch coverage as a guardrail metric.

Bot and fraud interactions. A seller pays for fake purchases that make their product co-occur with a bestseller; item-to-item tables now recommend it on the bestseller's page. CF is easy to poison because it trusts behaviour. Filter interactions from suspicious accounts, cap any single user's influence on a similarity, and monitor sudden jumps in an item's neighbour list.

Stale vectors. A nightly job fails silently and vectors are three days old; new items have none. Monitor model and index age, the share of shown items with no vector, and fall back to content-based or popularity sources for vector-less items.

Mismatched model versions. User vectors from one training run scored against item vectors from another produce nonsense, because factors are only defined up to rotation. Version user and item vectors together and refuse to serve mixed versions.

Accidental leakage in evaluation. Random splits, or test sets that include re-consumption, report excellent numbers that vanish online. Use temporal splits and test the product's actual task.

What to monitor

Training: objective by sweep, held-out recall@k and nDCG@k on a temporal split, by user-activity bucket. Outputs: catalogue coverage, Gini coefficient of recommendation counts across items (how concentrated they are), share of recommendations from the top 1% most popular items. Freshness: age of vectors and similarity tables, share of new items with vectors. Online: click-through and downstream conversion from CF-sourced candidates versus other sources, which tells you what this source contributes in the funnel from rec1.
myths: A missing entry in the user–item matrix means the user dislikes the item.

Almost always it means the user never saw it. With explicit ratings, missing entries are simply unknown, and treating them as zeros teaches the model that everything unseen is bad. With implicit feedback (clicks, plays), unobserved pairs are a mix of 'not interested' and 'never noticed', which is why implicit models treat them as weak negatives with low confidence rather than as firm zeros.
Matrix factorisation is SVD from linear algebra.

Classical singular value decomposition needs a fully observed matrix; a ratings matrix is more than 99% empty. What recommender papers call 'SVD' (after the Netflix Prize) is a learned factorisation that fits only the observed entries, with regularisation, by gradient descent or alternating least squares. The name stuck; the algorithm is different.
Lower RMSE on held-out ratings means better recommendations.

RMSE rewards predicting every rating accurately, including the many items a user would never be shown or would rate 2 versus 2.5. Users only see the top of a ranked list, so what matters is ranking quality at the top. Netflix itself reported that the extra accuracy of the Prize-winning ensemble did not justify its engineering cost, and its product moved from predicting stars to ranking what people actually watch.
Collaborative filtering needs deep learning to be competitive.

Well-tuned matrix factorisation and item-to-item neighbourhoods remain strong baselines; several reproducibility studies have found that carefully tuned classic methods match or beat many published neural recommenders on standard datasets. Deep models win when you have rich features, sequences and huge data, not automatically.
Implicit feedback is just explicit feedback with all ratings equal to 1.

Implicit signals differ in kind: they have no negative values, their strength (number of plays, minutes watched) measures confidence rather than preference, and unobserved does not mean disliked. Hu, Koren and Volinsky's model separates a binary preference from a confidence weight for exactly this reason, and fits all user–item pairs, not just observed ones.
lab:
Goal: implement item-to-item CF and matrix factorisation by SGD on a tiny ratings set, reproduce the lesson's ALS step, and compare with a popularity baseline. Python 3.12, standard library only.

  1. Create rec3_lab.py. Generate a synthetic ratings set: 200 users and 100 items. Give each user and item a hidden 3-number taste vector drawn from random.gauss(0, 1); a user's true affinity for an item is the dot product plus noise. Each user rates 15 random items, with rating = clamp(round(3 + affinity), 1, 5). Hold out each user's last 3 ratings as a test set.
  2. Write als_step(R, Y, lam) for k = 2 using the explicit 2×2 inverse formula, and check that on the lesson's 3×3 matrix it returns x1 ≈ (4.386, 0.900), x2 ≈ (3.570, 0.326), x3 ≈ (−0.825, 4.574).
  3. Implement MF with biases trained by SGD: pred = mu + bu[u] + bi[i] + dot(x[u], y[i]), k = 8, η = 0.01, λ = 0.05, 50 epochs, shuffling the training ratings each epoch. Print training and test RMSE every 10 epochs.
  4. Implement two baselines: the global mean, and mean + user bias + item bias only (k = 0). Compare test RMSE.
  5. Item-to-item CF: treat ratings ≥ 4 as "liked", compute cosine similarity between every pair of item columns, and for each user recommend the 10 unrated items with the highest summed similarity to their liked items. Compute hit rate@10: the share of users with at least one liked test item in their top 10. Compare with recommending the 10 most popular items.
  6. Vary k in 1, 3, 8, 20 and λ in 0, 0.05, 0.5 and note test RMSE.

What to look for. The bias-only model should already beat the global mean clearly; factors should improve on it modestly. With λ = 0 and large k, training RMSE should keep falling while test RMSE rises: overfitting. Item-to-item should beat popularity on hit rate, though not by a huge margin on such a small set. Because the data was generated with 3 hidden factors, k around 3 should be enough; much larger k adds little.
recap: Collaborative filtering recommends from behaviour alone: users who behaved alike before will probably like the same things, and items engaged with by the same people are probably related.
The user–item matrix is extremely sparse, typically well under 1% filled, and missing entries are unknown rather than negative.

Item-to-item neighbourhood methods compute similarities between items from the users who engaged with both, often by cosine similarity, and score a candidate by summing its similarity to the user's recent items; they are simple, explainable and precomputable.
Matrix factorisation learns a short vector per user and per item so that their dot product predicts the user's interest; regularisation stops it fitting noise.

SGD visits observed entries one at a time and nudges both vectors along the prediction error; ALS fixes item vectors and solves each user vector exactly with a small least-squares problem, then swaps, and parallelises easily.
In the worked ALS step, user 1's new vector comes from solving a 2×2 system: (YᵀY + λI) x = Yᵀr gives x = (4.39, 0.90), and one full sweep cuts the squared error on observed entries from 40.8 to 0.8.

For implicit feedback, Hu, Koren and Volinsky fit every user–item pair with preference 1 or 0 and confidence 1 + α·r (α = 40 in their TV study), and a trick with YᵀY keeps ALS linear in the number of observed pairs.

With SGD on implicit data you sample negatives from unobserved items, usually in proportion to popularity raised to a power below 1; BPR instead trains on pairs, pushing an observed item above a sampled unobserved one.
Collaborative filtering fails on new users and new items (cold start) and favours popular items; these weaknesses motivate content features, two-tower models and exploration later in the track.
glossary: ALS (alternating least squares)

A way to fit matrix factorisation by holding item vectors fixed and solving each user vector exactly as a least-squares problem, then holding user vectors fixed and solving each item vector, repeating until it converges.
BPR (Bayesian personalised ranking)
A pairwise training objective for implicit feedback: for a user, an observed item should score higher than a sampled unobserved item, trained with a log-sigmoid loss on the difference.
Bias terms
Per-user and per-item offsets added to the dot product, capturing that some users rate everything high and some items are liked by everyone.
Cold start
The problem of recommending to a user, or recommending an item, with little or no interaction history, where collaborative signals are missing.
Collaborative filtering
Recommending from the pattern of interactions among many users and items, without using the content of the items.
Confidence weight
In implicit-feedback models, how much the loss should trust an observed preference, growing with the strength of the signal such as number of plays.
Cosine similarity
The dot product of two vectors divided by the product of their lengths; for binary interaction columns it counts co-occurrence relative to how popular each item is.
Explicit feedback
Signals where users state their preference directly, such as star ratings or thumbs up and down.
Implicit feedback
Signals inferred from behaviour, such as clicks, plays, purchases and dwell time, which are plentiful but noisy and have no direct negatives.
Item-to-item collaborative filtering
Recommending items similar to the ones a user engaged with, where similarity comes from co-engagement across users; popularised by Amazon.
Latent factors
The learned numbers in user and item vectors; they often align loosely with interpretable traits such as genre or price level, but are not defined in advance.
Matrix factorisation
Approximating the user–item matrix as the product of a tall user matrix and a wide item matrix with a small number of columns, so each entry is a dot product of a user vector and an item vector.
Negative sampling
Choosing a few unobserved items per positive example to act as negatives during training, instead of using every unobserved item.
RMSE (root mean squared error)
The square root of the average squared difference between predicted and actual ratings; the Netflix Prize metric.
Sparsity
The share of the user–item matrix that is empty; recommender matrices are typically more than 99% empty.
User–item matrix
A table with a row per user and a column per item whose entries are ratings or interaction strengths, mostly missing.
drill:
Design: "customers also bought" for a grocery app

A grocery delivery app has 3 million weekly customers, 40,000 products and about 25 items per order. Product wants a "goes well with" row on every product page and a "you might have forgotten" row at checkout. The team proposes matrix factorisation on the customer × product purchase matrix. Critique the proposal and design something that will work, including how you handle milk and bananas, which are in 40% of all orders.

Answer

Critique. Customer-level MF learns long-term taste (vegetarian, family with toddlers, premium brands), which is good for a personalised home page, but "goes well with" is about items that go together in a basket, a session-level, item-to-item relation. The right unit is the order, not the customer.

Design. Build an item-to-item co-occurrence table from orders: for each pair of products, count the orders containing both, over the last 90 days with recent weeks weighted more. Compute a popularity-corrected similarity: raw co-occurrence would make milk and bananas the neighbours of everything, because they are in 40% of orders. Use lift, P(A and B) ÷ (P(A) × P(B)), with a minimum support (say 50 co-occurring orders) and shrinkage n/(n + 100) so rare pairs with tiny counts do not dominate. Keep the top 100 neighbours per product, recomputed nightly: 40,000 products × 100 entries is a small table, served from memory.

"Goes well with" on the page of pasta: look up its neighbours (pasta sauce, parmesan, basil), filter out-of-stock, re-rank lightly for variety (not five pasta sauces).

"You might have forgotten" at checkout: for each basket item, fetch neighbours; score each candidate by the sum of its similarities to the basket; add a personal signal, how often this customer buys it and how long since they last did (a repurchase model); drop items already in the basket. Here milk and bananas are legitimately good suggestions if this customer buys them weekly and they are missing; they should come from the personal repurchase signal, not from co-occurrence.

Where MF fits. Use implicit ALS on customer × product (confidence from purchase counts) as a separate candidate source for the personalised home page and for ranking features (customer–product affinity), alongside the co-occurrence table.

Evaluate. Offline: on held-out orders, hide one item per basket and measure how often it appears in the top 5 suggestions from the rest of the basket, versus a popularity baseline. Online: add-to-cart rate from the rows and basket size, with a guardrail on order cancellation or substitution rate.
qa: E
What is collaborative filtering and what does it need?

It recommends using only the pattern of interactions: people who liked the same things before will probably agree again, and items liked by the same people are related. It needs a log of who interacted with what (ratings, purchases, plays) and nothing about the items' content. That is its strength, because it captures taste that content cannot describe, and its weakness, because new items and users have no interactions.
E
Compare user-based and item-based neighbourhood methods.

User-based finds users similar to the target user and recommends what they liked; item-based finds items similar to what the user liked, where similarity comes from co-engagement. Item-based usually works better at scale: item similarities are more stable than user similarities, can be precomputed offline, there are often fewer items than users, and recommendations are easy to explain ('because you bought a tent').
E
Why is the user–item matrix so sparse, and why does it matter?

Each user interacts with a tiny fraction of the catalogue: a user who has watched 200 of 20,000 titles fills 1% of their row, and most users fill far less. Sparsity means most similarity estimates are based on few co-occurrences and are noisy, and that a model must generalise from very little data per user. Matrix factorisation helps by sharing statistical strength: each user vector is learned from all items they touched, and each item vector from all users.
M
Walk through one ALS update for a user.

Fix all item vectors. The user's vector x must minimise the sum over items they rated of (r − x·y)² plus λ|x|². That is ordinary ridge regression with the user's rated item vectors as rows of the design matrix Y and the ratings as targets, so x = (YᵀY + λI)⁻¹ Yᵀ r. With k factors this is a k × k system, cheap to solve, and every user's solve is independent, so millions run in parallel. Then fix users and solve items the same way.

Follow-up: Why does ALS converge? — Each half-step solves its subproblem exactly, so the loss never increases; it reaches a local minimum, not necessarily the global one, because the joint problem is non-convex.
M
When would you choose ALS over SGD for matrix factorisation?

ALS is attractive for implicit feedback, where the loss covers all user–item pairs: SGD would have to visit billions of zero entries or sample them, while ALS handles them in closed form with the YᵀY trick. ALS also parallelises cleanly and has no learning rate to tune. SGD is simpler, uses less memory per step, handles arbitrary losses (pairwise, with side features, sampled negatives) and works well for explicit ratings. Spark MLlib ships ALS for this reason.
M
How does implicit-feedback matrix factorisation differ from the explicit version?

Explicit MF fits only observed ratings. Implicit MF, as in Hu, Koren and Volinsky, turns each user–item pair into a binary preference (1 if any interaction, else 0) and a confidence (1 + α × interaction strength), and fits all pairs, weighting errors by confidence. Unobserved pairs act as weak negatives with confidence 1; heavily watched items get confidence 1 + 40 × plays in their setting. The result is a ranking model, not a rating predictor.

Follow-up: How do you pick α? — Treat it as a hyperparameter tuned on a ranking metric such as recall@k on held-out interactions; the paper found 40 worked for TV watching, and a log-scaled confidence is an option when counts have a long tail.
M
What is negative sampling and how should negatives be chosen?

With implicit data there are no labelled negatives, and using all unobserved items is too expensive for SGD, so for each positive you sample a few unobserved items as negatives. Uniform sampling mostly picks obscure items the model already scores low, which teaches little. Sampling in proportion to popularity (often raised to a power like 0.75) picks items the user plausibly saw and skipped, which are more informative. Harder negatives speed learning but risk being unlabelled positives.
M
Explain BPR in two sentences and when you would use it.

Bayesian personalised ranking trains on triples (user, observed item i, unobserved item j) and maximises the log-sigmoid of score(u, i) − score(u, j), so it learns to rank observed items above unobserved ones rather than to predict a value. Use it when the goal is a top-k list from implicit data and you are training with SGD; it is the pairwise counterpart to the pointwise implicit ALS objective.
M
Why did RMSE improvements in the Netflix Prize not translate into product impact?

RMSE measures accuracy on all held-out ratings, but users only see the top of a list, and ratings themselves are a biased sample of what people chose to rate. Netflix reported that it adopted two of the Prize's components, matrix factorisation and restricted Boltzmann machines (0.8914 and 0.8990 RMSE, about 0.88 blended), but not the final 100-plus-algorithm ensemble, because the extra accuracy did not justify the engineering effort, and its product had moved to streaming, where what people play matters more than what they rate.
H
Your item-to-item recommendations are dominated by bestsellers. Why, and how do you fix it?

Raw co-occurrence counts favour popular items: a bestseller co-occurs with everything simply because many people buy it. Cosine similarity divides by the square roots of both items' counts, which helps, and further fixes include stronger popularity normalisation (dividing by the candidate's count raised to a power), lift or pointwise mutual information (co-occurrence relative to what independence predicts), minimum support thresholds to avoid noisy rare pairs, and re-ranking for diversity. Check with a coverage metric: the share of the catalogue that ever appears in recommendations.

Follow-up: What does over-correcting look like? — Recommendations full of obscure items with two co-purchases each: high lift, tiny evidence. Require a minimum co-occurrence count and shrink similarities towards zero when support is small.
H
Size an ALS job for 50 million users, 5 million items, 4 billion interactions and 128 factors.

Each user solve costs about k² per observed item to build the system plus k³ to solve it: 128² = 16,384 per interaction, so 4 billion × 16,384 ≈ 6.6 × 10¹³ operations for the build, plus 50 million × 128³ ≈ 10¹⁴ for the solves; the item side is similar in build cost and 5 million × 2 × 10⁶ ≈ 10¹³ for solves. A full sweep is a few hundred teraflops, minutes on a modest cluster; 10-15 sweeps per run. Memory: 55 million vectors × 128 × 4 bytes ≈ 28 GB of factors, which must be shuffled between workers each half-step, often the real bottleneck.

Follow-up: How do you serve the factors? — Item vectors go into an ANN index; user vectors into a key-value store, or recomputed from the user's recent items with one least-squares solve at request time (fold-in).
H
How do you recommend for a user who signed up five minutes ago and has three interactions?

Matrix factorisation has no vector for them, but you can fold them in: hold item vectors fixed and solve the user's least-squares problem from their three interactions, which takes microseconds. Item-to-item methods work immediately from the three items. Blend with popularity and context (region, device, signup source) because three interactions are noisy, and add exploration so early pages gather informative signals. As interactions accumulate, shift weight from popularity to personal signals.

Follow-up: And a brand-new item? — It has no interactions, so CF cannot place it; you need content features (text, image, creator) mapped into the same space, which is what two-tower models (rec4) and cold-start strategies (rec11) provide.
H
When does collaborative filtering beat a content-based model, and vice versa?

CF wins when there is plenty of interaction data and taste is not captured by content: two songs with similar audio features can appeal to entirely different audiences, and CF learns that from listeners. Content models win for new items, niche items with few interactions, rapidly changing catalogues such as news, and when explanations must refer to attributes. Modern systems combine them: models whose item representation is built from both an ID embedding (collaborative) and content features, so new items start from content and drift towards collaborative signal as data arrives.

t: Two-tower models and embedding retrieval: in-batch negatives, sampling-bias correction and fresh indexes
sum: How modern retrieval learns user and item vectors from features: the two-tower architecture and why the towers must not interact, retrieval as extreme classification with a sampled softmax, in-batch negatives worked for a batch of 4 with and without the logQ correction, streaming frequency estimation, temperature and normalisation, hard and mixed negatives, serving with an ANN index, and keeping item embeddings, indexes and model versions fresh.
prereq: rec3
Matrix factorisation gives each user and item an ID vector whose dot product predicts interest, trained with sampled negatives; it cannot place a new item or use context.
lm10
Contrastive training pulls matching pairs together and pushes mismatches apart; an ANN index such as HNSW or IVF finds the nearest of millions of vectors in milliseconds at some loss of recall.
ml5
Cross-entropy with a softmax turns scores over classes into probabilities and penalises the log of the probability given to the correct class.
hd3
The feed design used two-tower retrieval with in-batch negatives and the logQ correction as one box; this lesson works through why each piece is there.
why:
A video platform has 20 million videos and a matrix-factorisation model from rec3. It works for established videos and regular users. Then three complaints arrive in the same week. Creators say their new uploads are invisible for days: the model has no vector for a video until the nightly retraining sees interactions, and it cannot get interactions without being recommended. The mobile team says recommendations ignore context: someone who watches cooking videos on the TV in the evening and short comedy clips on the phone on the train gets the same list on both. And the search team wants the same machinery for queries, but a matrix factorisation has no row for the text "easy vegan curry".

All three complaints have one root: matrix factorisation gives each user and item an ID vector, a free-floating set of numbers learned only from that ID's interactions. Anything without interaction history, a new video, a new query, a new context, has no vector. The fix is to compute vectors from features instead: a network reads the video's title, thumbnail, creator and category and outputs its vector; another network reads the user's recent history, device, time of day and (for search) the query text and outputs theirs. The score is still a dot product, so all the retrieval machinery, precomputed item vectors and an ANN index, still works. That is the two-tower model, and since the late 2010s it has been the standard learned retriever at YouTube, Pinterest, Meta, Spotify, Airbnb and most companies with a large catalogue.

Training it raises a problem that looks technical and turns out to be central. The model must learn to pick the right item out of millions, but computing a softmax over millions of items per training example is impossible. The cheap trick everyone uses, treating the other items in the training batch as negatives, quietly distorts what the model learns about popular items, and correcting that distortion was the subject of a well-known 2019 Google paper.

This lesson builds the two-tower model from MF, frames retrieval as classification, works the in-batch softmax loss for a batch of four with and without the correction, then covers temperature, harder negatives, serving with an ANN index and the unglamorous engineering of keeping millions of embeddings and an index fresh and consistent.
primer:
Think of a dating agency with millions of members that must suggest matches within a second. It cannot interview every pair. Instead, each member fills in a profile once, and the agency turns every profile into a point on a map, placed so that people who would get on well end up close together. To suggest matches, it places the new enquiry on the same map and looks at who is nearby. The expensive work, placing everyone on the map, is done in advance; the per-request work is one placement and one neighbourhood search.

A two-tower model is that agency. One network, the item tower, reads an item's features and places it on the map (outputs a vector). Another, the query tower or user tower, reads the user's features and context and places them on the same map. Closeness is measured by the dot product. The towers are trained together on past engagement, so that users land near the items they engaged with and away from the ones they did not. Because each item's position depends only on the item, all item positions are computed ahead of time and stored in a nearest-neighbour index.

Compare this with matrix factorisation from rec3. MF is a two-tower model whose towers are lookup tables: the user tower maps a user ID to a learned vector, the item tower maps an item ID to a learned vector, and nothing else goes in. Replace the lookup tables with networks that take features (still including the ID as one feature) and you gain three things: new items get vectors from their content, context such as time and device shapes the user vector, and a query's text can be a feature, so the same design serves search.

What does the learned map look like? Nobody tells the model what its 128 dimensions mean, but after training on billions of interactions, regions of the space correspond to recognisable tastes: beginner cooking videos cluster together, near but separate from professional chef content; a user who watches both lands between them. Because the user vector is computed from recent behaviour, it moves: after three football highlights in a row, the user's point drifts towards the football region and the next retrieval reflects it. Distances also carry popularity information unless you are careful, because items that many different users engage with are pulled towards many different user points; normalisation and the sampling correction below are partly about controlling that.

The analogy breaks at training. A dating agency could ask couples whether they got on; a recommender only sees which items users clicked from what they were shown, never what they would have thought of the millions of items they were not shown. So training must invent negatives: for each user–item pair that happened, pick some items that did not, and teach the model to put the real one first. How those negatives are picked turns out to shape the model as much as the architecture does, and that is the heart of this lesson.
body:
1. The towers and what goes in them

Each tower is usually a multilayer perceptron (a stack of fully connected layers with nonlinearities between them) on top of feature encodings. Categorical features such as item ID, creator ID, category and country become embeddings, looked up in tables and learned during training. Variable-length features such as "the last 50 videos watched" become the average (or a learned weighted combination) of the embeddings of those videos; YouTube's 2016 paper did exactly this, inspired by bag-of-words language models. Text such as a title or a query can be encoded by averaging token embeddings or by a pre-trained text encoder. Continuous features such as item age or user tenure are normalised. All of these are concatenated and fed through the layers, ending in a vector of, say, 64-256 numbers.

What goes in which tower follows one rule: the item tower may only use what is known about the item regardless of who is asking; the query tower may use anything about the user and the moment. So "number of likes this video got in the last hour" can go in the item tower (it is about the item), though it changes so fast that putting it there forces frequent re-embedding (more on that in section 8). "Whether this user has watched this creator before" cannot go in either tower: it is about the pair. That is a cross feature, and it belongs to the ranker.

Embedding tables that appear on both sides, for example video-ID embeddings used for the candidate item and for the user's watch history, are usually shared, so that a video's ID embedding learned from being watched also helps represent users who watched it. Yi et al. describe sharing input embeddings between the towers wherever a feature is available to both.

2. Retrieval as classification over the corpus

What should the model optimise? YouTube's 2016 paper gave the framing that most retrieval models still use: treat "which video will this user watch next?" as a classification problem with millions of classes, one per item. Given the query vector u and item vectors v1...vN, the model's probability that the user picks item i is a softmax over the whole corpus:

P(i | user) = exp(u · v_i / τ)  /  Σ_j over all N items  exp(u · v_j / τ)

where τ is a temperature (section 5). Training maximises the log-probability of the item the user actually engaged with, that is, minimises the cross-entropy loss −ln P(positive | user) (ml5). The softmax has a useful property: to raise the positive's probability it must push down every other item in proportion to how much probability the model currently gives it, so the items the model wrongly likes are corrected hardest.

The problem is the denominator. With N = 20 million items, each training example needs 20 million item vectors and dot products, and the gradient touches all of them. With billions of training examples a day, that is out of the question. The solution is to estimate the denominator from a sample of items, the sampled softmax: compute the softmax over the positive plus a handful of negatives. YouTube's 2016 system sampled several thousand negatives per example from a background distribution and corrected for the sampling with importance weighting, which it reported as more than 100 times faster than the full softmax.

3. In-batch negatives

Sampling negatives from a separate distribution still means computing item-tower outputs for those extra items. A cheaper trick has become standard: in-batch negatives. A training batch contains B examples, each a (user, positive item) pair. Compute all B user vectors and all B item vectors, then form the B × B matrix of dot products. Row i holds user i's score for every item in the batch: the diagonal entry is their positive, the other B − 1 entries are other users' positives, used as negatives. Apply a softmax across each row and take the loss on the diagonal. No extra item computation, and large batches give many negatives: Yi et al. used batches of 8,192, so 8,191 negatives per example.

Worked example: a batch of four. Four users each clicked one item; item 1 is a very popular video, item 4 fairly popular, items 2 and 3 niche. Both towers output vectors normalised to length 1, so dot products are cosines between −1 and 1. Here is the score matrix (rows: users, columns: items; the diagonal is each user's positive):

item 1 (popular)item 2item 3item 4
user 1 (clicked item 1)0.800.300.100.50
user 2 (clicked item 2)0.400.700.200.60
user 3 (clicked item 3)0.100.200.900.30
user 4 (clicked item 4)0.600.500.200.55

Use temperature τ = 0.2, so logits are scores × 5. For user 2 the logits are 2.0, 3.5, 1.0, 3.0. Exponentiate: e2.0 = 7.39, e3.5 = 33.12, e1.0 = 2.72, e3.0 = 20.09; sum 63.32. Softmax: 0.117, 0.523, 0.043, 0.317. Loss for user 2: −ln 0.523 = 0.648. The same computation for the others gives losses 0.289 (user 1, softmax on item 1 = 0.749), 0.094 (user 3, 0.910) and 1.175 (user 4, whose positive item 4 at 0.309 is beaten by item 1 at 0.397). Mean batch loss: 0.551.

Now the gradient. For a softmax with cross-entropy, the gradient of the loss with respect to each logit is (probability − 1) for the positive and (probability) for each negative. So in row 2, training raises item 2's logit with weight 1 − 0.523 = 0.477 and lowers item 1's with weight 0.117, item 3's with 0.043, item 4's with 0.317. Across the whole batch, item 1 is pushed down as a negative in rows 2, 3 and 4 with weights 0.117 + 0.017 + 0.397 = 0.53. That is the in-batch mechanism working as intended for this batch. The problem is what happens across millions of batches.

4. Sampling bias and the logQ correction

Which items end up as in-batch negatives? Whatever items are positives in the batch, and items appear as positives in proportion to how often they are clicked. If item 1 is clicked 40 times as often as item 3, it appears in batches 40 times as often, so it serves as a negative 40 times as often. In the full softmax every item is a negative in every example; in the in-batch version, popular items are hugely over-represented among negatives. The result: the model is pushed to under-score popular items, more than their true relevance warrants. Retrieval quality suffers, and in a feed this shows up as the retriever avoiding items that are popular for good reason.

The fix comes from the theory of sampled softmax. If negatives are drawn with probability pj for item j, then subtracting ln pj from each item's logit before the softmax makes the sampled loss a (consistent) estimate of the full-softmax loss. Intuitively, an item that shows up very often as a negative has its logit reduced so that each appearance counts for less; a rare item's logit is raised, so its rare appearances count for more. This is the logQ correction (Q being the sampling distribution). Yi et al. apply it to every logit in the row, positives included:

corrected logit(i, j) = u_i · v_j / τ  −  ln p_j

Back to the batch of four, with estimated sampling probabilities p = 0.02 (item 1), 0.002 (item 2), 0.0005 (item 3), 0.01 (item 4). The corrections −ln pj are +3.91, +6.21, +7.60, +4.61: rare items get the bigger boost. User 2's corrected logits become 2.0 + 3.91 = 5.91, 3.5 + 6.21 = 9.71, 1.0 + 7.60 = 8.60, 3.0 + 4.61 = 7.61. Softmax: 0.015, 0.679, 0.223, 0.082. Item 1, the popular one, now receives a push-down weight of 0.015 instead of 0.117: almost none. Niche item 3 now receives 0.223 instead of 0.043. Across the batch, item 1's total push-down falls from 0.53 to 0.09 (0.015 + 0.000 + 0.071).

Notice the corrected loss for this batch is higher (0.96 versus 0.55): the corrected problem is harder, because popular positives no longer get an easy win. User 1, whose positive is the popular item 1, now has a loss of 1.25 instead of 0.29; the model must raise item 1's raw score for user 1 to win, which is precisely the under-scoring of popular items being undone. At serving time the correction is not applied: retrieval ranks by the raw dot product, which now estimates true preference rather than preference distorted by batch composition.

Estimating pj. With a fixed catalogue you could count item frequencies in the training data. YouTube's corpus changes constantly, so Yi et al. estimate frequencies from the training stream itself. Keep two arrays of size H, indexed by a hash of the item ID: A records the last training step at which the item appeared, and B a running estimate of the average number of steps between its appearances, updated each time the item appears as B ← (1 − α)B + α(t − A), then A ← t. The estimated sampling probability is 1/B. An item seen every 50 steps on average has p ≈ 0.02 per step. This adapts as popularity changes, needs no fixed vocabulary, and costs two array lookups per item; collisions from hashing are reduced with several hash functions, an idea borrowed from count-min sketches. They used H = 50 million with α = 0.01.

5. Normalisation and temperature

Two small choices have outsized effects. Normalising both tower outputs to length 1 makes the dot product a cosine. Yi et al. report it "improves model trainability and thus leads to better retrieval quality". It also removes one route for popularity bias at serving: without normalisation, popular items can acquire large vector norms that inflate their dot products with every user.

The temperature τ divides the logits. Cosines live between −1 and 1, a narrow range; dividing by τ = 0.05 stretches it to −20..20, so a cosine gap of 0.1 becomes a logit gap of 2, a factor of e² ≈ 7.4 in probability. A small τ makes the softmax concentrate almost all its mass, and therefore all the gradient, on the few negatives that score close to the positive: a form of automatic hard-negative mining. Too small and training becomes unstable and over-reacts to noisy labels; too large and all negatives are pushed equally and learning slows. It is tuned on retrieval recall; Yi et al. reported Wikipedia link-prediction results for τ from 0.05 to 0.14 and used 0.05 in their YouTube live test.

6. Harder and broader negatives

In-batch negatives have a blind spot beyond popularity: items that are rarely or never positives (the long tail, and items uploaded minutes ago) almost never appear in a batch, so they are almost never pushed down. A model can then score some irrelevant niche items highly and nothing in training corrects it. Mixed negative sampling (Yang et al., 2020) adds a set of items sampled uniformly from the whole corpus to each batch's negatives, so every item has some chance of being a negative. Their item-tower vectors must be computed, which costs extra, but a few thousand shared uniform negatives per batch are affordable.

Hard negatives are items the current model scores high that the user did not engage with. Good sources: items that were shown and skipped (an impression without a click), and top ANN results for the user that were not clicked. They teach fine distinctions ("this user likes beginner yoga videos, not advanced ones") faster than random items. The risk is false negatives: most "unclicked" items were simply never seen, and a high-scoring unseen item might be exactly what the user wants. Prefer shown-and-skipped impressions over merely unclicked items, mix hard with easy negatives, and watch for the model suppressing good content.

What counts as a positive matters as much. A click is a weak signal (clickbait is clicked); Yi et al.'s live system weighted each clicked example by a reward reflecting real engagement with the video, such as watch time, with unwatched clicks getting zero weight. Choosing the label for retrieval is a product decision: retrieve what people click, what they watch, or what they return for?

7. Serving: one user vector, one index search

At request time: fetch the user's features, run the query tower once (a few milliseconds on CPU for a moderate MLP), and search the ANN index for the top K items by inner product (lm10 explains HNSW and IVF; db15 covers running them inside a database). With normalised vectors, inner product equals cosine, which every index supports. K is typically 200-2,000, feeding the merge with other candidate sources (rec1).

Index sizing is simple arithmetic. 20 million items × 128 dimensions × 4 bytes = 10.2 GB in float32; 2.6 GB with 8-bit quantisation, plus graph or cluster overhead. That fits in one machine's memory, so the index is replicated, not sharded: each request goes to one replica. If one replica answers 2,000 searches per second and peak traffic is 10,000 QPS, you need 5 replicas, about 8 with headroom and a spare zone. Filters (region, language, age rating) are best applied inside the search, either with separate indexes per major partition or filtered search; post-filtering a top 500 that turns out to be 60% ineligible is a common way to end up with too few candidates.

The user vector deserves the freshest inputs. If the query tower reads the last 50 watches including ones from 30 seconds ago (from a nearline session store), every action shifts the vector and the next page reflects it. The item index can be hours old for established items with little harm; Yi et al. rebuilt their index of about 10 million videos every few hours. The user side is where freshness pays.

8. Keeping embeddings and the index fresh

Three kinds of change force work, and each has a different pipeline.

A new model version (retrained towers) changes the whole vector space. Every item must be re-embedded with the new item tower and a new index built; then the new query tower and new index must go live together. If the old index is queried with the new user vector, or the reverse, the dot products are meaningless, and nothing errors: recommendations just quietly get worse. Version every artefact (model, item vectors, index) and make serving refuse mismatches. Re-embedding cost is modest: 50 million items through a moderate item tower at 20,000 items per second per GPU is about 40 GPU-minutes.

New items need vectors within minutes, not at the next rebuild. A streaming job embeds each new item with the current item tower and inserts it into the live index (HNSW supports incremental inserts; IVF assigns the vector to its nearest existing cluster). Deleted or ineligible items are removed or masked at query time, and periodic full rebuilds clean up and rebalance.

Changing item features are subtler. If the item tower takes "views in the last 24 hours" as input, an item's vector is stale the moment its view count changes. Either re-embed frequently-changing items on a schedule, or, more commonly, keep fast-moving statistics out of the item tower entirely: retrieval vectors encode what the item is (content, creator, long-run audience), and the ranker, which runs per request, uses what is happening to it now.

Training itself is usually continuous: Yi et al. trained sequentially on day-partitioned data, catching up on 15 days and then consuming each new day as it arrived, with the frequency estimator running inside the same stream. Continuous training plus periodic index rebuilds is the standard shape.

9. A query tower for search

The same design serves search: the query tower reads the query text (plus, optionally, the user's context), and the item tower reads the document or product. Training pairs are (query, clicked or purchased result) from search logs, again with in-batch negatives. The model learns what your users mean by their words: on a marketplace, "cheap phone" lands near the listings people who typed that actually bought, and "apple" lands near phones on an electronics site and near fruit on a grocery site, without anyone writing a rule.

This differs from the general-purpose text embedding models used for RAG (lm9, lm10) in what the training signal teaches. A general embedding model is trained to place texts with similar meaning close together. A behaviourally trained query tower learns what satisfies the query, which may not be semantic similarity at all: people searching "gift for dad" buy whisky glasses and wallets, which share no words or meaning with the query. The behaviourally trained model usually wins on head and torso queries with plenty of click data; the general model wins on rare queries, new products with no clicks and new markets, and needs no training data. Many search systems start from a general embedding model and fine-tune it on their query–click pairs, getting some of both.

Two practical differences from recommendation. Search queries are short and ambiguous, so the query tower benefits from context features (the category the user is browsing, their recent searches). And lexical matching remains essential for exact identifiers, which embeddings blur; rec5 combines both.

10. Evaluating a retriever

The standard offline metric is recall@K: on held-out (user, engaged item) pairs, does the engaged item appear in the top K retrieved? Use a temporal split (train on days before, test on the day after), as Yi et al. did, averaging over a week to cover weekly patterns. Report it for several K matching the funnel (100, 500, 1,000), and by slice: new items, new users, popular versus long-tail items.

Two cautions. Offline labels come from what the old system showed, so recall rewards imitating it; a retriever that surfaces good items the old system never showed is under-credited. And retrieval is one source among several: what matters is its marginal contribution. The more faithful offline evaluation is funnel recall from rec1, measured against the ranker's preferences on a large candidate set, plus the share of final impressions and engagements that come only from this source. The final judge is an online test of the whole system with and without the new retriever, which is how Yi et al. reported their result.
deep:
Why logQ makes the sampled softmax unbiased

The full softmax's normaliser is a sum over all N items, Z = Σj exp(sj). If you sample negatives j from a distribution Q with probabilities qj, then exp(sj)/qj is an unbiased estimate of Z for a single sample (importance sampling: E[exp(sj)/qj] = Σ qj exp(sj)/qj = Z). Dividing by qj inside the exponential is the same as subtracting ln qj from the logit. So the corrected logits make the sampled normaliser an estimate of the true one, and the gradient approximately matches the full softmax's gradient. The estimate is not exactly unbiased for the log-loss (the log of an expectation is not the expectation of a log), but it is consistent as the number of negatives grows, which with thousands of in-batch negatives is close enough. Jean et al. (2015) gave this derivation for machine translation; Yi et al. applied it to in-batch sampling, where qj is the item's frequency in the stream.

Why the towers cannot learn feature crosses, precisely

The score u(x) · v(y) is a sum of k products, each a function of the user times a function of the item. Any interaction the model expresses must be captured by k such products. A rule like "this user likes this creator's cooking videos but not their travel videos" needs the user side to know about creator × topic combinations and the item side to encode them; with enough dimensions it is representable in principle, but the model cannot compute an explicit conjunction of a user feature and an item feature, which a ranker with crossed inputs does trivially. In practice two-tower models capture broad affinity well and specific conditional preferences poorly. That is the formal reason the ranker exists, and why some systems add a lightweight "late interaction" step on retrieved candidates.

Multiple user vectors

One vector per user forces a single point to represent many interests: cooking, football and jazz end up averaged into a point near none of them, and nearest-neighbour search returns items from whichever interest dominates. Multi-interest approaches compute several user vectors, for example by clustering the user's recent items and embedding each cluster, and run one ANN search per vector, merging results. Pinterest's PinnerSage described this idea publicly, representing each user by several embeddings from clustered pin interactions. The cost is several searches per request; the gain is coverage of minority interests, which a single vector systematically suppresses.

Hashing IDs and the long tail of embeddings

An ID embedding table for 100 million items at 64 dimensions is 25.6 GB in float32, and most rows belong to items with too few interactions to learn anything.
