Common remedies: hash IDs into a fixed number of buckets (collisions share a row), use a frequency threshold below which items share an "unknown" embedding and rely on content features, or use several hash functions and sum their rows to reduce collision damage. Yi et al. assign out-of-vocabulary IDs to a fixed set of hash buckets and learn embeddings for each, noting this helps the model "capture new" content. The design choice decides how quickly a new item moves from content-only to collaborative representation.

Retrieval objectives beyond the next click

"Predict the next clicked item" is a convenient label, but it inherits clickbait and short-term bias. YouTube's 2016 paper noted that predicting the next watch performed much better in live tests than predicting a randomly held-out watch, because consumption is sequential and asymmetric (episode 2 follows episode 1, not the reverse), and that it deliberately represented the user's searches as an unordered bag of tokens, so the model could not learn to simply replay the search that immediately preceded a watch (the authors note the classifier is then "no longer directly aware of the origin of the label"). Its "example age" feature, the age of the training example, let the model learn time-dependent popularity, and was set to zero at serving to reflect "now". These are reminders that retrieval quality depends as much on how the training task is framed as on the network.

Temperature as a knob on hardness and calibration

With small τ, the gradient from each example is dominated by the negatives within a small cosine margin of the positive; this is similar in effect to a margin-based loss focused on hard negatives. With large batches, small τ plus in-batch negatives already performs implicit hard-negative mining, which is why explicit hard negatives sometimes add less than expected. Temperature also changes what the raw scores mean: they are not calibrated probabilities, so thresholds such as "retrieve only items with cosine above 0.6" are fragile across model versions; use top-K, not score thresholds, in retrieval.

Distillation from the ranker

A retriever trained on clicks and a ranker trained on clicks with richer features disagree about which items are best, and the funnel loses whatever the retriever misses. Some teams add a distillation term: on a sample of requests, run the ranker on a large candidate set and train the retriever to put the ranker's top items near the top as well. This aligns the stages (rec1), at the cost of making the retriever inherit the ranker's biases and of an offline pipeline that runs the ranker on many more items than are served.
prod:
The public case: YouTube's sampling-bias-corrected retrieval

Yi and colleagues' 2019 RecSys paper, "Sampling-Bias-Corrected Neural Modeling for Large Corpus Item Recommendations", describes a two-tower retriever deployed at YouTube to retrieve personalised suggestions from a corpus of tens of millions of videos, conditioned on a seed video the user is watching (the "watch next" setting). Both towers were three-layer networks with hidden sizes 1,024, 512 and 128; input embeddings were shared between towers where possible; training used Adagrad with learning rate 0.2 and batches of 8,192 on daily-partitioned data streamed into the trainer, with billions of clicked videos per day. Item frequencies for the correction came from the streaming estimator with H = 50 million and α = 0.01. An index of about 10 million videos was rebuilt every few hours and typically covered more than 90% of training examples.

Offline, the bias-corrected softmax beat the plain in-batch softmax at every temperature tested, and both beat a squared-loss baseline. In a live A/B test where the new retriever's candidates were added to the production system's, the plain in-batch softmax (τ = 0.05) improved the engagement metric by 0.20%, and the corrected version by 0.37%. Numbers that small are normal and meaningful at that scale: retrieval is one source among several, and a third of a percent of engagement across YouTube is a large effect. The case shows the whole lesson in one system: features rather than IDs, retrieval as sampled classification, the bias from in-batch negatives and its correction, normalisation and temperature, continuous training and periodic index rebuilds.

How two-tower retrieval fails in production

Version skew. The query tower is deployed before the index built with the matching item tower finishes; for an hour, retrieval quality collapses with no errors. Defence: version tags on every vector and index, a serving check that refuses mismatches, and an alert on retrieval-sourced engagement.

Index lag. The streaming embed job stalls; new uploads stop appearing in retrieval; creators complain before dashboards do. Monitor the age of the newest item in the index and the share of last-hour uploads that are indexed.

Popularity drift. After removing the logQ correction "to simplify", or after a frequency-estimator bug, the retriever over- or under-retrieves popular items. Monitor the distribution of retrieved items by popularity decile against what engaged users actually consume.

Embedding collapse. A bug or bad hyperparameters makes many item vectors nearly identical; ANN search returns essentially random items with high similarity. Monitor the spread of item vectors (average pairwise cosine on a sample, norms) per build, and fail the build if they shift sharply.

Filtered-out results. Retrieval returns 500 candidates, eligibility filters remove 70% in a small market, and the ranker sees a thin pool. Partition the index by market or use filtered search; monitor candidates surviving filters per market.

What to monitor

Index: build time, age, item count, share of eligible items present, recall of the ANN against exact search on a nightly sample (to catch index degradation separately from model quality). Serving: query-tower and ANN latency percentiles, candidates returned after filtering, fallback rate. Quality: share of impressions and engagements sourced only from this retriever, distribution of retrieved items by popularity and age, new-item time-to-first-impression. Training: loss with and without correction on a held-out day, recall@K by slice, frequency-estimator sanity (estimated versus counted frequencies for a sample of items).
myths: A two-tower model is just matrix factorisation with a neural network.

It generalises MF in a way that matters: the towers take features, not just IDs. The item tower can embed a brand-new video from its title, thumbnail and creator before anyone has watched it, and the user tower can include the time of day, the device and the last five things the user did. MF has neither, which is why it cannot handle cold start or context.
In-batch negatives are free, so they are always the right choice.

They are free in compute but not in statistics. Items appear in batches in proportion to their popularity, so popular items are used as negatives far more often than rare ones, and the model learns to under-score them. Without the logQ correction (subtracting the log of each item's sampling probability), in-batch training systematically biases retrieval against popular items. Items that rarely or never appear as positives are also almost never seen as negatives.
Better recall@k offline means better recommendations online.

Offline recall is measured against what users clicked from the old system's recommendations, so a retriever that imitates the old system scores well. A retriever that finds genuinely new, relevant items may look worse offline, because those items were never shown and never clicked. Retrieval changes must be judged in the full funnel, online, and by what the ranker and users do with the new candidates.
You can update the item tower and keep the old index.

Item vectors from one model version and user vectors from another live in different spaces; their dot products are meaningless. Every time the model changes, every item must be re-embedded and the index rebuilt, and the user tower and index must switch to the new version together. Mixing versions is a classic silent production bug.
Two-tower retrieval makes the ranker unnecessary.

Two towers cannot let user and item features interact before the final dot product, so they cannot use cross features such as 'how many of this creator's videos has this user finished'. That is the price of being able to precompute item vectors and search millions in milliseconds. A ranker with full feature interactions is still needed on the few hundred candidates.
lab:
Goal: compute the in-batch softmax loss by hand in code, see the logQ correction shift the gradient, and simulate how in-batch sampling biases a model against popular items. Python 3.12, standard library only (math, random).

  1. Create rec4_lab.py. Enter the lesson's 4 × 4 score matrix, τ = 0.2 and p = [0.02, 0.002, 0.0005, 0.01]. Write softmax(row) (subtract the max before exponentiating) and batch_loss(S, tau, p=None) that returns the mean loss and the matrix of gradient weights (probability, minus 1 on the diagonal). Check the plain mean loss is 0.551 and corrected 0.960, and user 2's probabilities match the lesson.
  2. Write the streaming frequency estimator: arrays A and B of size H = 1,000 indexed by hash(item) % H, α = 0.05. Generate a stream of 200,000 item draws from a Zipf-like distribution over 500 items (probability ∝ 1/rank). After the stream, compare the estimate 1/B with the true per-step probability for items of rank 1, 10, 100 and 400.
  3. Simulate training signal: draw 5,000 batches of 32 positives from the same Zipf distribution. For each batch, count how often each item appears as a negative (every item in the batch is a negative for the other 31 rows). Plot (print) total negative count per rank bucket versus what a uniform full softmax would give (every item a negative in every row).
  4. Repeat step 3 but weight each negative appearance by 1/pj (normalised). Confirm the weighted counts are roughly flat across ranks: that is what the correction achieves in expectation.
  5. Bonus: vary τ in 0.05, 0.2, 1.0 for user 2 and print how the push-down weights spread across the three negatives.

What to look for. The estimator should track frequent items well and rare items noisily (they appear rarely, so their gap estimates are based on few samples), and hash collisions with H = 1,000 should inflate some rare items' estimates. Step 3 should show the top-ranked items used as negatives hundreds of times more than tail items; step 4 should flatten that. Small τ should concentrate almost all push-down weight on item 4, the strongest negative.
recap: A two-tower model has a query (user and context) tower and an item tower, each a neural network that turns features into a vector; the score is the dot product, so item vectors can be computed ahead of time and searched with an ANN index.
The towers must not interact before the final dot product; that restriction is what makes retrieval over millions of items possible, and the reason a ranker is still needed for cross features.
Training treats retrieval as classification over the whole corpus: a softmax over all items is too expensive, so it is approximated with sampled negatives.
In-batch negatives reuse the other positives in the batch as negatives, which is free but samples items in proportion to popularity, biasing the model against popular items.

The logQ correction subtracts the log of each item's sampling probability from its logit during training, making the sampled softmax an unbiased estimate of the full one; in the worked batch of four, it moves the gradient off the popular item.

Yi et al. (2019) estimate sampling probabilities from the training stream itself with hashed arrays that track the average gap between an item's appearances, and reported +0.37% engagement with correction versus +0.20% without in a YouTube live experiment.
Normalising the vectors and dividing by a temperature (around 0.05 in that paper) controls how sharply the softmax separates positives from negatives.
Mixed negative sampling adds uniformly sampled items to the in-batch negatives so long-tail and fresh items are also pushed and pulled.

Serving needs one user-tower pass and one ANN search per request; item vectors are recomputed in batch for a new model, streamed in for new items, and the index, item vectors and user tower must always share a model version.
glossary: ANN index
A data structure (HNSW, IVF, ScaNN and others) that finds most of the nearest vectors to a query vector without comparing against every vector.
Extreme classification
Classification with millions of classes; retrieval can be framed as predicting which item, out of the whole corpus, the user will engage with.
Hard negative
A negative example the current model scores highly; informative to train on, but at risk of actually being a positive the user never saw.
In-batch negatives
Using the positive items of the other examples in the same training batch as negatives for each example.
Item tower
The network that maps item features (ID, text, image, creator, age) to the item vector; its output does not depend on the user.
logQ correction
Subtracting the log of an item's probability of being sampled as a negative from its logit during training, which removes the bias introduced by non-uniform negative sampling.
MIPS (maximum inner product search)
Finding the items whose vectors have the largest dot product with a query vector; what retrieval with a dot-product two-tower model needs.
Mixed negative sampling
Combining in-batch negatives with a set of items sampled uniformly from the corpus, so items that rarely appear in batches still serve as negatives.
Query tower
The network that maps the user and context (history, demographics, device, time, query text) to the query vector. Also called the user tower.
Sampled softmax
Approximating a softmax over all items by computing it over the positive and a sample of negatives, with a correction for how the negatives were sampled.
Sampling probability
How likely an item is to appear as a negative in a training batch; for in-batch negatives it is proportional to how often the item appears as a positive.
Temperature (τ)
A number that divides the logits before the softmax; small values make the distribution sharper and the training signal concentrate on the hardest negatives.
Two-tower model
A retrieval model made of two separate networks whose output vectors are compared with a dot product; also called a dual encoder or bi-encoder.
Fold-in / online user embedding
Computing the user vector at request time from the latest history, so it reflects what the user did seconds ago.
Embedding version
The identifier of the model that produced a set of vectors; vectors from different versions must never be compared.
drill:
Design: two-tower retrieval for a music streaming home screen

A music service has 80 million monthly users, 100 million tracks (of which 8 million account for 99% of plays), 150,000 new tracks uploaded per day, and a home screen requested 3,000 times per second at peak. The current retrieval is item-to-item co-occurrence from the user's last 20 plays. New releases take a week to appear and users complain the home screen only reflects what they played this morning. Design a two-tower retriever: features, training, negatives, serving, refresh, and how you will know it works.

Answer

Towers. Item tower: track ID embedding (hashed, with tracks below 50 plays sharing buckets), artist ID, album, genre and mood tags, audio embedding from a pre-trained audio model, language, release age bucket. Query tower: user ID embedding, the average of embeddings of the last 50 plays and separately of tracks saved in the last 90 days (long-term taste), skips in the session, time of day, day of week, device, country. Both towers are MLPs to 128 dimensions, normalised.

Labels and negatives. Positive: a play longer than 30 seconds, weighted by completion and by whether the user saved the track. In-batch softmax with batches of 8,192 and the logQ correction using streaming frequency estimates, since a few hit tracks dominate plays; plus 2,000 uniform negatives per batch from the 8 million track active catalogue so the tail is pushed too (mixed negatives). Temperature tuned around 0.05. Shown-and-skipped tracks from the home screen as a modest share of hard negatives.

Serving. Index the 8 million active tracks plus all releases from the last 90 days: about 9 million × 128 × 1 byte (int8) ≈ 1.2 GB, replicated; at roughly 2,000 searches per second per replica, 3,000 QPS needs 2, run 4-6 across zones. Query tower on CPU per request from features in the session store (last 50 plays updated nearline). Retrieve 500, merged with co-occurrence and a "new releases from followed artists" source.

Refresh. Daily continuous training; weekly or daily full re-embed (9 million tracks, minutes on one GPU) with index rebuild and version-locked switch. Streaming embed of the 150,000 daily uploads within minutes, from content features alone. That fixes the week-long delay.

Evaluation. Offline: recall@500 on the next day's plays, sliced by new releases, long-tail tracks and light users; funnel recall against the ranker. Online: A/B test adding the retriever; primary metric home-screen listening minutes per user, guardrails on skip rate and diversity (distinct artists per user per week), and new-release share of plays.
qa: E
What is a two-tower model and why is it used for retrieval?

It is two neural networks, one turning the user and context into a vector and one turning an item into a vector, scored by a dot product. Because the item vector does not depend on the user, all item vectors can be computed in advance and put in an ANN index; at request time you compute one user vector and search the index for the closest items in a few milliseconds. That makes it possible to retrieve from millions of items while still using rich features.
E
Why can't the two towers share information before the final dot product?

If the item's vector depended on the user, it would have to be recomputed for every request, for every item, which brings back the cost of scoring the whole corpus with a heavy model. Keeping the towers separate is what allows precomputation and indexing. The price is that the model cannot learn feature crosses between user and item; the ranker handles those on the few hundred retrieved candidates.
E
What are in-batch negatives?

In a batch of B (user, clicked item) pairs, each user's positive is scored against the other B − 1 items in the batch, which serve as negatives. It needs no extra item computation, because those item vectors were computed anyway for their own examples, and it gives many negatives per example for free: a batch of 8,192 gives 8,191 negatives each.
M
Explain the sampling bias of in-batch negatives and the logQ fix.

Items appear in a batch in proportion to how often they are positives, so popular items are negatives much more often than rare ones. The softmax then pushes popular items down too hard, and the model under-scores them. The fix, from sampled softmax theory, is to subtract log p_j, the log of item j's sampling probability, from every item's logit during training. That makes the sampled loss an unbiased estimate of the full softmax; at serving time you use the raw dot product.

Follow-up: Where do you get p_j? — Count item frequencies in the training stream; Yi et al. estimate it online with hashed arrays tracking the average number of steps between an item's appearances, which adapts as popularity changes.
M
Work through the softmax loss for one example in a batch of four.

Take user 2 with logits (cosine / 0.2) of 2.0, 3.5, 1.0, 3.0 for items 1-4, where item 2 is the positive. Softmax: exponentiate and normalise to 0.117, 0.523, 0.043, 0.317, so the loss is −ln 0.523 = 0.648. The gradient raises item 2's logit by 1 − 0.523 and lowers each other item's by its probability, so popular item 1 is pushed down with weight 0.117. With the logQ correction (item 1's sampling probability 0.02), its corrected probability drops to 0.015, so it is barely pushed.
M
What does the temperature do and how do you set it?

Logits are divided by τ before the softmax. A small τ, such as 0.05 on normalised vectors, stretches cosine differences into large logit gaps, so the softmax focuses on the few negatives that score close to the positive: effectively hard-negative mining. Too small and training is unstable and over-fits to noise; too large and every negative counts equally and learning is slow. It is a hyperparameter tuned on retrieval recall; Yi et al. reported results for 0.05 to 0.14.
M
How do you handle a brand-new item in a two-tower system?

The item tower embeds it from content features (title text, image or video embeddings, creator, category, price), so it gets a usable vector the moment it is uploaded, without any interactions. A streaming job computes the vector and inserts it into the ANN index within minutes. The ID embedding for the new item is untrained (or a shared hashed bucket), so content features carry it at first; its vector improves as the model retrains with its interactions. Exploration (rec11) gives it the impressions needed to learn.
M
What are hard negatives and what can go wrong with them?

Hard negatives are items the current model scores high for a user who did not engage with them, for example the top ANN results that were shown and skipped. They teach fine distinctions faster than random items. Risks: many are false negatives, items the user would like but never saw, so the model learns to suppress good items; and training only on hard negatives distorts the score distribution so random irrelevant items are no longer pushed down. Mix them with easy and in-batch negatives and prefer shown-and-skipped items over merely unclicked ones.
H
Your two-tower retriever's offline recall@100 improved 8% but the online A/B test is flat. What do you investigate?

First, whether the ranker uses the new candidates: measure the share of shown items that came only from the new retriever, and their engagement. If the ranker rarely picks them, the gain is invisible or the new candidates are ones the ranker dislikes. Second, whether offline recall rewards imitation: the labels are clicks on items the old system showed, so a retriever that copies the old system scores well without adding value. Third, staleness and version skew: index build lag, mismatched user and item model versions, or features computed differently at serving. Fourth, overlap with other sources: if its candidates are already supplied by co-occurrence, the funnel gains nothing.

Follow-up: How would you evaluate the retriever better offline? — Measure recall against the final ranker's choices on a large candidate set (funnel recall from rec1), and evaluate on engagements from all surfaces and from exploration traffic rather than only clicks on its own past recommendations.
H
Design the embedding refresh pipeline for 50 million items, a new model version weekly and 200,000 new items per day.

New model version: a batch job runs the item tower over all 50 million items (at, say, 20,000 items per second per GPU, about 40 GPU-minutes), builds a new ANN index, validates it (recall against exact search on a sample, distribution checks on norms), and then switches the user tower and index together, ideally with a canary. New items: a streaming job embeds each upload with the current item tower and inserts into the live index (HNSW supports inserts; IVF assigns to the nearest centroid), within minutes. Periodic full rebuilds clean up deleted items and keep the index balanced. Every vector and index carries a model-version tag, and serving refuses to mix versions.

Follow-up: Item features such as engagement counts change daily; must you re-embed everything daily? — Only if the item tower uses fast-changing features. Many teams keep fast-changing statistics out of the item tower (they belong in the ranker) so item vectors stay valid between model versions, and re-embed only items whose content changed.
H
How does a two-tower retriever learn popularity bias, and what can you do about it?

Training data is clicks on what was shown, which over-represents popular items; without logQ correction, in-batch training under-scores them, and with the correction the model faithfully learns their true popularity, so they dominate retrieval for everyone. Dot-product scoring adds another channel: popular items often get larger vector norms. Remedies: normalise vectors (cosine scoring), cap per-item exposure in re-ranking, use mixed negatives so the long tail is represented, add a fresh-items source, and measure coverage and the share of retrieved items from the long tail as guardrails.
H
When would you use a query tower that takes the text query as input, and how does that differ from RAG embeddings?

For product or video search, a two-tower model whose query tower reads the query text plus user context, trained on query–click pairs, learns what this audience means by queries ('cheap phone' maps to specific listings) and can personalise. An off-the-shelf text embedding model, as used in RAG, is trained on general semantic similarity between texts and does not know your users' behaviour or your catalogue's quirks. The trained tower usually wins on engagement; the generic model wins on cold start and on long-tail queries with no click history, which is why systems often use both (rec5).
refs: Sampling-Bias-Corrected Neural Modeling for Large Corpus Item Recommendations (Yi et al., RecSys 2019)
The public case: two-tower retrieval at YouTube, in-batch softmax with logQ correction, streaming frequency estimation, temperature and normalisation; +0.37% vs +0.20% engagement in a live test.
Deep Neural Networks for YouTube Recommendations (Covington, Adams, Sargin, RecSys 2016)
Retrieval as extreme multiclass classification over millions of videos, trained with several thousand sampled negatives and importance weighting, more than 100 times faster than a full softmax.
Mixed Negative Sampling for Learning Two-tower Neural Networks in Recommendations (Yang et al., WWW 2020 companion)
Adds uniformly sampled items to in-batch negatives to correct selection bias against items that rarely appear in batches.
A worked two-tower retrieval model with in-batch softmax and brute-force and ScaNN serving.
On Using Very Large Target Vocabulary for Neural Machine Translation (Jean et al., 2015)
The importance-sampling derivation behind sampled softmax with a correction for the proposal distribution.

t: Hybrid search and query understanding: lexical plus dense, rank fusion, spelling, expansion and intent
sum: How production search combines BM25 and embedding retrieval: why their failures are complementary, reciprocal rank fusion worked on two ranked lists (and why min-max score blending misleads), learned fusion in the ranker, query understanding (normalisation, spelling correction by the noisy-channel model, synonym and model-based expansion, category and attribute intent), and how semantic search for an LLM's context differs from search for people.
prereq: rec2
BM25 scores documents by rare-term matches with saturation and length normalisation, served from an inverted index; strong on exact words, blind to paraphrase.
rec4
A two-tower model embeds queries and items so that dot products reflect what satisfies users; it bridges paraphrase but blurs exact identifiers.
lm9
RAG pipelines already fuse BM25 and dense retrieval with RRF (c = 60) and re-rank with a cross-encoder; this lesson treats the same tools from the search-product side.
in11
Typeahead suggests completions from a prefix index of popular queries within 100 ms; it shapes which queries users actually submit.
why:
A podcast app's search runs on a well-tuned keyword engine. Type "Joe Rogan 1169" and you get exactly that episode. Type a guest's name and you get every show they appeared on. Then a listener types electric cars climate impact and gets nothing at all. There are hundreds of relevant episodes; their titles and descriptions say things like "Are EVs really greener?" and "The carbon cost of batteries". Not one contains all of the query's words, and the ones that contain some of them are about other things. Spotify described exactly this query returning no results in its 2022 write-up about adding natural-language search to podcasts.

The obvious fix is to switch to embedding search, which matches meaning. It handles the climate query beautifully. Then a listener searches for an episode number, a guest's unusual surname or a show's exact title, and gets a list of vaguely related episodes about similar topics, with the exact match somewhere on page two. Embeddings are good at "about the same thing" and bad at "this exact string".

Real search engines therefore do both and merge the results, which is called hybrid search. That raises a deceptively hard question: how do you merge two ranked lists whose scores mean completely different things? And before either retriever runs, there is the query itself to deal with: misspelled ("climat"), abbreviated ("ev"), ambiguous ("apple"), or carrying structure the words hide ("red nike running shoes under 100" is a category, a brand, a colour and a price filter). Making sense of the query before retrieval is query understanding, and on most search products it moves quality as much as the retrieval models do.

This lesson covers both halves. It shows why lexical and dense retrieval fail on different queries, works reciprocal rank fusion by hand on two ranked lists and shows why simple score blending misleads, then goes through query normalisation, spelling correction with the noisy-channel model, expansion and intent detection. It ends with a comparison that matters for AI engineers: retrieval for an LLM's context window (lm9, ev6) is not the same problem as search for people, even when the components are identical.
primer:
Imagine a library with two librarians. The first has memorised the card catalogue: give her exact words and she finds every book containing them instantly, but if you describe a book in your own words she is stuck. The second has read every book and understands what each is about: describe what you want and she suggests books on that theme, but ask for the book with a specific title and she hands you several on the same subject, unsure which you meant. A sensible visitor asks both and combines their suggestions, trusting most the books both of them pick.

That is hybrid search. The first librarian is lexical retrieval (rec2), the second is dense retrieval (rec4, lm10). Each returns a ranked list. Combining them well is the fusion step. The simplest robust method, reciprocal rank fusion, ignores how confident each librarian sounds (their scores, which are on incomparable scales) and uses only the order in which they listed books: a book near the top of both lists wins; a book at the top of one list still makes it.

Why not just pick the better librarian? Because which one is better depends on the question, and you do not know in advance which kind of question you have. On a typical product search box, a large share of traffic is short and specific (a brand, a model, a product name), where the catalogue librarian shines, and a long tail is descriptive ("something to stop the door slamming"), where the well-read librarian shines. Average quality is maximised by consulting both on every question and letting agreement and a learned ranker sort it out, at the price of running two retrievers. In latency terms that price is small, because they run at the same time, not one after the other.

The analogy breaks in two places, and both matter. Real librarians can tell you when they are unsure; retrievers always return a full list, so a dense retriever will happily return 200 "similar" documents for a query that has exactly one right answer. And the visitor's request is not fixed: a good search engine rewrites the request first, fixing typos, adding synonyms, recognising that "ev" means electric vehicle in this context and that "under 100" is a price limit. That rewriting, query understanding, is the first box in the picture, and a weak one caps everything after it.

One more piece of vocabulary before the details. A retriever that finds the right documents but ranks them badly has good recall and poor precision at the top; one that ranks a few documents perfectly but misses many has the reverse. Fusion is mostly a recall tool (union the candidates, reward agreement); the ranker is the precision tool. Keeping those roles separate makes design discussions much clearer.

A useful way to hold the whole lesson: query understanding decides what is being asked, retrieval decides which documents could answer it, fusion decides how to merge different opinions, and the ranker decides the order people see. Problems in search usually live in exactly one of those four, and the debugging question is always which.
body:
1. Two retrievers, two kinds of failure

It is worth being precise about why lexical and dense retrieval fail differently, because it decides when hybrid helps.

Lexical retrieval (BM25 over an inverted index) scores documents by shared terms, weighted by rarity. It fails on vocabulary mismatch: the relevant document uses different words ("EV" or "battery car" for "electric car", "carbon footprint" for "climate impact"). It also fails on conceptual queries with no distinctive words ("something relaxing to listen to while studying"). It succeeds on rare exact strings: identifiers, names, codes, quoted phrases, newly coined terms, where a match is strong evidence.

Dense retrieval (embeddings plus ANN) scores by learned similarity of meaning. It succeeds on paraphrase and concepts. It fails on exact-match needs: a model number becomes a few subword tokens whose embedding is dominated by "this is a product code", so all product codes look alike; a rare surname may be tokenised into fragments the model has no meaning for. It can fail on negation and precise constraints ("laptops without touchscreen" lands near touchscreen laptops). It also fails quietly: there is always a nearest neighbour, so it never returns "no results", only less relevant ones.

Because the failure sets overlap little, combining them helps most queries and hurts few, provided the fusion is sensible. BEIR (rec2) quantified the complementary strengths across 18 datasets; most production teams that publish on hybrid search report the same pattern on their own traffic.

2. Reciprocal rank fusion, worked

Suppose the query "electric car battery recycling" goes to both retrievers. BM25 returns, in order: D3, D1, D7, D2, D9, D5. The dense retriever returns: D1, D4, D3, D8, D2, D6. Their raw scores are useless for comparison: BM25's run from 18.2 down to 8.7, the dense cosines from 0.82 down to 0.77.

Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF), introduced by Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher in 2009, gives each document the sum, over the lists it appears in, of 1/(k + rank), with ranks starting at 1. Elasticsearch's RRF retriever defaults to k = 60 (the rank_constant), the value the original paper fixed in a pilot study and then validated. Compute each document:

DocBM25 rankDense rankRRF score (k = 60)
D1211/62 + 1/61 = 0.01613 + 0.01639 = 0.03252
D3131/61 + 1/63 = 0.01639 + 0.01587 = 0.03227
D2451/64 + 1/65 = 0.01563 + 0.01538 = 0.03101
D4—21/62 = 0.01613
D73—1/63 = 0.01587
D8—41/64 = 0.01563
D95—1/65 = 0.01538
D5, D66 / —— / 61/66 = 0.01515 each

Fused order: D1, D3, D2, D4, D7, D8, D9, D5/D6. Three observations. Documents both retrievers found (D1, D3, D2) take the top three, even D2, which neither ranked above fourth: agreement is strong evidence. Within the agreed set, ranks still matter, but only a little: D1 (2nd and 1st) edges D3 (1st and 3rd). And a document found by only one retriever at a high rank (D4, dense rank 2) still beats documents found only by one retriever lower down.

The role of k. With k = 60, the difference between rank 1 (1/61) and rank 5 (1/65) is small, about 6%; the scheme mostly rewards appearing in several lists. With k = 1, rank 1 is worth 1/2 and rank 5 only 1/6, so top positions dominate: on these lists, D1 scores 0.833, D3 0.750, D2 0.367 and D4 0.333, nearly tying D2 (found by both) with D4 (found by one). Large k is the conservative choice when you trust agreement more than either retriever's top pick. Elasticsearch also exposes rank_window_size, how deep into each list to look (default: the requested result size); fusing the top 100 of each list rather than the top 10 lets agreement deeper down count.

3. Why score blending misleads

The tempting alternative is to normalise each list's scores to 0-1 and take a weighted average, a convex combination. With min-max normalisation (subtract the list's minimum, divide by its range) and equal weights, on the same lists:

  • BM25 scores 18.2, 11.0, 10.4, 9.9, 9.1, 8.7 for D3, D1, D7, D2, D9, D5 become 1.00, 0.24, 0.18, 0.13, 0.04, 0.00. D3's unusually high score (perhaps it repeats a rare query term) squashes everything else towards zero.
  • Dense cosines 0.82, 0.80, 0.79, 0.78, 0.775, 0.77 for D1, D4, D3, D8, D2, D6 become 1.0, 0.6, 0.4, 0.2, 0.1, 0.0. A spread of 0.05 in cosine, which may be noise, is stretched across the whole range.

Averaging (missing documents count as 0): D3 0.70, D1 0.62, D4 0.30, D2 0.11, D8 0.10, D7 0.09. Now D4, found by one retriever, sits well above D2, found by both, and the order hinges on one outlier score. Change the depth of either list (fetch 50 instead of 6) and the minimums move, changing every normalised score. That fragility is why RRF is the robust default. Score blending can work, with per-query z-score normalisation, a tuned weight and a labelled set to tune on; OpenSearch's hybrid query offers min-max and L2 normalisation with weighted combination for teams that want it, and Elasticsearch supports both styles. But it must be tuned and monitored, because a change to either retriever's model shifts its score distribution and silently changes the blend.

4. Learned fusion: let the ranker decide

RRF is the right candidate-merging step, but the best final order usually comes from the learned ranker (rec6, rec7), which receives, for each candidate, the BM25 score per field, the dense cosine, each retriever's rank, whether the full query appears as a phrase, the attribute matches from query understanding, popularity, freshness and personalisation features. Trained on clicks or labels, it learns when to trust which signal: exact title matches dominate for navigational queries, the cosine matters more for long descriptive ones. Spotify's podcast search did exactly this: dense retrieval was added as an extra candidate source alongside Elasticsearch, and the query–episode cosine similarity was added as an input feature to the final re-ranking model.

The practical division of labour: the candidate stage unions both retrievers' top few hundred (RRF or plain union with quotas, rec1), and the ranker does the weighing. RRF on its own is the right final order when there is no learned ranker yet, as in many RAG systems and internal tools.

5. Query understanding: normalisation

Query understanding starts with the dull steps that prevent silly misses. Normalisation lowercases, folds accents (or not, per language), standardises Unicode, collapses whitespace, and handles units and numbers ("55in", "55 inch", "55\"" all become one form). Tokenisation of identifiers splits or joins consistently: "WH1000XM5", "WH-1000XM5" and "wh 1000 xm5" should all reach the same product. Language detection picks the analyser and the language-specific fields. These must mirror what the index does to documents (rec2's cardinal rule) or matches are lost.

6. Spelling correction with the noisy-channel model

Misspellings are common in typed search, especially on phones, and every one that goes uncorrected risks a null or poor result. The standard framing is the noisy channel: the user intended some query c, the act of typing corrupted it into the observed string t, and the corrector picks the c that best explains t:

best c = argmax over candidates c:   P(t | c) × P(c)

P(c), the language model or prior, says how plausible the intended query is: estimated from the query log and catalogue vocabulary, ideally with context ("running sheos" makes "shoes" more plausible than "sheds"). P(t | c), the error model, says how likely this particular typo is: adjacent-key substitutions and transpositions are common, dropped double letters are common, wholesale rewrites are rare. Candidates come from strings within a small edit distance (insertions, deletions, substitutions and, in the Damerau variant, transpositions of adjacent letters) of each query word.

Worked example: the user types sheos. Candidates within one edit include "shoes" (transpose e and o), "shes" (delete o), "sheds" (substitute o with d). From the query log, "shoes" was searched 200,000 times last month, "sheds" 2,000, "shes" 50. Suppose the error model gives a transposition probability of 0.002, and a substitution of a non-adjacent key 0.0005, and a deletion 0.001. Scores: shoes 0.002 × 200,000 = 400; sheds 0.0005 × 2,000 = 1; shes 0.001 × 50 = 0.05. "Shoes" wins by a factor of 400 over the runner-up. Also consider the original: "sheos" itself was searched 300 times (people do misspell it) but returns few results; with P(t | t) = 0.95 for "no typo", its score is 0.95 × 300 = 285, close to "shoes". This is why production systems compare the correction's score with the original's and the original's result count: correct automatically when the correction wins clearly and the original returns little; otherwise show results for the original with "Did you mean: shoes?".

The vocabulary is the trap. A dictionary-based corrector will "fix" brand names, product codes and new slang into common words. The candidates and the prior must come from your own query logs and catalogue, and any term that exists in the catalogue should be protected from correction. Error models are best learned from logs too: sequences where a user typed a query, got poor results and immediately retyped a close variant and clicked are free training pairs.

7. Expansion and rewriting

Query expansion adds terms to catch documents that do not use the query's words. Sources, from oldest to newest:

  • Curated synonyms: "tv" ↔ "television", "sofa" ↔ "couch". Precise, labour-intensive, domain-specific.
  • Behavioural mining: pairs of queries users reformulate into each other within a session, or queries that lead to clicks on the same items. "ev" and "electric car" share clicked results, so they are probably equivalent here.
  • Pseudo-relevance feedback: run the query, take the top 10 results, add terms that are frequent in them but not in the query, and run again. It helps when the first pass is mostly right and drifts badly when it is not.
  • Model-based expansion: an embedding model proposes related terms, or an LLM rewrites the query or generates a hypothetical answer to embed (rec14 discusses the cost at query rates).

Two rules keep expansion safe. Weight expanded terms below the original ones (in Elasticsearch, a bool query where the original is a must-match or boosted clause and expansions are optional should clauses), so documents matching the user's actual words still win. And make expansions context-aware: "apple" → "fruit" is right on a grocery site and wrong on an electronics site; "java" → "coffee" is right in a café chain's search and disastrous in a programming forum. Synonyms are often asymmetric: "iphone" implies "phone", but "phone" should not retrieve only iPhones.

Dense retrieval is, in a sense, implicit expansion: it matches documents that use related words without adding them to the query. This is one reason hybrid systems often need less hand-built expansion than pure lexical ones.

8. Intent: category, attributes and routing

Many queries hide structure. "red nike running shoes under 100" is not five words to match; it is a category (running shoes), a brand (Nike), a colour (red) and a price constraint (under 100). An attribute extractor, a sequence-labelling model or a rule set over a vocabulary of known brands and colours, tags each span, and the system turns tags into filters ("price < 100") or strong ranking features ("brand matches"). Without it, retrieval returns red socks and Nike headbands that happen to share words.

Category prediction classifies the query into the catalogue's taxonomy, using a model trained on which categories users clicked or bought from after each query. A confident prediction lets retrieval boost or filter to that category; a split prediction ("jaguar": cars 55%, animals 30%, guitars 15%) signals ambiguity, and the page should mix interpretations. Query-type classification distinguishes navigational queries (one known target: "nike air max 90", "netflix login"), where the exact item must be first and the rest barely matters, from exploratory ones ("comfortable shoes for standing all day"), where variety and dense retrieval matter more, and from questions, which might be routed to an answer system.

Intent outputs drive routing: identifier queries go lexical-first; long natural-language queries weight dense retrieval more; questions in a help centre may trigger a generated answer above the results. Routing is cheap and powerful, and its classifier needs the same care as any model: labelled data, per-class evaluation and monitoring.

9. Weighted fusion, more sources and personalisation

Real systems rarely fuse exactly two lists. A marketplace might merge BM25 on titles, BM25 on descriptions, a dense retriever, a "previously purchased by this user" source and a "popular for this category" source. RRF extends naturally: sum 1/(k + rank) over however many lists contain the document. Two refinements are common. Weighted RRF multiplies each list's contribution by a weight, ws/(k + rank), so a source known to be strong for this query class counts more; the weights can be set per query class from labelled data (for identifier queries, BM25 on titles might get weight 2 and dense 0.5). Per-source depth limits how far into each list fusion looks, which stops a weak source's long tail from diluting the pool.

Personalisation enters search in three places. Query understanding can use the user's context to resolve ambiguity: a user who has bought guitar strings is more likely to mean the guitar brand by "jaguar". Retrieval can add a personal source, such as items the user viewed or bought before that match the query (people re-find things constantly). And the ranker can take user features, as in recommendation. Search personalisation is usually lighter than feed personalisation, because the query is a strong, explicit statement of intent and users are surprised when two people get very different results for the same words; most teams personalise the order among relevant results rather than which results are relevant.

10. The latency budget of query understanding

Everything in sections 5-8 happens before retrieval starts, so it sits on the critical path of every search (rec1). A realistic budget for a search request of 150 ms at p99 might give query understanding 15-20 ms in total. That rules out a large model call per query: a hosted LLM rewrite takes hundreds of milliseconds. What fits: normalisation and identifier detection (microseconds), dictionary and query-log lookups for spelling (sub-millisecond with precomputed candidate tables), a small classifier for category and query type (a few milliseconds on CPU), an attribute tagger (a few milliseconds), and the query encoder for dense retrieval (5-20 ms on CPU for a small model, less on GPU).

Two tricks stretch the budget. Caching: the head of the query distribution repeats constantly, so the full understanding result (correction, category, attributes, query embedding) for the top million queries can be cached and served in a millisecond; Spotify cached query vectors for exactly this reason. Precomputation: for head queries, expensive rewrites, including LLM-generated expansions, can be produced offline in batch, reviewed, and stored as a lookup table, leaving live models only for the tail. The tail, where caching fails, is also where expensive understanding helps most, so some systems allow a slower path for rare, low-result queries only.

11. Evaluating hybrid search and query understanding

Evaluate each component and the whole, and always by query class. For retrieval and fusion, a labelled query set with graded relevance gives recall@100 (did the candidates contain the relevant items?) and nDCG@10 (are they in a good order?) for lexical alone, dense alone, RRF and the full ranker. The set must be stratified: if 70% of sampled traffic is head queries where BM25 already works, the average hides large changes on the tail. Report per class (navigational, identifier, descriptive, attribute-heavy, question-like) and per head, torso and tail.

For the speller, build pairs of (typed, intended) from logs and labelling, and measure correction precision (when it corrects, is it right?) and recall (of the misspellings, how many does it fix?), with special attention to false corrections of valid rare queries, which are far more damaging than missed corrections. For category and attribute models, standard classification metrics per class (ml7), plus the downstream effect: how often a wrong category filter removed the item the user eventually bought.

Online, the metrics are null-result rate, reformulation rate, click-through on the top results, and conversion per search, again per class. A healthy launch typically shows null results falling sharply for descriptive queries while navigational and identifier metrics stay flat; if navigational first-result click-through drops, fusion is overriding exact matches and needs routing or ranker features.

12. Semantic search for an LLM versus for people

AI engineers often build retrieval for RAG (lm9) and then for a product's search box, assuming the same pipeline serves both. The components overlap (BM25, embeddings, RRF, cross-encoder re-rankers), but the problems differ in ways that change the design.

Retrieval for an LLM (RAG)Search for people
UnitPassages of a few hundred tokensDocuments, products, episodes
ConsumerReads everything given, cannot click or skipScans the top few results, clicks one
GoalRecall of every needed passage within a token budgetBest few results first; satisfy or navigate fast
Harm from noiseHigh: irrelevant or contradictory chunks mislead the answerLow-moderate: users skip bad results
FeedbackLittle or none (no clicks); needs labelled evals (ev6)Clicks, dwell, purchases: abundant if biased (rec10)
QueriesOften generated or rewritten by the model; longTyped by people; short, misspelled, navigational
ExtrasAccess control per chunk, citation, freshness of factsSnippets, facets, personalisation, ads, latency

Practical consequences. For RAG, fuse deep (top 50-100 from each retriever) and re-rank with a cross-encoder to choose the 5-20 chunks that fit the budget; measure recall@k and groundedness (ev6). For people, invest in query understanding, navigational precision and the ranker; measure nDCG@5 or @10, click-through on the first results, null-result rate and conversion. And for people, latency is a hard product constraint (rec1), while for RAG the LLM call dwarfs retrieval time, so a slower, more thorough retrieval is often affordable.
deep:
Why RRF works as well as it does

RRF has three properties that explain its robustness. It is scale-free: monotone changes to either retriever's scores (a new model version with a different cosine range) do not affect it. It is bounded: no single list can contribute more than 1/(k + 1), so one retriever's overconfident outlier cannot dominate. And with large k it approximates a vote: the fused order is mostly decided by how many lists a document appears in, with rank as a tiebreak, which is exactly the right behaviour when each retriever is noisy but their errors are independent. Its weakness is the flip side: it throws away calibrated confidence. If one retriever is far better than the other for a query class, RRF still treats them equally; weighted RRF (multiplying each list's contribution by a per-retriever or per-query-class weight) or a learned ranker fixes that.

Normalisation choices if you do blend scores

If you blend scores, normalise per query, not globally, because BM25's scale changes with query length and term rarity. Z-score normalisation (subtract the list's mean, divide by its standard deviation) is less sensitive to a single outlier than min-max. Even better is calibrating each retriever's score to a probability of relevance with a small model fitted on labelled data (ml15), after which a weighted sum has meaning. Fix the depth of each list used for normalisation, or the statistics drift with the number of results. And re-tune whenever either retriever changes, which in practice means score blending is a maintenance commitment that rank fusion avoids.

Late interaction: a middle ground

ColBERT-style models keep one embedding per token for documents and queries and score a pair by summing, over query tokens, the maximum similarity to any document token. This preserves some exact-match behaviour (a rare token in the query must match some token in the document) while capturing meaning, and in BEIR it averaged slightly above BM25 out of domain. The cost is storage (one vector per token instead of per document, mitigated by compression) and a more complex index. It is a reasonable choice for corpora where both exact terms and paraphrase matter, such as technical documentation.

Learned sparse retrieval and document expansion

Another way to get hybrid behaviour from one index is to make the lexical side smarter: document-expansion models add likely query terms to each document before indexing, and learned sparse models assign weights to vocabulary terms (including ones not in the text). Both run on an inverted index with BM25-like efficiency and close part of the vocabulary gap while keeping exact-match strength. They are attractive when operating a separate vector index is costly, and they combine well with dense retrieval too.

Query understanding as a model, not a rule set

Early search teams built query understanding as dozens of rules. Mature teams consolidate it into a few models trained on behavioural data: a query-to-category classifier trained on click and purchase categories, a sequence tagger for attributes trained on queries whose clicked items' attributes reveal the labels, and a rewrite model trained on reformulation pairs. Training labels come almost for free from logs, which also means they inherit the logs' biases: a category that the old system never showed for a query will never be learned as its intent. Exploration traffic (rec11) and periodic human labelling of samples keep the models honest.

Typeahead shapes the queries you get

Query understanding does not start with a submitted query. Typeahead (in11) suggests completions on every keystroke, and on many products a large share of submitted queries are accepted suggestions. That has two consequences. Suggestions normalise queries towards popular, well-spelled forms, so the long tail of raw typed text is smaller than it would be, and spelling correction partly moves into the typeahead index. And whatever the suggestion system favours becomes what users search for, which feeds back into the query log that trains the speller, the synonym miner and the category classifier. A suggestion bug, such as dropping a brand from the suggestion index, can therefore look like a drop in search demand for that brand. Analysing search quality without knowing which queries came from suggestions misses this.

Null results and the long tail

Queries follow a long-tailed distribution: a few thousand head queries account for a large share of volume, and millions of tail queries occur once or twice. Head queries can be hand-tuned and have abundant click data; tail queries are where spelling, expansion, dense retrieval and robust fusion earn their keep, and where null results concentrate. A useful habit: review the top null-result and low-click queries weekly, classify the failure (spelling, vocabulary mismatch, missing inventory, intent misread, tokenisation), and feed each class to the right fix. Missing inventory is a business signal, not a search bug, and is worth reporting.
prod:
The public case: Spotify's natural-language podcast search

In March 2022 Spotify's engineering blog described adding natural-language search for podcast episodes. The existing system was Elasticsearch-based term matching, and the post gives the motivating failure directly: the query "electric cars climate impact" returned no results even though relevant episodes existed, because none matched the exact words. Spotify added dense retrieval as an additional candidate source rather than a replacement. The model was a bi-encoder (one shared transformer encoder for queries and episodes, compared with cosine similarity) starting from the Universal Sentence Encoder CMLM model, chosen because it produces sentence embeddings directly and covers more than 100 languages, then fine-tuned on Spotify's own data.

The training data came from four places: successful historical podcast searches from Elasticsearch logs, query reformulations (sessions where an unsuccessful query was followed by a successful one), synthetic queries generated with a BART model fine-tuned on MS MARCO, and a small manually curated set of semantic queries used only for evaluation. Training used in-batch negatives, producing B positive pairs and B² − B negative pairs per batch, with hard-negative mining and a margin loss added in later iterations. Episode vectors were indexed in Vespa, a search engine with native approximate-nearest-neighbour support, serving tens of millions of episodes; query vectors were computed by GPU inference on Google Cloud Vertex AI with a cache so repeated queries are not re-encoded. The final-stage re-ranking model received the query–episode cosine similarity as a new input feature alongside its existing ones. A/B testing showed a significant increase in podcast engagement, and the feature had rolled out to most users by publication.

Every idea in this lesson appears: complementary failure of lexical search, dense retrieval as an extra source, behavioural and synthetic training data, in-batch negatives, the cosine fed to a learned ranker as fusion, and online evaluation as the final word.

How hybrid search fails in production

Navigational regressions. After adding dense retrieval, exact-title and identifier searches lose their first-place result to "similar" items. Symptom: first-result click-through drops for navigational queries while overall metrics look flat. Fix with routing, exact-match features in the ranker, or per-class fusion weights.

Over-eager spelling correction. A new brand launches and its name is "corrected" to a common word; the brand's searches return nothing relevant. Symptom: a spike of reformulations and null results for one term. Protect catalogue vocabulary and monitor corrections by term.

Expansion drift. A mined synonym ("pink" ↔ "rose", learned from a perfume-heavy season) leaks into clothing search. Symptom: precision complaints for one category. Keep expansions category-scoped and review newly mined synonyms before activation.

Score-blend drift. A team blending normalised scores updates the embedding model; its cosine range shifts from 0.7-0.85 to 0.3-0.6, and the blend silently tilts towards BM25. RRF would not have noticed; a blend must be re-tuned. Monitor the share of final results contributed by each retriever.

Latency from the second retriever. The embedding service adds 20-40 ms of query encoding plus ANN search. Run it in parallel with lexical retrieval with a deadline (rec1), cache query embeddings for frequent queries (as Spotify did), and fall back to lexical-only if it is late.

What to monitor

Null-result rate and low-result rate; reformulation rate (a second query within seconds); first-result and top-3 click-through; conversion per search; all sliced by query class (navigational, identifier, descriptive, question) and by head versus tail. Per-retriever contribution: share of clicked results found by lexical only, dense only, both. Speller: correction rate, share of corrections followed by a reformulation back to the original (a sign the correction was wrong). Latency per retriever and fallback rate.
myths: Hybrid search means adding the BM25 score and the cosine similarity.

The two scores live on unrelated scales: BM25 is unbounded and query-dependent (a 3-term query scores higher than a 1-term one), cosine is between −1 and 1 and usually bunched in a narrow band. Adding them lets whichever has the larger spread dominate. Rank-based fusion such as RRF, or a learned ranker that takes both scores as features, avoids the problem.
RRF is a heuristic with a magic number, so a weighted score blend must be better.

RRF's constant of 60 came from a pilot study and was then validated across many test collections, where RRF beat both the best single system and score-based fusion such as CombMNZ. Score blends can beat it, but only after careful per-query normalisation and tuning on labelled data, and they break when one retriever's score distribution shifts. RRF is the robust default; a learned ranker is the upgrade.
Spelling correction should fix every word not in the dictionary.

Product names, brands, slang and new words are not in any dictionary, and 'correcting' them destroys the query: a search for a new brand gets rewritten into a common word. Good spellers use the query log and the catalogue as their vocabulary, correct only when the alternative is much more probable, and often show results for the original plus a 'did you mean' instead of silently rewriting.
Semantic search is the same problem whether the reader is a person or an LLM.

People scan a short list, judge the first few results harshly, click navigational results and need snippets and freshness; an LLM reads everything you put in its context, cannot click, is hurt by contradictory or irrelevant chunks, and needs passages rather than documents. The retrieval units, metrics, depth and fusion choices differ, as the last section explains.
Query expansion always improves recall.

It improves recall for vocabulary-mismatch queries and harms precision when the expansion drifts: expanding 'apple' with 'fruit' on an electronics site, or 'java' with 'coffee' in a programming help centre. Expansion must be context-aware, weighted below the original terms, and evaluated per query class.

Goal: implement RRF and score blending, reproduce the lesson's fused orders, and build a tiny noisy-channel speller. Python 3.12, standard library only.

  1. Create rec5_lab.py. Write rrf(lists, k=60) taking a list of ranked ID lists and returning documents sorted by fused score. Feed it the lesson's BM25 list (D3, D1, D7, D2, D9, D5) and dense list (D1, D4, D3, D8, D2, D6); check you get D1, D3, D2, D4, D7 at the top with scores 0.03252, 0.03227, 0.03101. Repeat with k = 1 and k = 1,000 and describe how the order changes.
  2. Write minmax_blend(score_dicts, weights) with missing documents scoring 0. Use the lesson's raw scores and confirm D2 falls below D4. Then change D3's BM25 score from 18.2 to 11.5 (no longer an outlier) and recompute: does the blend's order now resemble RRF's?
  3. Add a z-score blend (per list, subtract mean and divide by standard deviation) and compare its order with the min-max one.
  4. Speller: create a dictionary of 30 "query log" words with counts (include shoes 200,000; sheds 2,000; shes 50; and some brand names). Write edits1(word) generating all strings one deletion, transposition, substitution or insertion away (Norvig's approach). Score candidates by count × error probability, with transposition 0.002, deletion 0.001, insertion 0.001, substitution 0.0005, and the original word by its own count × 0.95.
  5. Test "sheos", "runing", "nikee" and a brand name from your list typed correctly. Add a rule: never correct a word that is in the dictionary with count ≥ 100.

What to look for. RRF orders should match the table, k = 1 should let single-list top results jump up, and k = 1,000 should make the order almost purely "how many lists". The min-max blend should change a lot when one outlier score changes, and RRF not at all, which is the robustness argument in one experiment. The speller should fix the typos, leave the correctly typed brand alone, and show how close "sheos" itself comes to its correction, which is why real systems use "did you mean" for borderline cases.
recap: Lexical and dense retrieval fail on different queries: BM25 misses paraphrases, embeddings miss exact identifiers and rare terms, so running both and fusing usually beats either alone.
Reciprocal rank fusion scores each document by the sum over retrievers of 1/(k + rank), with k = 60 by default in Elasticsearch; it uses only ranks, so it needs no score calibration.
In the worked example, RRF puts D1 (ranks 2 and 1) just ahead of D3 (ranks 1 and 3) and lifts D2, found by both retrievers at low ranks, above documents found by only one.
Min-max score blending on the same lists lets one outlying BM25 score dominate and drops D2 below a document only one retriever found, which is why rank fusion is the robust default.
The strongest fusion is a learned ranker that receives both retrievers' scores and ranks as features alongside everything else.
Query understanding runs before retrieval: normalisation, spelling correction, expansion, and classification of intent, category and attributes.

Spelling correction is best framed as a noisy channel: choose the candidate maximising P(typed | intended) × P(intended), with the prior learned from query logs and the catalogue, and correct only when confident.
Expansion adds synonyms, mined rewrites or model-generated terms, weighted below the original query and checked for drift; intent classification extracts category and attributes and routes the query.
Retrieval for an LLM optimises recall of the passages needed within a token budget; retrieval for people optimises the first few results, freshness, navigation and personalisation.
glossary: Attribute extraction
Recognising structured constraints in a query, such as colour, size, brand or price, and turning them into filters or features.
CombSUM / CombMNZ
Classic score-fusion methods: sum the (normalised) scores across systems, and for CombMNZ multiply the sum by the number of systems that retrieved the document.
Convex combination
A weighted blend of normalised scores, w × score_A + (1 − w) × score_B, with w between 0 and 1.
Dense retrieval
Retrieval by nearest-neighbour search over learned embeddings of queries and documents.
Edit distance
The minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions, substitutions (and, in the Damerau variant, adjacent transpositions) needed to turn one string into another.
Hybrid search
Running lexical and dense retrieval for the same query and combining their results.
Intent classification
Predicting what a query is after: a product category, a navigational target, a question to be answered, or a browsing need.
Noisy-channel model
A model of spelling errors in which the user intended a word, the typing process corrupted it, and the speller picks the intended word that best explains what was typed given how common each word is.
Null and low-result queries
Queries that return nothing or very few results; a key search health metric and the main source of spelling and expansion work.
Pseudo-relevance feedback
Expanding a query with terms frequent in the top results of a first retrieval pass, assuming those results are mostly relevant.
Query expansion
Adding terms (synonyms, related words, rewrites) to a query to retrieve relevant documents that do not contain its original words.
Query rewriting
Replacing or reformulating a query, for example correcting spelling or converting a question into keywords, before retrieval.
Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF)
Merging ranked lists by giving each document the sum over lists of 1/(k + rank), where k is a constant, usually 60.
Retrieval unit
What the index stores and returns: whole documents or products for people, passages or chunks for an LLM.
Routing
Sending a query to different retrieval strategies depending on its type, for example lexical only for product codes.
Synonym mining
Discovering equivalent terms from behaviour, such as queries users reformulate into each other or that lead to clicks on the same items.
drill:
Diagnose and design: hybrid search for a hardware retailer

A DIY retailer's search (1.2 million products, 4,000 queries per second at peak) is BM25-only. Analysis of a week of logs shows: 9% null-result queries; most are descriptive ("thing to stop door slamming", "paint for bathroom ceiling mould"); 22% of queries contain a part or model number; navigational queries ("bosch psb 1800") convert well today. The team proposes switching entirely to an off-the-shelf embedding model. Respond with a design and an evaluation plan.

Answer

Do not switch; add. Pure dense retrieval would likely fix many descriptive null results but damage the 22% of queries with part numbers and the navigational ones, which convert well and blur under embeddings. Run both retrievers in parallel and fuse.

Query understanding first. Normalise identifiers (strip spaces and hyphens in codes; "psb1800", "psb 1800", "PSB-1800" all match) and detect them with patterns plus a catalogue lookup; route identifier queries lexical-first with exact-match boosts. Spelling correction from the query log and catalogue vocabulary, protecting brand and model names. Category and attribute extraction for things like sizes ("2.5 l", "50 mm"), colours and finishes, applied as boosts or filters.

Retrieval and fusion. BM25 over title, brand, description and specification fields (BM25F-style), top 200; dense retrieval with the embedding model fine-tuned on the retailer's query–purchase pairs (in-batch negatives), top 200, run in parallel with a 30 ms deadline and a query-embedding cache for the head queries. Merge with RRF (k = 60) as the candidate list and as the ranking until a learned ranker exists; then feed BM25 per field, cosine, both ranks, exact-code match and attribute matches into the ranker.

Capacity. 4,000 QPS of query encoding: with a cache hit rate of, say, 60% on head queries, 1,600 encodes per second; a small encoder on a few CPU nodes or one GPU handles that. The product index: 1.2 million × 384 dimensions × 1 byte ≈ 0.5 GB, replicated.

Evaluation. Offline: a labelled set stratified by query class (descriptive, identifier, navigational, attribute-heavy, null-result), measuring recall@100 and nDCG@10 for BM25, dense, RRF and the ranker; ship only if identifier and navigational classes do not regress. Online A/B: primary metric revenue or conversion per search; secondary null-result rate and reformulation rate; guardrails on navigational first-result click-through and p99 latency. Expect the null-result rate to fall substantially for descriptive queries, and confirm the identifier segment is flat.
qa: E
Why combine lexical and dense retrieval instead of choosing one?

Their failure modes are complementary. BM25 finds exact identifiers, names and rare terms but misses documents that use different words for the same idea; embeddings bridge paraphrase but blur exact strings and struggle with unseen vocabulary. Running both and fusing the lists recovers most of each one's wins. The cost is a second index and a few extra milliseconds, usually well worth it.
E
What is reciprocal rank fusion?

Each document's fused score is the sum over the input lists of 1/(k + rank), where rank starts at 1 and k is a constant, typically 60; documents missing from a list get nothing from it. It uses only ranks, so it does not care that BM25 scores and cosine similarities are on different scales. Documents ranked well by both lists rise to the top; a document strongly ranked by one list still gets in.
E
Give three examples of query understanding steps.

Spelling correction ('sheos' to 'shoes'), expansion with synonyms or related terms ('tv' also matches 'television'), and intent or attribute extraction ('red nike running shoes under 100' becomes category = running shoes, brand = Nike, colour = red, price < 100, applied as filters or features). Others include language detection, tokenising model numbers and classifying navigational queries.
M
Fuse these two lists with RRF, k = 60: BM25 returns D3, D1, D7, D2, D9; dense returns D1, D4, D3, D8, D2.

D1: 1/62 + 1/61 = 0.0325. D3: 1/61 + 1/63 = 0.0323. D2: 1/64 + 1/65 = 0.0310. D4 (dense rank 2 only): 1/62 = 0.0161. D7 (BM25 rank 3 only): 1/63 = 0.0159. Then D8 0.0156, D9 0.0154. So D1, D3, D2, D4, D7: documents both retrievers agree on come first, even D2, which neither ranked highly.

Follow-up: What does a smaller k do? — It sharpens the reward for top ranks: with k = 1, rank 1 is worth 0.5 and rank 5 only 0.17, so a single retriever's first result can outweigh agreement; large k flattens differences and rewards agreement more.
M
Why does min-max normalising and averaging scores often go wrong?

Min-max maps each list's top score to 1 and bottom to 0, so the result depends on the outliers and on how deep each list goes. One BM25 document with an unusually high score (because it repeats a rare query term) pushes every other BM25 result towards 0, and dense cosine scores bunched in 0.77-0.82 get stretched to 0-1, exaggerating tiny differences. In the lesson's example this drops D2, found by both retrievers, below a document only one found. It can work with per-query z-scores and tuning, but it is fragile.
M
How would you build a spelling corrector for an e-commerce search box?

Use the noisy-channel model: generate candidates within edit distance 1-2 of each query word (and of the whole query), score each by P(typed | candidate), from an error model learned from logged corrections (users retyping a query), times P(candidate), from query-log frequency and catalogue vocabulary, ideally with context from neighbouring words. Correct automatically only when the best candidate is much more likely than the original and the original returns few results; otherwise show 'did you mean'. Never correct brand or model names that exist in the catalogue.

Follow-up: How do you evaluate it? — Labelled pairs of misspelled and intended queries for precision and recall of corrections, plus the online null-result rate and click-through after correction; watch especially for false corrections of valid rare queries.
M
Where do synonyms come from in a production search engine, and what are the risks?

From curated lists for the domain, from query reformulations (users who search A then immediately search B and click), from co-click data (queries leading to clicks on the same items), and increasingly from embedding similarity or an LLM. Risks: drift (expanding 'apple' to 'fruit' on an electronics site), asymmetric synonyms ('iphone' implies 'phone' but not the reverse), and expansions that swamp the original terms. Apply expansions with lower weight than original terms, make them category-aware and test them per query class.
M
How does intent classification change retrieval and ranking?

Predicting the category ('running shoes') lets retrieval filter or boost that category, avoiding accessories and unrelated items that match words; extracting attributes turns 'under 100' into a price filter; recognising a navigational query ('nike air max 90') says one exact product should come first; detecting a question routes it to an answer or help-content system. Each step narrows the candidate set or adds strong features, so the ranker spends effort on plausible items.
M
When should a query bypass dense retrieval?

When it is an exact identifier (a SKU, order number, error code, part number), a quoted phrase, or a navigational query for a known item, dense retrieval adds noise and latency. A lightweight classifier or pattern rules can route those to lexical-only retrieval, or keep dense results but with low fusion weight. Conversely, long natural-language questions benefit most from dense retrieval.
H
Your hybrid search improved offline nDCG by 6% on a labelled set but users complain that exact product searches got worse. What happened and how do you fix it?

The labelled set probably over-represents descriptive queries, where dense retrieval helps, and under-represents identifier and navigational queries, where fusion can push the exact match down: with RRF, an item ranked first by BM25 but absent from the dense list can lose to items both retrievers placed moderately. Fix by slicing the evaluation by query class, routing identifier-like queries to lexical-first ranking, adding exact-match features (full model number match, title match) to the ranker so it can override fusion, and possibly weighting retrievers per query class in RRF.

Follow-up: How would you detect this before launch? — Evaluate per query class with a sample stratified by class, not by traffic share alone, and check the share of queries where the old first result drops below position 3.
H
Design the retrieval stack for an internal knowledge assistant (RAG) versus for the company's public help-centre search. What differs?

For RAG, the unit is a passage of a few hundred tokens, the goal is recall of every passage needed to answer within a token budget (say 8-20 chunks), there are no clicks, contradictory or stale chunks are actively harmful, and access control must filter per user. For the help centre, the unit is an article, users look at the top 3-5 results, navigational queries ('reset password') must hit the exact page, snippets and freshness matter, and clicks give training signal. Both benefit from hybrid retrieval and a cross-encoder re-ranker, but metrics differ (recall@k of passages and groundedness for RAG; nDCG@5, click-through and deflection for the help centre) and so do depth and fusion weights.
H
How would you evaluate whether to add a dense retriever to an existing lexical search system?

Offline: build a labelled set stratified by query class (head, tail, natural-language, identifier, null-result queries), and measure recall@100 and nDCG@10 for lexical, dense and fused retrieval with the existing ranker on top, since the ranker decides what users see. Check the dense retriever's marginal contribution: how many relevant results only it finds. Measure added latency and cost. Online: A/B test with search conversion and null-result rate as primary metrics, and guardrails on navigational success (click on first result) and latency. Spotify's 2022 podcast search did exactly this, adding dense retrieval as a source and the cosine as a ranker feature, and reported a significant engagement increase.
refs: Introducing Natural Language Search for Podcast Episodes (Spotify Engineering, March 2022)

The public case: dense retrieval with a fine-tuned multilingual sentence encoder added alongside Elasticsearch as an extra candidate source, the cosine fed to the re-ranker, served from Vespa; a significant engagement increase in A/B testing.
