t: Ranking metrics: precision, recall, MRR, MAP, nDCG, beyond-accuracy metrics, and why offline gains vanish online
sum: How to measure a ranked list: precision and recall at k, MRR, average precision and MAP, nDCG with linear and exponential gains (all worked by hand for one recommendation list), how to aggregate over users, catalogue coverage, intra-list diversity, novelty and calibration, the evaluation protocol choices that quietly decide the answer (temporal splits, sampled negatives), and the reasons a ranker that wins offline so often loses or ties online.
prereq: ml7
Precision is the share of predicted positives that are correct and recall the share of actual positives found; both depend on the threshold, and ROC-AUC measures separation across all thresholds.
ev6
For RAG retrieval, hit rate, recall@k, precision@k, MRR and nDCG@5 were defined and worked for one query with graded chunks; this lesson applies them to recommendation lists and goes further.
rec7
Learning-to-rank losses such as LambdaRank optimise a metric at a chosen depth with a chosen gain function, so the metric definition shapes the model.
ml16
Offline metrics are proxies; an A/B test measures the business metric directly, and the two often disagree.
why:
Two teams at a streaming service each claim a better home-page ranker. Team A reports "+6% nDCG@10". Team B reports "+11% hit rate@10 against 100 sampled negatives". Leadership asks which to ship. Nobody can answer, because the two numbers measure different things in different ways, and, as it turns out, either could be positive while the true effect on members is zero or negative. Team A's labels came from what the old ranker showed. Team B's protocol, ranking each held-out title against a hundred random titles instead of the whole catalogue, is one that a 2020 paper by Google researchers showed can reverse which of two models looks better.

Ranking metrics look simple, a few formulas with logarithms in them, and they are where an enormous amount of recommender and search work quietly goes wrong. The metric decides what the model is tuned towards (rec7's LambdaRank literally optimises it), what the team believes about its progress, and which experiments get run. A metric that rewards the wrong thing or an evaluation protocol that leaks information produces months of "progress" that never shows up for users.

Senior interviews probe this hard. "How would you evaluate this recommender?" is a standard question, and the strong answer is not a list of acronyms but a protocol: which metric for which surface and why, at what depth, computed how, against what baseline, sliced how, with what confidence, alongside which beyond-accuracy measures, and with what expectations about the online result.

The stakes are concrete. A ranking team ships perhaps ten to twenty model changes a year, and each needs weeks of A/B testing to measure. Offline evaluation decides which candidates get those scarce test slots. If the offline metric is biased towards imitating production, the team spends its year testing models that cannot win; if it is measured with a protocol that reverses comparisons, it ships worse models with confidence. Good offline evaluation is therefore a throughput multiplier for the whole team, not a formality before launch.

This lesson builds the toolkit. ev6 introduced recall@k, MRR and nDCG for RAG retrieval; here we compute the full set, precision@k, recall@k, MRR, MAP and nDCG with both gain conventions, by hand for one recommendation list, then cover how to aggregate them, the beyond-accuracy metrics (coverage, diversity, novelty, calibration), the protocol choices that quietly decide the answer, and the main reasons offline gains so often vanish online. Experiment design itself is rec13's subject.
primer:
Picture a friend who recommends five films. How would you grade them? You might count how many of the five you enjoyed (that is precision). You might ask how many of the films you would have enjoyed they managed to mention (recall). If you only wanted one film for tonight, you would care how far down their list the first good one was (reciprocal rank). If some films were wonderful and others merely fine, and you would mostly watch the first one or two, you would want the wonderful ones first: that is what nDCG measures, giving each film credit for how good it is, discounted by how far down the list it sits.

And then there are things none of those capture. If all five films are sequels in the same franchise, the list is accurate and dull (diversity). If all five are the year's biggest hits that you already know about, it adds nothing (novelty). If you love comedies and documentaries in equal measure but the list is all comedies, it misrepresents you (calibration). A real evaluation looks at both kinds of measures, because the second kind is where accuracy-optimised systems drift.

Notice that the metrics in the box disagree about how good the list is: reciprocal rank says perfect (1.0), precision says 60%, nDCG with exponential gains says under 50%. None is wrong. Reciprocal rank asks "was the first thing good?", and it was, a little. Precision asks "how much of the list was good?". nDCG asks "were the best things first?", and the best title was third while another excellent one was missing. Choosing a metric is choosing which of these questions your product cares about, which is why the first step of any evaluation is describing how people use the list: do they take the first acceptable result and leave, scan a short row, or scroll through dozens of items?

A second habit worth building early: always compute a metric for a trivial baseline next to your model. "Recommend the most popular titles" or "rank by BM25" gives a floor. If your model's nDCG@10 is 0.31 and popularity's is 0.29, the model is adding little, however sophisticated it is. If popularity scores 0.05, the problem is genuinely personal and the model is doing real work. Absolute metric values mean little on their own; the gap to sensible baselines and to production is what carries information.

The analogy breaks in an important way. Your friend's list can be graded by asking you about every film. A recommender's list is graded using what users actually did, and users only act on what they were shown. A film never recommended has no "enjoyed" or "ignored" label at all, so the grades we compute are always partial and shaped by the system that produced the data. Much of the "offline gains vanish online" story at the end of this lesson follows from that one fact.
body:
1. The setting: per-user lists, labels and depth

Offline evaluation of a recommender or search ranker needs three things. A set of evaluation units: users (for recommendations) or queries (for search). For each unit, the model's ranked list of items. And relevance labels: which items are relevant for that unit, ideally with grades. In recommendation, labels usually come from held-out behaviour (what the user watched, bought or rated after the training cut-off); in search, from human judgements or behaviour (rec7).

Every metric is computed per unit on the top k of the list, the cut-off, and then averaged over units. Choose k to match the product: the number of items visible without scrolling, the number of slots in a carousel, the number of chunks sent to an LLM (ev6). A metric at k = 100 says nothing about a carousel of 6.

The worked example used throughout: one user, a top-5 list from a streaming service, graded by what the user did in the next week: 2 = finished the title, 1 = started it, 0 = did not watch. The list's grades by rank are 1, 0, 2, 0, 1. The user also finished one title that the list did not include (grade 2, not retrieved). So there are four relevant titles in total: two with grade 2 (one at rank 3, one missing) and two with grade 1 (ranks 1 and 5).

2. Precision@k and recall@k

Precision@k is the share of the top k that is relevant. Counting any grade above 0 as relevant, the top 5 contains 3 relevant titles: precision@5 = 3/5 = 0.60. Recall@k is the share of all relevant items that appear in the top k: 3 of 4, recall@5 = 0.75.

They pull in different directions. Lengthening the list can only raise recall and usually lowers precision. Precision suits surfaces where every slot costs attention (a short carousel); recall suits stages whose job is not to miss things, like retrieval (rec1, rec4). Hit rate@k is a third variant: 1 if any relevant item is in the top k, else 0; it suits "the user needs just one good option" and is common in next-item recommendation papers. None of the three care about order within the top k: the list 0, 0, 1, 2, 1 has the same precision@5 and recall@5 as ours.

3. Reciprocal rank and MRR

The reciprocal rank (RR) is 1 divided by the rank of the first relevant item, or 0 if none is in the list. Our first relevant title is at rank 1, so RR = 1.0. If we count only "finished" (grade 2) as relevant, the first one is at rank 3 and RR = 0.33. MRR (mean reciprocal rank) averages RR over users or queries.

MRR is the right metric when there is one answer and the user stops when they find it: navigational search, a known-item lookup, question answering with one correct passage (MS MARCO's official metric is MRR@10, rec7). Its blind spot is everything after the first hit: moving our grade-2 title from rank 3 to rank 2 leaves MRR unchanged. Its scale is also very non-linear: dropping from rank 1 to rank 2 halves the score, while dropping from rank 9 to 10 barely moves it, which matches how people use search results.

4. Average precision and MAP

Average precision (AP) rewards placing all relevant items early. Walk down the list; at each rank where a relevant item appears, compute precision at that rank; sum those values and divide by the total number of relevant items (including ones not retrieved). For our list: rank 1 is relevant, precision@1 = 1/1 = 1.0; rank 3 is relevant, precision@3 = 2/3 = 0.667; rank 5 is relevant, precision@5 = 3/5 = 0.6. AP = (1.0 + 0.667 + 0.6) / 4 = 0.567. The missing fourth relevant title contributes 0, which is how AP penalises incomplete recall. (Some libraries divide by the number of relevant items retrieved instead, here 3, giving 0.756; check which definition a tool uses.) MAP averages AP over users or queries.

AP is binary: it does not distinguish "finished" from "started". It was the standard metric of the TREC evaluations for years and remains common for tasks with binary relevance.

5. nDCG, worked with both gain conventions

Discounted cumulative gain (Järvelin and Kekäläinen, 2002) gives each item a gain from its grade and divides it by a discount that grows with rank, log2(rank + 1):

DCG@k = Σ over ranks r = 1..k:  gain(grade_r) / log2(r + 1)
nDCG@k = DCG@k / IDCG@k

where IDCG@k is the DCG of the best possible ordering of all known relevant items. The discounts for ranks 1-5 are 1.000, 0.631, 0.500, 0.431, 0.387: rank 2 counts 63% as much as rank 1, rank 5 under 40%.

Linear gains (gain = grade), as in ev6. DCG@5 = 1 × 1.000 + 0 + 2 × 0.500 + 0 + 1 × 0.387 = 2.387. The ideal list orders all four relevant titles by grade: 2, 2, 1, 1. IDCG@5 = 2 × 1.000 + 2 × 0.631 + 1 × 0.500 + 1 × 0.431 = 2 + 1.262 + 0.5 + 0.431 = 4.193. nDCG@5 = 2.387 / 4.193 = 0.569.

Exponential gains (gain = 2grade − 1, common in web search and in LambdaMART, rec7): grades 0, 1, 2 give gains 0, 1, 3. DCG@5 = 1 + 0 + 3 × 0.5 + 0 + 1 × 0.387 = 2.887. IDCG@5 = 3 + 3 × 0.631 + 1 × 0.5 + 1 × 0.431 = 5.824. nDCG@5 = 0.496.

Same list, two different nDCGs. The exponential version makes a "finished" title worth three "started" ones, so the list is punished more for having its best item at rank 3 and for missing the other grade-2 title entirely. Neither is wrong; they encode different beliefs about how much better "finished" is than "started". The point is to choose deliberately, use the same definition for training (rec7) and evaluation, and state it when reporting.

Two more definitional traps. If the IDCG is computed only from relevant items that the model retrieved, rather than all known relevant items, the missing documentary no longer counts against the list, and nDCG rises (here to 2.387 / (2 + 0.631 + 0.5) = 0.762 with linear gains). And users with no relevant items in the test period have IDCG = 0; they must be excluded or assigned a fixed value, and the choice changes averages. Libraries differ on both.

6. Aggregating over users, and confidence

Metrics are computed per user (or query) and then averaged. Macro-averaging (each user counts once) is standard and protects light users from being drowned out by heavy ones. Weighting by activity answers a different question (how good is the average impression?). Report which.

Averages hide distributions. Slice by user activity (cold, light, heavy), by country, device, and content type; a model can raise the average by improving heavy users while hurting new ones. And attach uncertainty: per-user metric values are noisy, so compute a confidence interval by bootstrapping users (resample users with replacement, recompute the mean, take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles), and compare two models on the same users with a paired bootstrap of the per-user differences (ev7 covers both). A 0.5% nDCG gain with an interval of ±0.8% is not a gain.

7. Coverage and concentration

Accuracy metrics are computed per user, so they cannot see what the system does to the catalogue as a whole. Catalogue coverage is the share of items recommended to at least one user in a period: a system that recommends the same 2,000 titles to everyone may have decent accuracy and 4% coverage of a 50,000-title catalogue. Coverage is a minimum; the distribution of exposure matters more. The Gini coefficient of impressions across items summarises inequality (0 if all items get equal exposure, near 1 if a few items get almost all), and simpler versions are "share of impressions going to the top 1% of items". These matter for catalogue economics (licensed content nobody sees is wasted money) and for marketplaces and creator platforms, where exposure is income (rec12 covers fairness of exposure).

8. Diversity, novelty and serendipity

Intra-list diversity measures how different the items in one list are from each other: the average over pairs of items of (1 − similarity), where similarity might be the cosine of item embeddings or simply "same category". A list of five Marvel films has low diversity; one comedy, one documentary, one thriller has high diversity. Averaging it over users gives a system-level number.

Novelty measures how unfamiliar the recommended items are likely to be. A common definition is the average self-information of recommended items, −log2(pi), where pi is the share of users who have interacted with item i. An item 20% of users have watched contributes −log2(0.2) = 2.3 bits; one only 0.1% have watched contributes 10.0 bits. A list of blockbusters has low novelty. Serendipity tries to capture "relevant and surprising": items the user engaged with that a simple baseline (popularity, or "more of the same genre") would not have recommended. It is harder to measure and usually estimated against a baseline model.

These metrics are not goals in themselves: a list of random obscure items is maximally novel and diverse and useless. They are guardrails and trade-off dials, reported next to accuracy so that a model which gains 1% nDCG by collapsing diversity is visible before launch.

9. Calibration of the list

Steck's 2018 paper at Netflix pointed out a specific accuracy failure. A user who has watched 70% romance and 30% action titles often gets a list that is nearly all romance, because romance titles have slightly higher predicted scores for them, and the top-10 of a ranked list amplifies small score differences into a winner-takes-all mix. The minority interest disappears, and with it part of what the user wanted.

He defined calibration as how well the distribution of genres in the recommended list, q(g), matches the distribution in the user's history, p(g), measured with the KL divergence, Σg p(g) log(p(g) / q(g)), where q is smoothed slightly towards p so that a genre missing from the list does not give an infinite value. For the 70/30 user, a list of 9 romance and 1 action titles has q = (0.9, 0.1): KL = 0.7 ln(0.7/0.9) + 0.3 ln(0.3/0.1) = 0.7 × (−0.251) + 0.3 × 1.099 = −0.176 + 0.330 = 0.154. A 7/3 list has KL = 0. Calibrated re-ranking (rec12) trades a little accuracy for a much lower KL. The word "calibration" here is distinct from probability calibration (ml15, rec6): this is about the mix of the list, not the meaning of a predicted probability.

10. Choosing metrics per surface

Putting the pieces together, a reasonable default per surface:

  • Retrieval stage (rec1, rec4): recall@K at the depth passed to ranking (K = 200-2,000), and funnel recall against the ranker's preferences. Precision and order do not matter here.
  • Navigational or question search: MRR@10 and success@1 (was the first result right?), because users stop at the first good answer.
  • Result pages and product search: nDCG@10 with graded labels, plus click-through and conversion online.
  • Home-feed carousels and rows: nDCG or recall at the number of visible slots, plus diversity, novelty and calibration, because the row is consumed as a set.
  • Playlists and autoplay: metrics over the whole sequence (completion, skips per hour), because every item is consumed in order.
  • RAG retrieval (ev6): recall@k of the passages needed, at the number of chunks sent to the model, and downstream groundedness.

Whatever the surface, pair one primary accuracy metric with two or three beyond-accuracy guardrails and the slice view, so that a trade-off is always visible rather than discovered after launch.

11. Protocols that quietly decide the answer

The same model and metric can produce very different numbers depending on how the evaluation is set up. Four choices dominate.

Temporal versus random split. Random splits let the model train on a user's later behaviour and test on earlier behaviour, and let it learn item popularity from the future. A temporal split (train before a date, test after) matches deployment. Numbers drop, honestly.

Re-consumption. On many services people re-watch, re-listen and re-buy. Predicting "the user will play the same podcast they play every morning" is trivially easy and inflates every metric. Decide whether the product goal is discovery (exclude already-consumed items from both list and labels) or re-engagement (include them), and evaluate that goal.

Full ranking versus sampled negatives. Ranking each held-out item against the entire catalogue is expensive for large catalogues, so many papers rank it against a small random sample, often 100 items, and report hit rate or nDCG on that. Krichene and Rendle (KDD 2020) showed that these sampled metrics are "inconsistent with their exact version, in the sense that they do not persist relative statements, e.g., recommender A is better than B, not even in expectation". The intuition: against 100 random items, a held-out item only needs to beat mostly irrelevant, often unpopular items, so the metric mostly measures whether the model scores relevant items above random ones, which is AUC; indeed they show that as the sample shrinks, all top-k metrics collapse towards AUC. Top-of-list quality against the real competition, other plausible items, is lost.

Candidate set for ranking models. A ranker evaluated on logged impressions only sees items the old funnel produced. If the new ranker will serve on a different candidate set (because retrieval also changed), its offline metrics are for the wrong inputs.

12. Why offline gains vanish online

Every team that ships rankers learns that a meaningful offline gain often becomes a neutral online test, and occasionally a negative one. The reasons are structural, not bad luck.

Logged-data bias. Offline labels exist only for items the old system showed, at the positions it showed them. A new model that would show different items is evaluated mostly on the old model's choices; its genuinely new picks have no labels and count as non-relevant. This systematically favours models that imitate production and penalises exploratory ones (Wide & Deep's deep-only model, with lower offline AUC and higher online gain, is a public example, rec6). Counterfactual evaluation with logged propensities (rec10) is the principled fix.

Position and presentation bias. Clicked items were often clicked because they were on top. Labels encode the old ranking, and a model that reproduces it scores well offline without being better.

Proxy mismatch. nDCG on next-week watches is a proxy for what the business wants: satisfied members who stay subscribed. A model can move the proxy without moving the goal, for example by recommending titles people start but do not enjoy.

User adaptation and novelty effects. Users react to change: a new ranker may get a burst of curiosity clicks that fade, or an initial dip while users adjust (rec13). Offline metrics assume behaviour is fixed.

Funnel and system effects. The ranker's offline gain is measured on a fixed candidate set; online, retrieval, re-ranking, business rules and latency fallbacks all interact with it. A gain at positions the re-ranker overrides does not reach users.

Statistical power. Offline gains are measured on millions of past events with tiny error bars; online effects are often an order of magnitude smaller in relative terms and need large samples to detect. A flat test can be an underpowered test.

The practical response is to treat offline metrics as a filter, not a forecast: they remove clearly bad models and rank candidates for online testing. Track, over many launches, the ratio between offline and online gains for your system; it calibrates expectations and exposes metrics that do not predict anything. Use fast online methods such as interleaving (rec13) to check direction cheaply before full A/B tests.
deep:
Why the log2 discount?

Järvelin and Kekäläinen chose a logarithmic discount because it decays smoothly, models a patient user who may look several results deep, and is easy to compute; the base controls how fast it decays, and log2(rank + 1) has become the convention. Other user models give other metrics. Rank-biased precision assumes the user moves from each result to the next with a fixed persistence probability p and stops otherwise, so position r is reached with probability pr−1; expected reciprocal rank assumes the user stops at the first satisfying result, with satisfaction probability rising with grade, so a highly relevant item early lowers the value of everything after it. These "user model" metrics make assumptions explicit and can be fitted to click logs, which is an argument for preferring them when you can.

The sampled-metric problem in a little more depth

Krichene and Rendle's analysis shows that for a sampled metric the expected value depends on the rank of the held-out item among all items through a smooth function determined by the sample size. With 100 samples out of a million items, an item ranked 50th and one ranked 5,000th in the full catalogue both very likely land at rank 1 among the 100 sampled competitors, so the metric barely distinguishes them; differences in the true top-10 are washed out. They propose corrected estimators that recover the exact metric's expectation from sampled ranks, but recommend avoiding sampled evaluation where possible. For production systems, full-catalogue ranking is usually affordable offline with an ANN index or brute force on GPUs; the cost argument for sampling is weaker than it looks.

Graded labels from implicit feedback

Converting behaviour into grades is a design choice with consequences. Watch fraction thresholds (finished = 2, started = 1), purchase over add-to-cart over click, explicit likes and saves as the top grade: each mapping encodes what the business values, and changing it can reorder models. Two cautions: dwell-time thresholds depend on item length (a 30-second watch is a full song and a fraction of a film), so normalise per item type; and negative signals ("not interested", quick skips) are informative and are lost if every non-positive becomes grade 0. Some teams use negative gains for explicit negative feedback, which nDCG can handle if the ideal ordering is computed accordingly.

Metrics for slates and sessions

Per-item metrics assume each item's value is independent of the others on the page. Real users experience slates: a page with two near-duplicates is worse than nDCG says. Diversity-aware variants such as α-nDCG discount an item's gain when it covers subtopics already covered higher up. For feeds, session-level metrics (time spent, number of satisfied interactions per session, return the next day) capture what per-list metrics cannot, at the cost of being measurable only online or with simulators.

Metrics on a funnel, not a model

Each stage of the funnel (rec1) needs its own metric, and the stages interact. Retrieval is judged by recall at its output depth, the ranker by nDCG at the visible depth on the candidates it actually receives, the re-ranker by diversity and calibration on the final page. A frequent mistake is evaluating a new ranker on the old retrieval's candidates and a new retriever with the old ranker, then shipping both together: the combination was never measured. Another is evaluating the ranker on a fixed candidate set that includes the held-out relevant items by construction, which ignores the chance that retrieval would have missed them; in production, the ranker's ceiling is retrieval's recall. End-to-end offline evaluation, in which the full pipeline produces the list from scratch for each test user and the list is scored, is slower but is the only offline number that corresponds to what users would see. Teams usually run per-stage metrics on every change and the end-to-end evaluation before any A/B test.

Simulators and replay

Between static offline metrics and live experiments sit two intermediate tools. Replay (or rejection-sampling) evaluation uses traffic where the old system chose items at random, for example an exploration slot (rec11): for each logged event, ask whether the new policy would have chosen the same item; if yes, count the outcome, if not, discard the event. Because the logged choice was random, the kept events are an unbiased sample of what the new policy would have experienced, at the cost of discarding most data. User simulators model how users respond to slates and run candidate policies against them; they make long-horizon effects (fatigue, return visits) explorable offline, but are only as good as their behaviour models and are easily over-fitted. Both are used to pre-screen policies, never as a substitute for an online test.

Offline metrics that predict online outcomes

The most useful offline metric is the one whose changes correlate with online changes on your system. Teams with a long history of experiments compute, across past launches, the correlation between each offline metric's delta and the online metric's delta, and retire metrics that never predict anything. This is the same idea as validating a proxy in causal inference: a surrogate metric is only as good as its demonstrated relationship with the outcome.
prod:
The public case: sampled metrics reverse conclusions

In the late 2010s it became common in recommender research, especially in papers on neural sequential recommendation, to evaluate by ranking each user's held-out item against 100 (sometimes 50 or 1,000) randomly sampled items the user had not interacted with, and reporting hit rate@10 and nDCG@10 on that small list. It made evaluation cheap on large catalogues. Krichene and Rendle's KDD 2020 paper "On Sampled Metrics for Item Recommendation" examined the practice formally. Their central finding, in the abstract's words: sampled metrics "are inconsistent with their exact version, in the sense that they do not persist relative statements, e.g., recommender A is better than B, not even in expectation". They also showed that "the smaller the sampling size, the less difference there is between metrics, and for very small sampling size, all metrics collapse to the AUC metric".

The consequence was concrete: published comparisons between recommenders made with sampled metrics could not be trusted to reflect which model was better at the top of a real, full-catalogue list. The paper proposed corrections that estimate the exact metric from sampled results, and recommended avoiding sampled metrics where possible. Follow-up replication work in the community re-evaluated several popular sequential recommenders with full ranking and found some reported gains shrank or disappeared. For a practitioner the lesson is general: the evaluation protocol is part of the metric, and a cheap protocol can produce confident, wrong conclusions.

How evaluation fails in production teams

Metric drift by definition. Two teams report nDCG@10 with different gains, IDCG definitions or treatment of empty users; a dashboard averages them. Pin definitions in a shared library and version them.

Leaky splits. Features computed over the whole dataset (an item's total popularity, including the test period) leak the future into training. Compute features as of the training cut-off.

Average hides harm. A model improves heavy users and degrades new users; the average rises. Slice by user activity and other key segments and set per-slice guardrails.

No uncertainty. Small evaluation sets produce differences within noise that are reported as wins. Bootstrap intervals per metric and paired comparisons per model pair.

Offline-online ratio ignored. Teams keep promising online gains equal to offline gains and keep missing. Track the historical ratio and set expectations from it.

Building the evaluation harness

Mature teams turn all of this into a shared harness rather than per-project notebooks. It owns the splits (fixed, dated, reproducible), the label definitions and gain tables, the metric implementations (with unit tests against hand-worked examples like this lesson's), the baselines (popularity, item-kNN, production), the slices and the bootstrap intervals, and it writes every run to a results store keyed by model version and data snapshot. Two benefits matter most: results from different teams are comparable because they share definitions, and every launch adds a data point to the offline-versus-online history that tells you which metrics predict anything. The harness also runs in CI for model changes, the recommendation-system counterpart of the eval gates in ev12.

What a good offline report contains

The surface and its depth k; label definition and gains; split dates; whether re-consumption is excluded; full-catalogue or sampled ranking (and why); per-user macro averages with bootstrap 95% intervals for recall@k, nDCG@k, MRR or MAP as appropriate; beyond-accuracy metrics (coverage, exposure Gini, intra-list diversity, novelty, calibration KL); slices by user activity, region, device, item age; comparison against production and against simple baselines (popularity, item-kNN) on the same users; and a stated expectation for the online test based on past offline-online ratios.
myths: nDCG is one well-defined number.

It is a family. Linear versus exponential gains, the cut-off k, how the ideal ranking is built (from all relevant items or only those retrieved), and how users with no relevant items are treated all change the value. In this lesson's example the same list scores 0.569 with linear gains and 0.496 with exponential gains. Two papers or two teams reporting nDCG@10 may not be measuring the same thing.
Evaluating against 100 randomly sampled negatives is a cheap, harmless approximation.

Krichene and Rendle (KDD 2020) showed that sampled top-k metrics are inconsistent with their exact versions: they can reverse which of two recommenders is better, even in expectation, and with very few samples all metrics collapse towards AUC. Rank against the full catalogue, or at least use corrected estimators.
Higher accuracy metrics mean users are happier.

Accuracy metrics reward predicting what users would have engaged with anyway, which favours popular items and more of the same. A list can score well while being repetitive, obvious and narrow. Coverage, diversity, novelty and calibration exist because accuracy alone systematically misses these, and users and creators notice.
If the offline metric improves, the online test should show the same improvement.

Offline data is logged from the old system, so it only contains feedback on items the old system chose to show, at the positions it chose. A new model that surfaces different items is evaluated on the wrong evidence. Add metric mismatch, feedback loops and novelty effects, and offline-online disagreement is the normal case, not an anomaly.
MRR and nDCG measure the same thing.

MRR looks only at the first relevant item and ignores everything after it, which suits navigational search with one right answer. nDCG credits every relevant item with a position discount and supports graded relevance, which suits feeds and result pages where several items matter. A change that adds relevant items at ranks 2-5 improves nDCG and leaves MRR unchanged.
lab:
Goal: write a small ranking-metrics library, reproduce the lesson's numbers, and see sampled metrics mislead. Python 3.12, standard library only.

  1. Create rec8_lab.py. Implement precision_at_k, recall_at_k, reciprocal_rank (with a grade threshold), average_precision (dividing by all relevant items), and ndcg_at_k(grades_in_order, all_relevant_grades, k, gain="linear"|"exp").
  2. Check against the lesson: grades 1, 0, 2, 0, 1 with relevant grades {2, 2, 1, 1}: P@5 0.60, R@5 0.75, RR 1.0 (0.33 at threshold 2), AP 0.567, nDCG@5 0.569 (linear) and 0.496 (exponential). Also compute the "IDCG from retrieved only" variant (0.762).
  3. Add novelty(list, popularity) (mean −log2p) and calibration_kl(history_mix, list_mix, alpha=0.01) with smoothing q̃ = (1 − α)q + αp; check the 70/30 example gives about 0.15 for a 9/1 list.
  4. Sampled-metric experiment: simulate a catalogue of 10,000 items and 1,000 users, each with one held-out item. Model A ranks the held-out item at a true rank drawn so that it is often in the top 10 but has a long tail; model B is rarely in the top 10 but almost never terrible (for example A: rank = int(exp(gauss(2.5, 2.0))), B: rank = int(exp(gauss(3.5, 0.5)))), clipped to 1-10,000.
  5. Compute exact hit rate@10 for both. Then compute sampled hit rate@10: for each user, draw 100 random negatives; the held-out item's sampled rank is 1 + the number of sampled negatives whose true rank is better than its rank. Compare which model wins under each protocol.
  6. Bootstrap a 95% interval for the difference in exact nDCG@10 between A and B by resampling users 1,000 times.

What to look for. All of step 2's numbers should match. In the sampled experiment, model A should win on exact hit rate@10 (it often puts the item in the true top 10) while model B, which is consistently "pretty good", should look as good or better under 100-sample evaluation, because against 100 random items being consistently in the top 1% of the catalogue is enough to land at sampled rank 1. That reversal is the Krichene and Rendle finding in miniature.
recap: Ranking metrics are computed per user or per query on the top k of the list, then averaged; the choice of k should match how many items people actually see.
Precision@k is the share of the top k that is relevant; recall@k is the share of all relevant items that appear in the top k.
Reciprocal rank is 1 divided by the rank of the first relevant item; MRR averages it and suits tasks with one right answer.
Average precision averages precision at each rank where a relevant item appears, divided by the number of relevant items; MAP averages it over users or queries.
nDCG discounts each item's gain by log2(rank + 1) and divides by the ideal DCG; in the worked list it is 0.569 with linear gains and 0.496 with exponential gains.

Beyond-accuracy metrics measure what accuracy misses: catalogue coverage, intra-list diversity, novelty as average self-information of recommended items, and calibration as how well the list's mix matches the user's interests.
The evaluation protocol matters as much as the metric: temporal splits, excluding already-consumed items, and ranking against the full catalogue rather than sampled negatives.

Offline gains vanish online because logged data reflects the old system's choices and positions, offline metrics are proxies for long-term goals, users react to change, and systems feed back on their own data.
glossary: Average precision (AP)
For one list, the mean of precision@k taken at each rank k where a relevant item appears, divided by the total number of relevant items.
Calibration (of a recommendation list)
How closely the mix of categories or genres in a list matches the mix in the user's history; measured with a divergence such as KL.
Catalogue coverage
The share of items in the catalogue that appear in at least one user's recommendations over a period.
Cut-off k
The depth at which a metric is computed, such as the top 10 results; items below it are ignored.
DCG (discounted cumulative gain)
The sum over positions of each item's gain divided by log2(position + 1).
Gini coefficient (of exposure)
A measure of how unequally recommendations are spread across items: 0 means every item is shown equally, near 1 means a few items get almost all exposure.
Ideal DCG (IDCG)
The DCG of the best possible ordering of the known relevant items, used to normalise DCG to between 0 and 1.
Intra-list diversity
The average dissimilarity between pairs of items in one recommendation list.
KL divergence
A measure of how one probability distribution differs from another; zero when they are identical.
MAP (mean average precision)
Average precision averaged over all users or queries.
MRR (mean reciprocal rank)
The average over users or queries of 1 divided by the rank of the first relevant item.
nDCG
Normalised discounted cumulative gain: DCG divided by ideal DCG, rewarding relevant items near the top with support for graded relevance.
Novelty
How unfamiliar recommended items are likely to be, often measured as the average of −log2 of each item's popularity.
Off-policy (logged) evaluation
Evaluating a new ranker on data logged while a different ranker was serving, which only contains feedback on what the old ranker showed.
Precision@k
The share of the top k items that are relevant.
Recall@k
The share of all relevant items for the user or query that appear in the top k.
Sampled metric
A metric computed by ranking each relevant item against a small random sample of non-relevant items instead of the full catalogue.
Temporal split
Holding out data after a cut-off time for testing, so the model is evaluated on the future as it would be in deployment.
drill:
Evaluate: two candidate rankers for a podcast app's home screen

The home screen shows a carousel of 8 episodes. Model X (new) and Model Y (production) are compared offline on four weeks of data. Model X: nDCG@50 +7%, hit rate@10 against 100 sampled negatives +9%, catalogue coverage −30%, intra-list diversity −18%. Model Y is unchanged. The team trained on a random 80/20 split of all plays. Leadership wants to ship X next week. What do you say, and what evaluation do you run before an A/B test?

Answer

Problems with the evidence. (1) Depth: the carousel shows 8, but the metrics are at 50 and at 10; neither measures what users see. Use nDCG@8 and recall@8. (2) Sampled hit rate against 100 negatives can reverse model comparisons (Krichene and Rendle); rank against the full episode catalogue. (3) A random split of plays leaks the future and, on a podcast app where people replay the same shows daily, rewards predicting re-listening; use a temporal split and decide whether the carousel's goal is discovery (exclude shows the user already follows) or continuation. (4) Coverage −30% and diversity −18% suggest X gains accuracy by concentrating on popular episodes; that may hurt discovery, creators and long-term engagement. (5) No confidence intervals or slices.

What to run. Rebuild the evaluation: temporal split (train to day 21, test days 22-28); labels graded (listened over 75% = 2, 25-75% = 1, under 25% or skipped = 0); separate evaluations for "continue listening" and "new shows" if those are distinct goals; full-catalogue ranking; nDCG@8, recall@8, MRR; per-user bootstrap intervals and a paired bootstrap for X − Y; slices by user tenure, listening frequency and language. Beyond accuracy: coverage, exposure Gini, share of impressions to the top 1% of shows, novelty, calibration KL across podcast categories, new-show share.

Decision rule. If X's gain survives the corrected protocol at depth 8 with intervals excluding zero, and coverage and diversity losses are moderate or fixable by re-ranking (rec12), run an A/B test with listening minutes per user as primary metric and new-show discovery, diversity and 28-day retention as guardrails, long enough to see past novelty effects (rec13). If the gain disappears under the corrected protocol, it was an artefact of evaluation, not a better model.
qa: E
Define precision@k and recall@k for a recommendation list.

Precision@k is the number of relevant items in the top k divided by k: how much of what we showed was good. Recall@k is the number of relevant items in the top k divided by the total number of relevant items for that user: how much of what was good we showed. For a list of 5 with 3 relevant items and 4 relevant items overall, precision@5 = 0.6 and recall@5 = 0.75.
E
When would you use MRR instead of nDCG?

When there is essentially one right answer and the user stops at it: navigational search, question answering with one correct passage, 'find this exact product'. MRR rewards putting the first relevant item high and ignores the rest. When several items matter or relevance is graded, as in feeds and result pages, nDCG is the better choice.
E
Why normalise DCG?

Because raw DCG depends on how many relevant items a user or query has and how relevant they are; a user with ten relevant items can reach a much higher DCG than one with one. Dividing by the ideal DCG for that user makes every value lie between 0 and 1, so users and queries can be averaged fairly.
M
Compute nDCG@5 and MRR for this list: grades by rank 1, 0, 2, 0, 1, with one more grade-2 item not retrieved.

Discounts for ranks 1-5 are 1, 0.631, 0.5, 0.431, 0.387. With linear gains, DCG = 1 + 0 + 2 × 0.5 + 0 + 1 × 0.387 = 2.387. The ideal list is 2, 2, 1, 1: IDCG = 2 + 1.262 + 0.5 + 0.431 = 4.193, so nDCG@5 = 0.569. With gains 2^g − 1, DCG = 2.887, IDCG = 5.824, nDCG = 0.496. MRR counting any grade above 0 as relevant is 1 (rank 1); counting only grade 2 it is 1/3.

Follow-up: Why does the exponential version score lower? — It gives grade-2 items three times the gain of grade-1 items, so having the best item at rank 3 and missing the other grade-2 item costs more.
M
What is MAP and how does it differ from mean precision@k?

Average precision for one list is the mean of precision@k at every rank where a relevant item appears, divided by the number of relevant items; it rewards putting relevant items early and penalises missing them. Mean precision@k just counts relevant items in the top k, ignoring their order. For the example list, precision at the hits is 1.0, 0.667 and 0.6, so AP = (1.0 + 0.667 + 0.6) / 4 = 0.567 when there are four relevant items, while precision@5 is 0.6.
M
Why are sampled metrics (rank the held-out item among 100 random negatives) problematic?

Ranking against 100 random items is much easier than against the full catalogue, so absolute values are inflated, and worse, Krichene and Rendle showed the sampled versions are inconsistent with the exact ones: they can reverse the order of two models, even in expectation. With very small samples every top-k metric behaves like AUC, which ignores the top-of-list focus that top-k metrics are supposed to provide. Use full ranking where feasible, or their corrected estimators, and never compare papers that used different sampling.
M
How would you measure diversity and novelty of recommendations?

Intra-list diversity: average pairwise dissimilarity (1 − cosine of item embeddings, or different-category rate) within each list, averaged over users. Coverage: share of the catalogue recommended to anyone in a period, and the Gini coefficient of exposure. Novelty: average −log2 of each recommended item's popularity share, so a very popular item contributes little and a niche one a lot. Report these next to accuracy metrics so trade-offs are visible.
M
What is calibration in the sense of Steck's calibrated recommendations?

A user who watches 70% romance and 30% action should get a list that roughly reflects that mix, not 100% romance because romance items have slightly higher predicted scores. Measure it with the KL divergence between the genre distribution of the user's history and that of the recommended list (with a little smoothing so empty genres do not give infinite divergence). Accuracy-optimised lists tend to over-represent the user's main interest and crowd out the minority ones; calibrated re-ranking (rec12) fixes it.
M
How should you split data to evaluate a recommender offline?

By time: train on interactions before a cut-off and test on those after, as in deployment. Random splits leak the future (the model trains on a later interaction to predict an earlier one) and inflate scores. Decide whether re-consumption counts (recommending a show the user watches weekly is easy and usually not the product's goal), restrict test users to those seen in training if the model cannot handle new users, and report results by user-activity bucket.
H
Your new ranker beats production by 4% nDCG@10 offline, but the A/B test is flat. List the most likely reasons and how you'd check each.

One, logged-data bias: offline relevance only exists for items production showed, so a model surfacing different items is under-credited or over-credited; check how often its top 10 contains items with no logged feedback. Two, metric mismatch: nDCG@10 on clicks may not track the online success metric (watch time, retention); check correlation between per-user offline gains and online outcomes. Three, position bias in labels: gains may come from reproducing production's order; compare on randomised or interleaved traffic. Four, train-serve skew: features online differ from those in the offline data. Five, the funnel: candidates online differ from those in the offline set. Six, statistical power: 4% offline may translate to 0.2% online, below detection.

Follow-up: How would you make offline evaluation more predictive? — Counterfactual estimators with logged propensities (rec10), evaluation on exploration traffic, interleaving as a fast online check (rec13), and tracking the historical ratio between offline and online gains to calibrate expectations.
H
Design the evaluation suite for a video recommender before any change can reach an A/B test.

Offline accuracy: recall@500 for retrieval against next-day watches; nDCG@10 and MAP for ranking with graded labels (complete watch 3, partial 1, skip 0), per user, with bootstrap confidence intervals (ev7), on a temporal split, full-catalogue ranking. Beyond accuracy: coverage, Gini of exposure, intra-list diversity, novelty, calibration KL, new-item share. Slices: new versus heavy users, countries, devices, content types. Guardrails: no slice regresses beyond its noise band. Counterfactual estimate of the online metric using logged propensities where available. Only then an A/B test with long-term metrics.
H
When can optimising nDCG make the product worse?

When relevance labels encode short-term engagement and the product needs long-term value: a model that ranks compulsive, clicky content first raises nDCG on click labels and erodes satisfaction and retention. When the list is consumed as a set and nDCG scores items independently, so ten near-duplicates score well. When it narrows exposure to popular items, hurting creators and catalogue health. And when gains improve on easy users while hurting the minority slices. Pair nDCG with beyond-accuracy metrics, satisfaction labels and long-term online metrics.

t: Features and data for ranking: real-time and batch features, log-and-wait, label joins and training/serving skew
sum: The data machinery behind a ranker: the four feature families (user, item, context, user-item cross) and their freshness tiers, windowed counters computed with event time, why ranking systems log features at serving time and wait for labels instead of recomputing them, the joiner that attaches clicks and conversions to impressions (sized for 200,000 impressions per second), attribution windows and delayed conversions, the specific ways training/serving skew appears in ranking, and how ByteDance's Monolith trains on a stream with minute-level parameter sync.
prereq: ml14
Training/serving skew happens when a feature is computed one way for training and another way at serving; logging served features and point-in-time joins prevent it; PSI detects drift.
hd8
A feature store keeps one feature definition with an offline store for training and an online key-value store for millisecond serving, with point-in-time correct training data.
rec6
The ranker uses counters, rates, embeddings, user histories and cross features; its quality depends on those inputs matching between training and serving.
rec1
Computation is split into offline, nearline and online lanes; the request path should mostly read what slower lanes prepared.
why:
A team adds a feature to its video ranker: "how many times was this video clicked in the last hour?". Offline, it is the best feature they have added all year: AUC up half a point. Online, the A/B test is flat. Two weeks of investigation later, the cause is embarrassingly simple. In the training data, the feature had been computed by a batch job the next morning, with complete data, so for each impression it included clicks that arrived after the impression, including, for clicked impressions, the click itself. Online, the same feature came from a streaming counter that lagged by a few minutes and missed late events. The model had learned to read the answer off a feature that would never contain it in production.

Versions of this story are the most common way ranking projects fail, and they rarely involve the model. They involve data: which features exist, how fresh they are, how they are computed, how labels are attached to the right impressions, and whether the numbers the model trained on are the numbers it will see. ml14 introduced training/serving skew and hd8 designed a feature store; this lesson is the ranking-specific deep dive: the families of features rankers use, the freshness tiers and where each is computed, why mature systems log features at serving time and wait for labels rather than recomputing them, how the joiner that builds training data works and what it costs, how delayed outcomes like purchases are labelled, and the particular shapes skew takes in ranking.

The stakes are large. A ranker's quality is bounded by its features, and its offline evaluation is only meaningful if training data matches serving. Several of the "offline gains vanish online" causes from rec8 are, underneath, data problems. And at scale the data path is the expensive part of the system: rec1 and hd3 noted that impression logs dominate the data platform, at tens of terabytes per day.

Interviewers probe this area because it separates people who have run rankers in production from people who have trained models in notebooks. Questions like "how do you make sure the feature the model trained on is the feature it sees?", "how do you attach a purchase that happens four days later to the right impression?" and "what happens to your training data during an outage?" have concrete, experience-based answers, and this lesson aims to give you those answers with the numbers behind them.

The lesson ends with a public case, ByteDance's Monolith system, which takes freshness to its limit: training continuously on a stream and pushing updated embeddings to serving every few minutes, with measurements of what that buys.
primer:
Think of a weather forecaster who predicts tomorrow's rain from today's observations: temperature, pressure, humidity, wind. Imagine two ways of building their training data. In the first, every evening they record the observations exactly as they saw them on their instruments that day, and the next day they note whether it rained. In the second, they skip the recording and, months later, reconstruct "what the observations were" from a weather archive. The archive has been cleaned, corrected and filled in with readings that arrived late. The second dataset looks better, and models trained on it look more accurate, but it describes a world the forecaster never sees at forecast time, with complete, corrected, slightly-later data. Their real forecasts, made from raw instruments, disappoint.

Ranking has the same choice. The model's inputs at serving time are whatever the feature systems returned at that millisecond: possibly stale, possibly missing, possibly computed by a different code path from the training pipeline. Log-and-wait is the first method: record the inputs the model actually saw with each impression, wait for the outcome, and train on that. Recompute-and-join is the second: rebuild features later from the warehouse. Both are used; the first is safer, the second more flexible, and the difference between them is a source of bugs that never raise an error.

The analogy breaks in one useful way. A forecaster's observations do not change because of the forecast. A recommender's data does: what it shows decides what gets clicked, which decides tomorrow's counters and training labels. That feedback loop is rec10's subject; here it matters only because it means the training data is always data the system itself produced, which is one more reason to record exactly what the system did and saw.

It helps to picture the volumes involved, because they drive every design choice that follows. A feed serving 10,000 requests per second, with 20 items per page, produces 200,000 impressions every second. Each impression is a small record: who, what, where on the page, which model, and the few hundred numbers the model looked at. Clicks, watches and purchases trickle in afterwards, seconds to days later, each needing to find its impression among the billions logged that day. The training pipeline is therefore a large, continuous matching problem, and the feature systems are a set of caches and counters that must answer within a few milliseconds for every one of those impressions. Neither is glamorous, and both decide whether the model works.

A final framing before the details: every feature has three versions that should be identical and often are not. There is the feature as defined (a sentence in a design doc, "clicks on this item in the last hour"), the feature as served (whatever the streaming counter returned at that millisecond), and the feature as trained on (whatever ended up in the training table). Most data bugs in ranking are a gap between two of those three, and most of the practices in this lesson exist to close the gaps.

With that picture, the rest of the lesson is about four questions: what features to have, how fresh each must be, how labels get attached to the right impression, and how to make sure training and serving agree.
body:
1. Four families of features

Ranking features fall into four families, and knowing which family a feature belongs to tells you where it can be computed and what it costs.

User features describe the person regardless of candidate: account age, country, language, subscription tier, long-term affinities (share of watch time per category over 90 days), recent history (the last 50 items with watch fractions), and learned user embeddings. They are fetched once per request, usually as one row from a key-value store.

Item features describe the candidate regardless of user: category, creator, duration, upload age, content embeddings from text, image and audio models, and above all engagement statistics: impressions, clicks, completion rate, likes and hides over several time windows. They are the same for every user, so hot items' features can be cached in the ranker's memory.

Context features describe the request: time of day, day of week, device, operating system, network quality, location, the surface (home feed, search, item page), and, in training only, the position the item was shown at (rec10 explains why position is handled specially).

User-item cross features depend on both: how many of this creator's videos the user finished in the last 30 days; whether the user follows the creator; time since the user last engaged with this category; the similarity between the candidate's embedding and the user's recent items. These are often the most predictive features a ranker has, because they directly encode "this person and this kind of thing", and they are the most expensive to serve, because they must be computed per candidate per request. The standard trick: fetch per-user maps once per request (creator → engagement stats, category → stats), then each candidate's cross features are local hash-map lookups.

2. Freshness tiers and where each is computed

Every feature has a freshness requirement, and rec1's three lanes map onto it.

TierExamplesComputedTypical staleness
Staticitem category, duration, creator; content embeddingson ingest, re-run on editnone until the item changes
Batch90-day affinities, 7-day item rates, user embeddingsoffline, daily or hourlyhours to a day
Near-real-timeclicks in the last hour, session history, trending scoresnearline stream processingseconds to minutes
Request-timetime, device, query, crosses from fetched mapsonline, in the requestnone

The design rule is to compute each feature in the slowest lane that meets its need, because faster lanes cost more to build and run, and are harder to make consistent with training. A user's 90-day genre mix moves slowly; computing it per request wastes money. A user's last five clicks move every few seconds; a daily batch makes the feed feel unresponsive. Many features exist in several windows at once (item clicks over 1 hour, 1 day and 7 days), letting the model combine a noisy fresh signal with a stable slow one.

3. Counters and rates, computed correctly

Engagement counters are the backbone of ranking features, and they are full of traps.

Event time versus processing time. A click that happened at 10:00:05 may reach the stream processor at 10:00:40 or, from a phone that was offline, at 14:30. Counting by processing time puts events in the wrong window. Stream processors such as Flink and Kafka Streams support windows by event time, with watermarks that decide how long to wait for late events before closing a window.

As of the impression. In training data, each impression's counters must reflect only events before the impression time. Worked example: an item had 4,000 impressions and 120 clicks in the 24 hours before an impression at 09:00, a click rate of 3.0%. A training pipeline that computes "clicks in the last 24 hours" at midnight, after the fact, includes the next 15 hours: say 500 more impressions and 30 more clicks, giving 150 / 4,500 = 3.3%. Two things went wrong. The feature is systematically fresher than it can ever be at serving time. And, more insidiously, for impressions that were clicked, the counter includes their own click, so clicked impressions have slightly higher counter values than unclicked ones: label leakage. For a popular item the effect per impression is tiny; for a new item with ten impressions, one click moves the rate from 10% to 20%, and the model learns to cheat. Point-in-time correctness (hd8) is the cure for recomputed features; logging is the cure for served ones.

Smoothing. Rates from small counts are noise. A smoothed rate, (clicks + α × prior) / (impressions + α), with a prior such as the category's average rate, keeps new items near the prior until evidence accumulates (rec6 worked one). Feeding both the smoothed rate and the raw impression count lets the model decide how much to trust it.

Exact versus approximate. Counting distinct users per item per window exactly needs memory per user; at scale, approximate structures such as HyperLogLog (distinct counts) and count-min sketches (frequencies) are used. Their error is small and predictable, which is usually fine for features, but must be the same in training and serving.

4. Two ways to build training data

A training example for the ranker is (features as of the impression, labels observed afterwards). There are two ways to get the features.

Recompute-and-join. Store raw events in the warehouse; when building training data, recompute every feature for every impression as of its timestamp with point-in-time logic, and join the labels. Its strength is flexibility: a new feature can be backfilled over months of history and trained on immediately. Its weakness is fidelity: the recomputation is a different code path from serving, run with complete data and today's code, so any difference in logic, defaults, lag or late data becomes skew.

Log-and-wait. At serving time, write the full feature vector the model used, plus the request ID, the item, the position and the model version, to an impression log. Join labels as they arrive. Train on the logged features. Its strength is fidelity: training sees exactly what serving saw, including stale values, missing lookups and defaults, so the model learns to cope with real serving conditions. Its weakness is the wait: a new feature must be logged for days or weeks before there is enough data to train on, and logging every feature for every impression is expensive (next section). Google's Rules of Machine Learning recommends this directly: save the features used at serving time and pipe them into training.

Most mature systems use log-and-wait as the default and allow recomputation for backfilling new features, carefully checked against logged values on the overlap period. hd8's deep dive called this the log-and-train versus compute-and-join trade-off; for rankers, with their fast-moving counters and cross features, logging usually wins.

5. The joiner, sized

The joiner is the job that matches engagement events to the impressions that caused them. Both carry the request ID (and item ID); the joiner holds impressions until their attribution window closes, attaches any events that arrive in time, and emits training examples: positives with their labels, and negatives when the window closes without an event.

Size it for a feed at 10,000 requests per second with 20 impressions per request: 200,000 impressions per second. If each logged feature vector is 1.5 KB compressed, the impression stream is 300 MB/s, about 26 TB per day. To attach clicks within a 30-minute window, the joiner must hold 30 minutes of impressions: 200,000 × 1,800 s × 1.5 KB ≈ 540 GB, spread across the joiner's workers. That is feasible but expensive; a 7-day purchase window would need 7 × 48 = 336 times as much, about 180 TB, which no one holds in memory. Hence the standard design, described in Monolith's paper: keep recent impressions in an in-memory cache, spill older ones to an on-disk key-value store, and when an engagement event arrives, look in the cache first and the disk store second.

Three more details matter. Events arrive out of order, so joins are by ID, not by arrival time. Duplicates happen (retries, double-logged clicks), so the joiner de-duplicates by event ID. And the joiner is a natural place to down-sample negatives (rec6), recording the sampling rate so the model can be re-calibrated, and to drop impressions from bots or internal test accounts.

Storage can be cut further: log full features only for a sample of negatives, or log compact references (feature-store version and keys) for slow-moving features and full values only for fast-moving ones, at the cost of a small recomputation step for the referenced values.

6. Labels with delay

Clicks arrive within seconds; watch completion when the session ends; purchases, subscriptions and churn days or weeks later. Delayed labels force a trade-off between accuracy and freshness. Waiting a full 7-day window before emitting an example gives correct labels for week-old impressions, so the model is always a week behind. Emitting after one day mislabels late conversions as negatives, biasing the model against items whose buyers deliberate longer (expensive items, for example). Chapelle's 2014 work on display advertising modelled this explicitly: learn, alongside the conversion probability, a distribution of the delay between click and conversion, so an impression without a conversion after one day is treated as "probably negative, with some probability of converting later" instead of a firm negative.

A common practical structure: train the fast labels (click, short watch) on fresh data continuously; train slow labels (purchase, 7-day return) on older, complete data; combine heads in the value model (rec6). Each head can have its own window and its own training cadence.

7. The shapes of skew in ranking

Training/serving skew (ml14) is any difference between what the model trained on and what it sees online. In rankers it takes recognisable forms.

Two code paths. A Spark job computes "hours since the user's last visit" in UTC for training; the serving service computes it in the user's local time zone. Every value is off by the zone offset. Logging served values, or sharing one library between batch and serving, removes this class.

Missing values and defaults. Online, a feature-store lookup that times out returns 0; in training data the same feature was never missing, or was missing for different reasons (new users). The model has never seen "0 because of a timeout" and treats it as "user has zero affinity". Log missingness explicitly (a separate "was missing" flag), use the same default everywhere, and monitor missing rates online.

Freshness mismatch. As in the opening story, recomputed counters are complete and current; served counters lag. The model over-trusts fresh counters. Train on logged values, or reproduce serving lag in recomputation.

Self-inclusion. The counter used for an impression includes that impression (or its click), in training but not at serving. Compute "as of just before" the impression.

Embedding versions. Content or user embeddings used as features were refreshed with a new encoder model; the ranker was trained on the old ones. Values are in a different space. Version embeddings and retrain or keep the old encoder until the ranker is retrained.

Population skew. Training data over-represents some traffic (heavy users, one country, desktop), or excludes traffic served by fallbacks (rec1). Not a code bug, but the same symptom: offline metrics that do not hold online.

8. Detecting and preventing skew

Three checks catch most skew. Logged versus recomputed: for a sample of impressions, compare the logged serving features with the training pipeline's values; any feature whose distributions differ systematically is a bug or a lag effect. Distribution monitoring: each feature's online distribution and missing rate versus the latest training data, with a drift statistic such as PSI (ml14) and alerts on sudden changes. Prediction parity: re-score a sample of logged requests offline with the exact served model version and logged features; predictions should match the logged predictions to numerical precision. A mismatch means the offline scoring path (feature transforms, model loading) differs from serving.

Prevention is structural: one feature definition shared by batch and serving (a feature store, hd8), shared transformation code (the same library for normalisation and bucketing), logging served features, explicit missing flags, and versioned embeddings.

9. New features: the cost of log-and-wait

Log-and-wait has one real cost: a brand-new feature has no history in the logs. Teams handle it three ways. Start logging the new feature immediately in production (even before the model uses it) and wait one or two weeks before training on it; slow but safe. Backfill it by recomputation over months of history to experiment quickly, then validate the backfill against the logged values on the overlap and, if they differ, train the production model only on logged data. Or "shadow log": compute the feature in serving, log it, but do not feed it to the model, so the data accumulates while experiments run. A feature-request process that starts logging early saves weeks on every model iteration.

10. Sequence features and how to log them

The strongest modern ranking signal is the user's recent behaviour sequence: the last 50 to several thousand items they interacted with, each with an action type, a timestamp and sometimes a duration (rec6's target attention and sequence models consume it). Sequences raise their own data questions. Logging cost: writing a 1,000-event history with every impression would multiply log volume many times. The usual answer is to log a reference (user ID and a sequence version or timestamp) and store the sequences once per user in a time-versioned store from which training reconstructs "the sequence as of the impression". This is recomputation, so it must be checked against what serving fetched. Freshness: the serving sequence comes from a nearline store that may lag by seconds; training must reproduce that lag or the model learns to rely on the very latest event, which serving sometimes lacks. Leakage: the sequence as of the impression must exclude the impression's own outcome; an off-by-one in a timestamp comparison silently includes it.

11. Choosing, pruning and paying for features

Features are not free. Each one costs storage in the logs, a lookup or computation at serving time, a pipeline to keep it fresh and an on-call burden when it breaks. Mature teams periodically prune: measure each feature's contribution (by ablation, retraining without it, or with importance scores from the model, which GBDTs give directly and which permutation tests give for neural models), and remove features whose contribution is within noise. Facebook's 2014 ads paper reported that a small fraction of features carried most of the model's accuracy, a common pattern. Also prune for robustness: a feature with marginal accuracy value and a history of outages is a net negative.

When adding a feature, the questions to answer up front are: which lane computes it (rec1), how fresh it must be, what its value is when the lookup fails, whether it is logged at serving, how it is computed point-in-time for any backfill, and who owns it. A feature that cannot answer those questions should not reach production, however good it looks in a notebook.
deep:
Why logged features make models robust to serving failures

Logged data contains the system's real imperfections: features that were missing because a store timed out, counters that lagged during an incident, defaults for new users. A model trained on it learns how much to trust each feature under those conditions. A model trained on clean recomputed data has never seen a timeout default and can misbehave badly during the next incident, exactly when you would want it to degrade gracefully. This is one reason to mark degraded requests explicitly (rec1): you want the model to learn from realistic data, but not to treat an outage day as normal behaviour.

Point-in-time joins at scale

Recomputing features as of millions of impression timestamps is an "as-of join": for each impression at time t, find the latest feature value with timestamp ≤ t (and, for availability-time correctness, the latest value that was actually available to serving by t, hd8). Done naively it is quadratic; done well it sorts both sides by entity and time and merges them in one pass. Feature-store tools (Feast, Tecton, the platforms at large companies) implement this. The subtle part is the timestamp to use: the time the underlying event happened, the time the feature value was computed, or the time it reached the online store. Only the last reproduces what serving could have seen.

Negative sampling and its bookkeeping

Down-sampling negatives in the joiner (rec6) saves storage and training time but changes the label rate, so the sampling rate must travel with each example for re-calibration and for any weighted metric. If different surfaces or time periods use different rates, store the rate per example, not as a global constant. A subtle bias appears if sampling depends on anything correlated with features (for example, keeping all negatives for new users and 5% for others): the model learns a distorted base rate per segment unless each example is weighted by the inverse of its sampling probability.

Expiring and filtering embeddings

Online-trained models face an ever-growing set of IDs. Monolith's approach: a collisionless hash table (cuckoo hashing) for embeddings, so different IDs never share a row; frequency filtering, so an ID gets an embedding only after it has appeared a minimum number of times (rare IDs would not learn anything useful and would waste memory); and expiry, so an ID inactive for a configured period is evicted. These are the online counterparts of the hashing and thresholds in rec6, and they turn "memory grows forever" into a tunable steady state.

Fresh features versus fresh models

There are two ways to react quickly to change: fresh features (the model is a day old, but its inputs include the last hour's counters and the user's last five minutes) and fresh parameters (the model itself updates every few minutes). Fresh features capture changes the model already knows how to interpret ("this video is suddenly popular"); fresh parameters capture things it has never seen (a brand-new item's ID embedding, a new trend's pattern). Most systems get most of the value from fresh features and daily or hourly retraining; continuous training pays off where new IDs dominate, such as short video and ads.

Label quality: what counts as an engagement

Labels look objective ("clicked: yes") and are full of judgement calls. Accidental taps on mobile, especially near scroll gestures, produce clicks followed by an immediate back; many teams drop or down-weight clicks with dwell under a couple of seconds. Bots and scrapers generate impressions and clicks with no human behind them and must be filtered before joining, or they teach the model their patterns. Autoplay makes "watched" ambiguous: a video that played in the background for 30 seconds while the user scrolled past was not chosen. Repeated impressions of the same item to the same user (the user scrolled past it three times) need a policy: one example per impression, or de-duplicated per session. Each of these choices changes the label distribution and therefore the model, so they should be written down, versioned with the training data and changed only with an experiment, exactly like model changes.

Data volume as a design variable

At 26 TB of impression logs per day, retention is a cost decision. Thirty days of full logs is nearly 800 TB. Common choices: keep full feature logs for a few weeks, keep down-sampled negatives longer, aggregate older data into per-user and per-item statistics, and keep a small uniformly sampled slice indefinitely for long-term studies and reproducing old experiments. The training window itself is a modelling choice: more history helps rare items and slow trends, while recent data reflects current behaviour; many rankers weight recent days more.
prod:
The public case: Monolith, ByteDance's real-time training system

Monolith, described by ByteDance engineers at the ORSUM workshop of RecSys 2022 and used in the BytePlus Recommend product, is a public example of pushing feature and model freshness to their limits. The authors' motivation: recommendation data is mostly sparse IDs whose population changes constantly, and user interests shift fast, so a model that is hours old is already behind.

The data path is the one this lesson describes, made real-time. User actions (clicks, likes, conversions) go to one Kafka queue and the features used at serving go to another; a Flink streaming job acts as the online joiner, pairing actions with features by a unique request key, because the two streams arrive without time-order guarantees. Because some actions arrive days later ("a user may take a few days before they decide to buy an item they were presented days ago"), the joiner keeps recent features in an in-memory cache and spills older ones to an on-disk key-value store, looking in the cache first and the disk store on a miss. Joined examples go through negative sampling into a training-example queue that feeds both batch training (to bootstrap or change architecture) and online training.

On the model side, embeddings live in a collisionless cuckoo hash table with frequency filtering and expiry. During online training, the system tracks which IDs were updated since the last sync and pushes only those sparse parameters from the training parameter servers to the serving ones at a minute-level interval; dense parameters, which change slowly, are synced less often. Parameter servers are snapshotted daily; the authors argue that losing up to a day of updates on one failed server among many is a negligible loss.

Their measurements make the freshness argument concrete. On the public Criteo display-ads dataset, simulating online training, average online-serving AUC rose as the parameter sync interval shortened: 79.66 at 5 hours, 79.78 at 1 hour and 79.80 at 30 minutes, against about 79.4 for batch training. They also report a live A/B experiment on an ads model in which online training outperformed batch training on every day of the test. The case shows both what freshness buys and what it costs: streaming joins, late-event storage, parameter synchronisation and fault tolerance are all needed before a model can learn from what happened ten minutes ago.

How the data path fails in production

Silent logging loss. A client release stops sending one engagement event type (say, likes on one platform). The like head's label rate drops by a third; the model learns that likes are rarer and down-weights likeable content. Monitor label rates per head, per platform and per app version, with alerts on step changes.

Joiner backlog. The joiner falls behind during a traffic spike; impressions age out of the in-memory window before their clicks arrive and are emitted as negatives. The training data's click rate dips for exactly the busiest hours. Monitor joiner lag and the share of positives arriving after window close.

Feature outage baked into training. A feature service returns defaults for six hours; logged data faithfully records them; the next model learns that the default value predicts low engagement. Mark degraded requests and exclude or down-weight them.

Backfill mismatch. A new feature is backfilled by recomputation and trained on; online, the served values differ (lag, different source). The offline gain does not appear. Validate backfills against logged values before training a production model on them.

Clock problems. Device clocks are wrong; event-time windows put events in the future or far past. Use server receipt time as a sanity bound and clamp outliers.
