What to monitor

Per feature: online missing rate, distribution versus training (quantiles or PSI), freshness (age of the newest data behind the value). Logging: impressions logged versus served (they should match), bytes per impression, schema changes. Joiner: lag, cache hit rate, examples emitted per minute, label rates per head, share of late events. Training data: example count per hour, positive rate per head, sampling rates recorded. Parity: daily logged-versus-recomputed comparison for a sample, and offline-versus-online prediction match for re-scored requests.
myths: A feature store solves training/serving skew.

A feature store gives one definition and point-in-time joins for features it manages, which removes a large class of bugs. It does not cover features computed inside the serving code (request context, candidate-dependent crosses), defaults applied differently when a lookup fails, embeddings served from a different model version, or counters whose update lag differs online. Logging the exact feature values the model saw at serving time is still the most reliable defence.
Recomputing features later for training is equivalent to logging them.

Recomputation reproduces what the feature would be under today's code and data, not what the model saw. Counters may include events that arrived late, lookups may succeed now that failed then, a bug fixed last week changes historical values, and an item's metadata may have been edited. Log-and-wait records the served values, at the cost of waiting for new features to accumulate history before they can be trained on.
Fresher features are always better.

Freshness costs infrastructure, and some features are better smoothed: a click rate over the last minute is mostly noise for most items. The right window depends on how fast the underlying quantity changes and how much data arrives per window. Typical rankers combine several windows (1 hour, 1 day, 7 days, 90 days) and let the model weigh them.
A missing label means a negative example.

For delayed outcomes such as purchases or subscriptions, an impression without a conversion yet may still convert in a few days. Training on it as a negative too early teaches the model to under-predict conversions, especially for items whose buyers take longer to decide. Attribution windows, waiting periods and delayed-feedback corrections exist for this.
Online learning is just batch training run more often.

Training continuously on a stream changes the engineering: labels must be joined in real time, late events handled, negatives sampled consistently, parameters synchronised to serving without pauses, and bad data can reach the live model within minutes. Monolith's design (a streaming joiner with an on-disk store for late actions, minute-level sparse parameter sync, daily snapshots) shows how much machinery it takes.
lab:
Goal: build a toy event stream, compute counters correctly and incorrectly, join labels with a window, and watch leakage inflate offline performance. Python 3.12, standard library only.

  1. Create rec9_lab.py. Simulate one day of a feed: 50 items with hidden true click probabilities between 1% and 10%, and 100,000 impressions at random times across 24 hours, each assigned to an item in proportion to its popularity. Each impression is clicked with its item's probability; the click arrives 0-300 seconds later (uniform), and 5% of clicks arrive 1-3 hours late.
  2. For each impression, compute three versions of "item click rate in the previous 6 hours": correct (events with event time strictly before the impression), lagged (correct but ignoring events in the last 5 minutes, as a stream with lag would), and leaky (all events in the 6 hours before the impression plus the 6 hours after, including its own click).
  3. Join labels with a 30-minute attribution window by impression ID; count how many true clicks become negatives because they arrived late.
  4. Train a one-feature logistic regression (by SGD) on the first 18 hours with each counter version, and evaluate log loss on the last 6 hours using the lagged counter (what serving would have).
  5. Print the training log loss and the "serving" log loss for each version.
  6. Repeat with items that have only 20-50 impressions per day (new items) and compare the size of the leakage effect.

What to look for. The leaky version should look best on training data and do worst when evaluated with serving-time features, and the gap should be much larger for low-traffic items, where one click moves the rate a lot. The lagged version trained and evaluated consistently should be close to the correct version. The 30-minute window should turn the late-arriving 5% of clicks into negatives, a small, measurable label bias.
recap: Ranking features fall into four families: user, item, context and user-item cross features; crosses are usually the most predictive and the most expensive to serve.
Features have freshness tiers: static metadata, daily batch aggregates, near-real-time streaming counters and request-time context, each computed in the slowest lane that meets its need.
Counters and rates must be computed with event time and as of the moment of the impression, or they leak the future into training.
Log-and-wait means logging the feature values the model saw at serving time with each impression and waiting for labels, so training uses exactly the served inputs.

A joiner attaches engagement events to impressions by request ID within an attribution window; at 200,000 impressions per second with 1.5 KB of features each, holding 30 minutes in memory needs about 540 GB, which is why late events go to an on-disk store.
Delayed outcomes such as purchases need longer windows and corrections, because an impression without a conversion yet is not yet a negative.

Training/serving skew in ranking appears as different code paths, different defaults for missing values, counters with different lag, embedding version mismatch and features that include the current impression.

Skew is caught by comparing logged serving features with recomputed or expected values, monitoring feature distributions and missing rates, and checking that offline and online predictions match on the same requests.

Monolith trains continuously from Kafka through a Flink joiner and pushes updated sparse embeddings to serving every few minutes; on Criteo data, shorter sync intervals gave higher online AUC (79.66 at 5 hours, 79.80 at 30 minutes).
glossary: Attribution window
The time after an impression during which an engagement event is credited to it, such as 30 minutes for a click or 7 days for a purchase.
Context features
Features of the request rather than the user or item: time, device, network, location, page, position.
Cross features (user-item)
Features that depend on both the user and the candidate, such as the user's past watch rate for this creator.
Delayed feedback
Outcomes, such as conversions, that arrive long after the impression, so recent impressions have incomplete labels.
Event time
The time an event actually happened, as opposed to the time the system processed it.
Feature freshness
How old the data behind a feature value is at the moment it is used.
Feature logging
Recording, with each impression, the exact feature values the model used to score it.
Joiner
The batch or streaming job that matches engagement events to the impressions that caused them and emits training examples.
Label leakage
Information about the label reaching the features, for example a counter that already includes the click being predicted.
Log-and-wait
Building training data from logged serving features and waiting for labels, rather than recomputing features afterwards.
Online training
Updating a model continuously from a stream of fresh training examples while it serves.
Point-in-time correctness
Computing each training example's features only from data available at the example's timestamp.
Request ID
A unique identifier for one recommendation request, logged with impressions and engagement events so they can be joined.
Smoothed rate
A ratio such as click-through rate stabilised by a prior, (clicks + α·prior) / (impressions + α), so items with few impressions do not get extreme values.
Training/serving skew
Any difference between the feature values or data distribution used in training and those seen at serving.
Windowed counter
A count of events over a sliding or tumbling time window, such as an item's clicks in the last hour.
drill:
Diagnose: a conversion model that gets worse every Monday

An e-commerce ranker predicts P(purchase within 7 days | impression) and is retrained daily on impressions from 8 to 1 days ago, joined with purchases. Features are recomputed from the warehouse at training time. The team notices the model's calibration is poor on Mondays (it under-predicts purchases by about 15%), and that items with long consideration times (furniture, electronics) are consistently under-ranked. A new feature, "item add-to-cart rate in the last hour", gave +0.4% AUC offline but nothing online. Explain the likely causes and redesign the data path.

Answer

Causes. (1) Truncated attribution: training on impressions from 8 to 1 days ago with a 7-day purchase label means impressions from 1-6 days ago have incomplete windows; recent impressions' late purchases are labelled negative. Long-consideration categories are hit hardest, so they are under-predicted and under-ranked. (2) The Monday effect: weekend browsing converts later (people buy on Monday or Tuesday), so the most recent days in Monday's training run, the weekend impressions, are the most truncated; the model trained on Monday learns an artificially low rate. (3) The add-to-cart feature: recomputed from the warehouse with complete data, including events after the impression and possibly the user's own add-to-cart, while the serving value comes from a lagging stream. That is leakage plus freshness skew, so the offline gain was not real.

Redesign. Log served features with each impression (request ID, item, position, model version, full feature vector) and train on logged values; backfill new features only for experiments, validated against logged values. Labels: train the purchase head only on impressions whose 7-day window has closed (8-14 days old), and add a fast head for add-to-cart on fresh data; combine both in the value model. Alternatively, use a delayed-feedback model that learns the conversion-delay distribution so recent impressions count as partial negatives. Compute counters as of the impression, with the same lag as serving. Monitor calibration per category and per weekday, label completeness per day, and logged-versus-recomputed differences for every feature.

Check it worked. Calibration ratio (predicted / observed) near 1 for every weekday and category on a held-out week; long-consideration categories' share of impressions back to their historical level; any new feature's offline gain measured on logged values before an A/B test.
qa: E
Name the main families of ranking features with an example of each.

User features: tenure, country, long-term category affinities, recent history. Item features: category, creator, age, content embeddings, click and completion rates. Context features: time of day, device, network, the page and position. User-item cross features: how often this user engaged with this creator, similarity between the item and the user's recent items. Crosses tend to be the most predictive and must be computed per candidate per request.
E
What is log-and-wait?

At serving time, the system logs every feature value the model used, together with the impression and a request ID. It then waits for engagement events (clicks, watches, purchases) to arrive, joins them to the logged impressions, and trains on the result. Training therefore uses exactly the inputs the model saw, avoiding skew from recomputation; the cost is that a new feature can only be trained on after it has been logged for a while.
E
Why must counters be computed as of the impression time?

Because otherwise they contain the future. An item's 'clicks in the last 24 hours' computed at training time, after the fact, may include the very click being predicted and clicks that happened after the impression; the model learns to rely on information it will not have at serving, looks excellent offline and disappoints online.
M
Show with numbers how a leaky counter inflates a feature.

An item had 4,000 impressions and 120 clicks in the 24 hours before an impression: CTR 3.0%. If the training pipeline recomputes the counter at the end of the day, it includes the next 12 hours, say 500 more impressions and 30 more clicks, among them the click on this impression: (120 + 30) / (4,000 + 500) = 3.3%. Worse, for impressions that were clicked the counter is systematically higher than for those that were not, which is pure label leakage that the model happily exploits.
M
Size the streaming joiner for 10,000 requests per second with 20 impressions each.

That is 200,000 impressions per second. With 1.5 KB of logged features each, the stream is 300 MB/s, about 26 TB per day before compression. Holding impressions for a 30-minute click window in memory takes 200,000 × 1,800 × 1.5 KB ≈ 540 GB across the joiner fleet; feasible but costly, and a 7-day purchase window is impossible in memory. So keep a short window in memory, spill older impressions to an on-disk key-value store keyed by request ID (as Monolith does), and emit negatives when windows close.
Follow-up: When do you emit a negative? — When the attribution window closes without a positive; for long windows, emit a provisional negative early and correct later, or use delayed-feedback models.
M
What is training/serving skew in a ranker, concretely? Give three causes.

It is any difference between what the model saw in training and what it sees online. Causes: two code paths compute the same feature (a Spark job for training, a Java service for serving) with subtle differences such as time zones or tokenisation; a lookup that fails online returns a default that differs from the training data's default or from its natural missing rate; counters are fresher in training data (computed after the fact) than online (lagging minutes behind a stream); an embedding table at serving is from a different model version than the one used to build training features.
M
How do you detect skew?

Compare, for a sample of requests, the features logged at serving with features recomputed by the training pipeline; any systematic difference is skew. Monitor each feature's distribution and missing rate online versus in the latest training data (PSI or simple quantile comparisons, ml14). Re-score logged requests offline with the served model version and check that predictions match the logged predictions. Alert on sudden changes in any of these.
M
How should conversions with a 7-day delay be handled in training?

Options: wait the full window before labelling (accurate but the model trains on week-old data); label after a shorter window and accept that some positives are mislabelled negatives (biased, faster); or model the delay explicitly, training a delay distribution alongside the conversion model so that recent unconverted impressions count as partial negatives. Many systems also train a fast proxy (click, add-to-cart) on fresh data and the slow label on older data, combining them in the value model.
M
What features belong in the online path versus precomputed?

Precompute anything that depends only on the user or only on the item and changes slowly: long-term affinities, item metadata and embeddings, daily aggregates. Compute nearline anything that must reflect minutes-old behaviour: session history, counters by hour. Compute online only what depends on the request: context, and user-item crosses derived by looking up the candidate in per-user maps fetched once per request. The goal is that serving does lookups and arithmetic, not aggregation.
H
Design the data pipeline for a feed ranker that must react to the last five minutes of behaviour.

Events (impressions, clicks, watch progress, likes) go to a log stream partitioned by user. A streaming job maintains per-user session state (last 50 items with watch fractions, categories in the last 30 minutes) in a low-latency key-value store, and per-item counters with event-time windows (1 hour and 24 hours, updated every few seconds) in another. At request time the ranker fetches one user row and per-item counters for candidates (hot items cached in-process). Every impression logs its full feature vector and request ID. A streaming joiner attaches clicks within 30 minutes and watch completion when sessions close, writing training examples to a stream that feeds continuous training, with daily batch backfills for long-window labels.

Follow-up: How do you protect the model from a bad stream? — Validate example volumes and label rates per hour, quarantine anomalous windows, gate checkpoint promotion on held-out metrics, and keep the ability to roll back.
H
Your new feature improves offline AUC by 0.5% but the online test is neutral. The feature is 'item clicks in the last hour'. What do you suspect?

Skew between offline and online values of the feature. Offline it was probably computed by a batch job with complete data, possibly including events after the impression (leakage) and with no processing lag; online it comes from a stream that lags by minutes and may miss late events, so it is systematically lower and noisier, especially for fresh items where it matters most. Check by comparing logged online values with the offline ones for the same impressions. Fix by training on logged values only (log-and-wait) or by reproducing the stream's lag in the offline computation.
H
When is online (continuous) training worth its complexity?

When the data distribution changes on a timescale of hours: news, short video, ads, trending content, many new items per hour whose ID embeddings must be learned quickly. Monolith's Criteo experiment showed online AUC improving with shorter parameter sync intervals, and Facebook's 2014 ads work measured about 1% better normalised entropy from daily versus weekly retraining. For catalogues that change slowly (books, long-form films), daily batch training plus fresh features captures most of the value with much less risk.
refs: Monolith: Real Time Recommendation System With Collisionless Embedding Table (Liu et al., ByteDance, ORSUM@RecSys 2022)

The public case: Kafka action and feature logs joined by a Flink online joiner with an on-disk store for late actions, collisionless cuckoo-hash embedding tables with expiry and frequency filtering, minute-level sparse parameter sync, and sync-interval experiments on Criteo.
Practical Lessons from Predicting Clicks on Ads at Facebook (He et al., 2014)
Data freshness (daily versus weekly retraining), an online joiner, negative down-sampling and the value of historical versus contextual features.
Rules of Machine Learning (Martin Zinkevich, Google)
Rules on training/serving skew, logging features at serving time and reusing code between training and serving.
Modeling Delayed Feedback in Display Advertising (Chapelle, KDD 2014)
A conversion model that jointly learns the delay distribution so recent unconverted clicks are not treated as firm negatives.
How an open-source feature store builds point-in-time correct training data from event timestamps.

t: Biases and feedback loops: position, selection and popularity bias, inverse propensity weighting and counterfactual evaluation
sum: Why a recommender's own data lies to it: position bias and the examination model, selection (exposure) bias and data missing not at random, popularity bias and rich-get-richer loops, inverse propensity weighting worked with position click-through rates, how propensities are estimated by randomised swaps, unbiased learning to rank (Joachims et al.), counterfactual evaluation of a new policy with IPS and self-normalised IPS worked on six logged events, and what is and is not known about filter bubbles.
prereq: rec7
Learning-to-rank trains on query groups with pairwise or listwise losses; clicks as labels are biased by position and need correction.
rec8
Offline metrics are computed on data logged from the old system, which only contains feedback on what it showed; that is one main reason offline gains vanish online.
rec6
A ranker can learn position with a separate shallow tower during training and drop it at serving.
ml16
An A/B test randomises users between variants so that the difference in outcomes is caused by the variant, not by who chose it.
why:
A news app ranks articles by a click model. Every morning, the top article on the home screen gets 10% of visitors to click it; the article in fifth place gets 2%. The team trains tomorrow's model on today's clicks, and tomorrow's model, unsurprisingly, learns that the articles that were at the top are the good ones. It puts them, or ones like them, at the top again. The clicks confirm it. After a few months, an editor notices that a certain kind of article, long investigative pieces, has almost disappeared from the top three, even though readers who open them spend twelve minutes reading. They were never placed high enough to be clicked enough to be placed high.

That is the central problem of this lesson: a recommender learns from data that it produced itself. What users clicked depends on what was shown, where it was shown and to whom. So the data contains the system's own past decisions mixed in with users' real preferences, and a model trained naively on it learns both, unable to tell them apart. This produces several named biases. Position bias: things higher on the page get more attention. Selection or exposure bias: things never shown have no data at all. Popularity bias: already-popular items get more exposure and so look even more popular. Together they form feedback loops that can entrench the old system, starve new and niche items, and, some worry, narrow what users see.

The good news is that the tools to separate preferences from the system's own influence are well understood, borrowed from causal inference and statistics. If you know, or can estimate, the probability with which the system showed each item at each position, you can reweight the data so that it behaves like data from a randomised experiment. That idea, inverse propensity weighting, powers unbiased learning to rank and counterfactual evaluation: estimating offline how a new ranker would have performed, using logs from the old one.

This lesson covers each bias with its mechanism, works inverse propensity weighting with real position click-through rates, shows how propensities are measured with randomised swaps, follows Joachims and colleagues' unbiased learning to rank from theory to a live search engine, computes counterfactual estimates (IPS and self-normalised IPS) by hand on six logged events, and ends with popularity bias, feedback loops and the honest state of the evidence on filter bubbles. Exploration, which generates the data these corrections need, is rec11's subject.
primer:
Imagine judging which restaurants in a city are best by counting how many diners each has. The restaurants on the main square are always full; the ones down side streets are half empty. Does that mean the square's restaurants are better? Partly, perhaps, but mostly they are easier to see. Tourists walk past them first. If you wanted to know which restaurants diners actually prefer, you would compare how many people choose a restaurant given that they walked past it. A side-street restaurant that only 100 people pass and 30 of them enter is more appealing than a square restaurant that 2,000 pass and 300 enter.

A recommender's page is a city where the top positions are the main square. Clicks per impression are like diners per restaurant: they mix appeal with visibility. The examination hypothesis makes the split precise: a user clicks an item only if they look at it (examine it) and like what they see, so

P(click) = P(examined | position) × P(clicked | examined, item)

The first factor is about the page; the second is about the item. To learn about items, divide out the first factor. That is inverse propensity weighting: count each click as worth 1 / P(examined) clicks, so a click on position 6, where only 20% of users look, counts five times as much as one on position 1, where everyone looks.

The analogy breaks, usefully, in two places. In a city you can count passers-by; on a page you cannot directly observe whether a user examined position 4. Examination probabilities must be estimated, usually by running small randomised experiments that move items between positions. And a city's restaurants do not move; a recommender rearranges the page for every request based on its beliefs, which is why its data is so entangled with those beliefs. Breaking the entanglement requires the system to deliberately add some randomness and record the probabilities, the theme that connects this lesson to exploration in rec11.

Why not simply run an A/B test for every question? Because experiments are slow and scarce: each one takes weeks of traffic and answers one question about one change. Debiasing logged data lets a team learn from all the traffic it already serves, and counterfactual evaluation lets it screen dozens of candidate models offline, sending only the promising ones to the expensive online test. The two are complements: randomised experiments give unbiased answers to few questions; propensity-corrected logs give approximately unbiased answers to many.

One sentence summary to carry through the lesson: logged data tells you what happened under the old policy; to learn what would happen under a new one, you need to know how likely the old policy was to produce each thing you observed. That likelihood is the propensity, and almost every technique below is a way to estimate it or use it.
body:
1. The loop: why recommender data is not like other data

Most supervised learning assumes training examples are drawn independently from the same distribution as future data. Recommender data violates this in a specific way. The system chooses which items to show (the action), in what order, to which users (the context), and only then observes outcomes (the reward: click, watch, purchase). The probability distribution over actions given context is the logging policy. Every logged example is therefore (context, action chosen by the logging policy, reward), and the reward is only observed for the action that was taken.

This is the structure of a bandit problem (rec11 builds on it): you see the outcome of the arm you pulled, never of the arms you did not. Three consequences follow. Outcomes depend on presentation (position, layout), not only on the item. The distribution of items in the data is set by the logging policy, not by users. And the next model is trained on data from this one, so its errors and preferences propagate. Each named bias below is one of these consequences.

2. Position bias and the examination model

Position bias is the best measured of the biases. Joachims and colleagues' 2005 eye-tracking and click studies of web search found that users scan results largely from the top down, look at the first one or two results far more than lower ones, and click the top result much more often even when the order of the top two results is secretly swapped. The click on the top result is partly a vote for relevance and partly a reflection of trust in the ranking and of attention.

The examination model (also called the position-based model) formalises it. For an item i shown at position k:

P(click | i, k) = p_k × r_i

where pk = P(examined | position k) is the position propensity, the same for every item, and ri = P(click | examined, item i) is the item's relevance-driven click probability. Propensities are usually expressed relative to position 1 (p1 = 1). The model is a simplification: in reality examination also depends on the items above (a great result at position 1 means fewer people look further, which the "cascade" model captures), on layout (grids, carousels, autoplay) and on device. But the position-based model is the workhorse for correction, and it is often good enough.

Worked example. Use illustrative propensities p = (1.0, 0.6, 0.4, 0.3, 0.25, 0.2) for positions 1-6. Item A was shown 10,000 times at position 1 and clicked 800 times: raw click rate 8%. Item B was shown 10,000 times at position 4 and clicked 300 times: raw 3%. A naive model concludes A is far better. Under the examination model, A's relevance-driven rate is 800 / (10,000 × 1.0) = 8%, and B's is 300 / (10,000 × 0.3) = 10%. B is the more appealing item; it was handicapped by being shown where fewer people look. Equivalently, each of B's clicks is worth 1/0.3 = 3.33 "examined-and-clicked" events, and each of A's is worth 1.

This is inverse propensity weighting (IPW). In training, every click (or every example) is weighted by 1/pk for the position k it was shown at. In expectation, the weighted click count for an item equals the number of clicks it would have received if every impression had been examined, which is proportional to ri, its relevance.

The cost: variance. B's estimate rests effectively on 10,000 × 0.3 = 3,000 examinations, not 10,000, so it is noisier. At position 20 with a propensity of 0.1, each click gets weight 10, and a handful of lucky clicks can swing an item's estimate. Practical systems clip weights at a maximum (for example 1/p ≤ 10), which introduces a little bias but bounds the variance.

3. Estimating propensities with randomised interventions

We cannot see examination, so propensities are estimated from experiments in which an item's relevance is held fixed and only its position changes. The cleanest is the swap intervention. On a small share of traffic, take the ranker's top item and swap it with the item at a random position r. Because the same item (with the same relevance) now appears at r instead of 1, the ratio of its click rate at r to its click rate at 1 estimates pr/p1: relevance cancels out. Average over many queries and items.

Joachims, Swaminathan and Schnabel did exactly this for their live experiment: for 7 days, before presenting each ranking, they swapped the top-ranked document with the document at a uniformly random rank j from 1 to 21, and used the ratio of click rates to estimate pj/p1, smoothing the noisy estimates by interpolating with overall click rates by position. The resulting propensities decayed with rank, with the smallest around 0.12.

Swapping costs some user experience (a worse result at the top for some users), so it runs on a small share of traffic for a limited time. Alternatives reduce the cost. RandPair-style interventions swap only adjacent or nearby pairs, a smaller harm. Intervention harvesting uses naturally occurring variation: the same item appears at different positions for the same query across different rankers (A/B test arms) or days, which acts like a free randomisation when the variation is unrelated to the item's relevance. Click models fit examination and relevance parameters jointly to logs with repeated queries. And neural approaches learn a position tower jointly with the ranker: YouTube's multi-task ranker (rec6) added a shallow tower fed with position and device features whose output is added to the main logit during training, then dropped at serving, so the main tower is trained as if positions were equal.

4. Unbiased learning to rank

Combine the pieces and you can train a ranker on clicks without inheriting position bias. Joachims and colleagues (WSDM 2017) set this up as counterfactual empirical risk minimisation. Imagine the loss you would compute if you knew true relevance: for each query, a rank-based loss summed over the relevant documents. With clicks you only see some relevant documents, those that were examined. But if each clicked document's contribution is divided by the propensity of the position where it was shown, the expected value of this propensity-weighted loss equals the loss with full relevance information. Minimising it learns a ranker for relevance, not for the old presentation order, without needing queries to repeat (unlike click models) and without randomising every ranking.

They implemented it as a propensity-weighted ranking SVM (a pairwise linear ranker, close in spirit to RankNet in rec7, with the pairwise loss weighted by 1/p of the clicked document's position). On synthetic click data generated from the Yahoo! LTR dataset, it recovered most of the quality of training on true labels, and degraded gracefully when propensities were misspecified. On a live search engine for scientific articles, trained on 21 days of clicks under the hand-tuned production ranker with propensities from the 7-day swap experiment, it was compared using interleaving (rec13): against production it won on 87 queries, lost on 48 and tied on 83; against a naive click-trained ranking SVM it won 95, lost 60, tied 102. Both differences were statistically significant.

The same correction applies to any learning-to-rank loss: LambdaMART (rec7) with propensity-weighted lambdas, neural rankers with weighted softmax losses. XGBoost's learning-to-rank tutorial, for instance, includes position-debiasing options for click data.

5. Selection bias: what was never shown

Position bias concerns how items were shown; selection bias (or exposure bias) concerns whether they were shown at all. Logged data contains outcomes only for items the logging policy chose. An item the old ranker scored low is shown rarely, collects few interactions, and remains scored low. The data is missing not at random (MNAR): whether an outcome is observed depends on what the system believed about it, which is correlated with the outcome itself.

The same structure appears in explicit ratings: people rate films they chose to watch, which they expected to like, so observed ratings skew high (rec3). Schnabel and colleagues' 2016 paper "Recommendations as Treatments" treated recommendation exactly like a medical study with non-random treatment assignment: each rating's propensity is the probability that the user rated (was "treated" with) that item, estimated from data, and training and evaluation are reweighted by 1/propensity so that the observed ratings stand in for the full matrix.

Exposure propensities in a recommender are the probabilities that each item was shown to the user, which depend on the whole funnel (retrieval, ranking, re-ranking, rules). They are only known if the system has a stochastic component and logs its probabilities, which a deterministic top-k ranker does not. That is the fundamental reason mature systems add controlled randomness (exploration slots, randomised tie-breaking, small perturbations) and log the probabilities: without them, the propensity of every unshown item is zero and nothing can be learned about it from logs.

6. Counterfactual evaluation: estimating a new policy from old logs

The same reweighting answers a different question: how would a new ranker have performed, had it been serving? rec8 explained why ordinary offline metrics on logged data are biased towards the logging policy. Counterfactual (or off-policy) evaluation fixes this when the logs record propensities.

Simplify to one slot: in each logged event, the logging policy π0 showed one item a from some candidates in context x, with probability π0(a | x), and observed reward r (1 for click, 0 otherwise). A new, deterministic policy π would choose π(x). The inverse propensity scoring (IPS) estimate of π's average reward is:

IPS = (1/n) Σ over events:  r × 1[π(x) = a] / π0(a | x)

Events where the new policy agrees with what was logged count, weighted by how unlikely the logging policy was to take that action; disagreeing events count zero. In expectation over the logging policy's randomness, this equals the new policy's true average reward, provided every action the new policy takes had a non-zero probability under the old one.

Worked example: six logged events.

EventLogged itemπ0(item)RewardNew policy picksMatchWeight 1/π0Reward × weight
1A0.51Ayes2.002.00
2B0.30Ano—0
3A0.50Ayes2.000
4C0.21Cyes5.005.00
5B0.31Byes3.333.33
6A0.51Bno—0

The logging policy's own average reward: 4 clicks / 6 events = 0.67. IPS for the new policy: (2 + 0 + 0 + 5 + 3.33 + 0) / 6 = 10.33 / 6 = 1.72. That is an impossible click rate: one event with a small propensity (event 4, weight 5) dominates. This is IPS's well-known weakness: unbiased on average, with very high variance on small samples.

Self-normalised IPS (SNIPS) divides by the sum of the weights of matching events instead of the number of events: 10.33 / (2 + 2 + 5 + 3.33) = 10.33 / 12.33 = 0.84. It is slightly biased but always lies within the range of rewards and has much lower variance. Clipping caps weights (say at 4), which would turn event 4's weight from 5 to 4. Doubly robust estimators add a reward model's prediction for every event and use IPS only to correct the model's error, accurate if either the model or the propensities are good. The effective sample size, (Σw)² / Σw², here 12.33² / (4 + 4 + 25 + 11.1) = 152 / 44.1 ≈ 3.4, says these six events carry the information of about three unweighted ones; always report it.

Bottou and colleagues' 2013 paper on computational advertising at Microsoft showed this machinery working at production scale: by randomising some ad-placement decisions slightly and logging probabilities, they could estimate offline, with confidence intervals, the effect of changes to the ad system that had never been deployed.

For full rankings, the action space is enormous (every permutation of items), so exact matching almost never happens. Practical estimators work per position or per item, using the position-based model (an item's probability of being shown at each position under the old and new policies) or assume the reward decomposes across slots. These estimators are an active research area; in production they serve as a filter before online tests, alongside interleaving.

7. Popularity bias and the rich-get-richer loop

Popularity bias combines the previous mechanisms over time. Popular items are retrieved by more sources and ranked higher, so they get more impressions; more impressions mean more clicks and more training data; more data means more confident and usually higher scores; so they are shown even more. Meanwhile the long tail and new items get few impressions, so their estimates stay uncertain and usually low. Some of an item's popularity reflects genuine broad appeal, and some reflects accumulated exposure; naive training cannot tell the two apart.

Several earlier lessons met specific channels of this bias: in-batch negatives in retrieval (rec4), where the logQ correction compensates; inner-product scoring with large vector norms for popular items (rec3, rec4), where normalisation helps; and position bias, which gives top-ranked popular items extra clicks. The cumulative effect is measured at the system level: the Gini coefficient of impressions across items, the share of impressions going to the top 1% of items, catalogue coverage, and the time a new item takes to reach some threshold of exposure (rec8 defines these). Watching them over months shows whether the loop is tightening.

Mitigations act at each stage: exploration traffic that gives uncertain items impressions (rec11); propensity-weighted training so popular items' many clicks are not over-counted; retrieval sources dedicated to fresh and long-tail items; re-ranking with exposure constraints or diversity (rec12); and long-term holdouts that measure what the loop does to user satisfaction and the catalogue over months (rec13).

8. Filter bubbles: what is and is not known

The "filter bubble" concern is that personalisation narrows each user's information diet to content similar to what they already consume, with possible effects on the users and on society. Mechanistically, it is a user-level feedback loop: the model recommends more of what you engaged with; you engage with what you are shown; the model becomes more confident.

Simulation studies show the mechanism can operate: Chaney, Stewart and Engelhardt (RecSys 2018) simulated recommenders retrained on data from their own recommendations and found this "algorithmic confounding" increased the homogeneity of users' behaviour and reduced utility compared with an ideal recommender. Empirical evidence on real platforms is more mixed, depends on how narrowing is measured (diversity of recommendations, of consumption, of opinions) and on the platform, and has changed as platforms changed their algorithms; some studies find recommendations expose users to more variety than they would choose themselves, others find narrowing in specific settings.

The engineering position that survives scrutiny: do not assume either answer for your system; measure it. Track per-user diversity of recommendations and of consumption over time (for example, the entropy of the category distribution of what each user watched each month), compare against a holdout with a less personalised or more diverse policy, and design in calibration and diversity (rec8, rec12) where narrowing appears, especially where the content has civic or health consequences.

9. A debiasing checklist for a new system

Pulling the lesson together, a team building or inheriting a recommender can work through a short list. Log the presentation: every impression's position, surface, layout and device, and the model version, so position effects can be modelled at all. Add controlled randomness and log its probabilities: an exploration slot, randomised tie-breaking among near-equal scores, a small swap experiment; each random decision's probability goes in the log. Estimate propensities per surface and re-estimate after interface changes. Correct training: inverse propensity weights (clipped) or a position tower removed at serving, compared against each other on randomised traffic. Correct evaluation: counterfactual estimates with effective sample sizes for candidate models, interleaving for fast online checks (rec13), and ordinary metrics only on randomised traffic when possible. Watch the loop: concentration and coverage metrics over months, new-item exposure, per-user diversity, and a long-running holdout.

None of these steps requires exotic modelling. They require deciding, early, that the system's own influence on its data is a first-class engineering concern, because retrofitting propensity logging after years of deterministic serving leaves all of that history uncorrectable.
deep:
Why IPW is unbiased: one line of algebra

For an item at position k, let C be the indicator of a click and E of examination, with C = E × R where R is the relevance-driven click. Under the examination model E and R are independent given the item and position, so E[C / pk] = E[E] × E[R] / pk = pk × r / pk = r. The weighted click is an unbiased estimate of relevance, whatever position the item was shown in. The derivation also shows the assumptions: examination depends only on position (not on the items above it, which the cascade model relaxes), the propensity is known, and it is not zero. If position 30 is never examined, no reweighting can recover information about items shown there.

Trust bias and other violations of the simple model

Users do not just examine top results more; they also trust them more, clicking a top result they would have skipped lower down. This trust bias breaks the clean factorisation, because the second factor now depends on position too. Corrections model it with position-dependent false-positive and false-negative click rates. Grid layouts (two-dimensional examination), carousels (horizontal swipes), autoplay and rich snippets all need their own propensity models. The lesson is not that correction fails, but that propensities should be estimated per surface and layout, and re-estimated when the interface changes, because a redesign can shift attention patterns overnight and silently invalidate weights.

Doubly robust estimation in one paragraph

A direct method estimates a new policy's reward by training a reward model on logs and averaging its predictions for the new policy's choices; it has low variance but inherits the model's bias, especially for actions rarely logged. IPS has no model bias but high variance. The doubly robust estimator combines them: for each event, take the model's predicted reward for the new policy's action, then add an IPS correction for the model's error on the logged action when the policies agree: DR = (1/n) Σ [ r̂(x, π(x)) + 1[π(x) = a] × (r − r̂(x, a)) / π0(a | x) ]. If the reward model is accurate, the correction terms are small and variance is low; if the propensities are accurate, the correction removes the model's bias. It is consistent if either is right, which is where the name comes from, and it is the default choice in many off-policy evaluation libraries.

The bias-variance trade-off in off-policy estimators

IPS is unbiased with variance that grows with the squared importance weights. Clipping trades bias for variance; self-normalisation does too, more gently; doubly robust estimators reduce variance when the reward model is decent. A useful diagnostic is how far the new policy is from the logging policy: if they agree on most decisions, estimates are stable; if the new policy mostly takes actions the old one rarely took, no estimator will be reliable, and an online test is the only honest option. This is why logging policies with a little randomness everywhere (rather than a lot in a few places) make far more future policies evaluable.

Exposure is a decision, so log its probability

The single most valuable practice this lesson implies is mundane: whenever any stage of the system makes a random choice (an exploration slot, a randomised tie-break, a sampled candidate, a swap experiment), log the probability with which it made it. Without that number, the data cannot be reweighted later, and the randomness was wasted. With it, every future model can be trained and evaluated with corrections. Systems that log propensities from the start accumulate an asset; systems that add them later can only use data from that point on.

Debiasing through features versus through weights

Two families of methods address position bias. Weighting methods (IPW, unbiased LTR) change how much each example counts. Feature methods give the model the bias variables (position, device, layout) during training and neutralise them at serving, such as YouTube's shallow position tower or simply feeding position as a feature and setting it to a constant (often position 1) at inference. Feature methods have lower variance and need no explicit propensities, but rely on the model separating position effects from relevance effects correctly, which can fail when position and relevance are strongly correlated in the logs (the best items are always on top). Randomised data helps both: it breaks that correlation.

Long-term loops are slower than experiments

Many feedback effects play out over weeks or months: a creator who gets no exposure stops uploading; a user who sees narrower content gradually engages less. A two-week A/B test measures the first-order effect of a change and misses these. Long-running holdouts (a small group kept on an older or more exploratory policy for months) and ecosystem metrics (creator retention, catalogue coverage, new-item success) are the tools for seeing them; rec13 covers their design.
prod:
The public case: unbiased learning to rank on a live search engine

Joachims, Swaminathan and Schnabel's WSDM 2017 paper "Unbiased Learning-to-Rank with Biased Feedback" is a clean, complete example of the lesson's ideas moving from theory into a running system. The theory: treat learning to rank from clicks as counterfactual empirical risk minimisation, with click models providing propensities, so the propensity-weighted training objective is an unbiased estimate of the objective with full relevance labels, even when queries do not repeat. The method: a ranking SVM whose pairwise loss for each clicked document is weighted by the inverse of its position's propensity.

The deployment was on a live search engine for scientific articles, using a linear scoring function over a 1,000-dimensional vector of query-document features. The production ranker had a hand-crafted weight vector. Clicks from 21 days of production traffic provided training data. To estimate propensities, the authors ran a 7-day randomised intervention: for each query, swap the top-ranked document with the document at a uniformly random rank j between 1 and 21, and estimate pj/p1 from the ratio of that document's click rate at j to its rate at 1, smoothed with overall click rates by position; the estimates decayed with rank to a minimum around 0.12, and ranks beyond 21 were assigned p21.

The trained propensity-weighted ranker was compared with production and with a naive click-trained ranking SVM using balanced interleaving, which mixes two rankers' results on one page and credits clicks to the ranker that contributed each result (rec13). Against production: 87 query wins, 48 losses, 83 ties (two-tailed sign test p = 0.001). Against the naive click-trained ranker: 95 wins, 60 losses, 102 ties (p = 0.006). On synthetic experiments built from the Yahoo! LTR data, the method was robust to click noise and to moderately misspecified propensities. The case shows the whole chain: small randomised interventions to measure bias, propensity-weighted training, and an online comparison method that itself resists position bias.

How bias handling fails in production

Stale propensities. A redesign moves from a list to a two-column grid; position propensities from the old layout are still used. Corrections are now wrong, sometimes worse than none. Re-estimate propensities after every layout change, per surface and device.

Exploding weights. Propensities for deep positions are tiny; a few clicks there receive weights of 50 and dominate training batches, producing unstable models. Clip weights and monitor the distribution of weights per batch.

No logged probabilities. The team wants to evaluate a new policy counterfactually, but the system is deterministic and never logged propensities; the estimator is undefined for anything the old policy did not show. Add controlled randomness and log probabilities now; the payoff comes later.

Correlated randomisation. "Random" exploration that depends on something correlated with outcomes (only for new users, only at night) biases the corrected estimates. Randomise independently of user and item features, or log and model the dependence.

Popularity creep. Over a year, the share of impressions going to the top 1% of items rises from 30% to 45% with no single launch responsible. Each change was small and positive in its two-week test. Ecosystem metrics on a dashboard, reviewed monthly, and a long-term holdout catch this.

What to monitor

Click-through rate by position over time (a shift indicates changed attention patterns); propensity estimates per surface with their confidence intervals and last re-estimation date; weight distributions in training; share of traffic with randomisation and logged probabilities; off-policy estimates for candidate models with effective sample sizes; concentration metrics (Gini of impressions, top-1% share, coverage, new-item exposure time); and per-user diversity trends against a holdout.
myths: Users click what is most relevant, so clicks measure relevance.

Users click what they see and find relevant, and what they see depends on position. In web search the top result receives far more clicks than the second even when their order is swapped in experiments. A click is evidence of relevance given examination; the probability of examination must be accounted for, or clicks mostly measure the old ranking.
If we train on all the logged data, the model sees an unbiased picture of user preferences.

Logged data only contains outcomes for items the system chose to show. Items it never showed have no labels, and items it showed often have many. The data is missing not at random, and a model trained on it inherits the old system's choices. Exploration and propensity weighting exist to break this.
Inverse propensity weighting removes bias for free.

It removes bias at the cost of variance: dividing by small propensities produces huge weights, so a few examples dominate and estimates swing wildly. Practical estimators clip weights, self-normalise or combine IPW with a model (doubly robust estimation), trading a little bias for much less variance. Propensities must also be known or estimated well; wrong propensities give wrong corrections.
Popularity bias is fine because popular items are what people want.

Some popularity is genuine quality; some is exposure begetting exposure. A system that recommends popular items gets more interactions on them, which makes them look even better to the next model. Without correction, the long tail is starved of the impressions it would need to show its quality, new items struggle, and the catalogue a platform pays for goes unseen.
Recommenders definitely trap users in filter bubbles.

The evidence is mixed and depends on the platform and how bubbles are measured. Simulation studies show feedback loops can homogenise recommendations, and some audits find narrowing on specific platforms; other empirical studies find recommendation exposes users to more diversity than their own choices would. The defensible engineering position is to measure diversity and concentration on your own system and design against narrowing, not to assume either answer.
lab:
Goal: simulate position bias, correct it with inverse propensity weighting, and run IPS and SNIPS on a simulated logging policy. Python 3.12, standard library only.

  1. Create rec10_lab.py. Reproduce the worked example: compute raw and propensity-corrected click rates for A and B (8% vs 8%; 3% vs 10%).
  2. Simulate a feed: 30 items with hidden relevance ri drawn uniformly from 2% to 15%; propensities by position p = 1/(1 + 0.6 × (k − 1)) for positions k = 1..10. A deterministic "old ranker" orders items by a noisy guess of relevance (true r plus Gaussian noise with SD 4 percentage points) and shows the top 10 on each of 50,000 page views. Generate clicks as Bernoulli(pk × ri).
  3. Estimate each item's relevance by naive click rate (clicks / impressions) and by IPW (Σ clicks/pk / impressions). Compare both with the true ri using Spearman rank correlation (write it yourself: rank both lists and compute Pearson on ranks). Items never shown get no estimate: count them.
  4. Add a 5% exploration share where the 10 shown items are a random sample of all 30 in random order. Repeat step 3 using all data with IPW, and note which items now have estimates.
  5. Counterfactual evaluation: on the exploration traffic only, treat the logging policy for position 1 as uniform over 30 items (π0 = 1/30). Define a new policy that puts the item with the highest IPW-estimated relevance first. Estimate its position-1 click rate with IPS and SNIPS, and compare with the truth (p1 × r of that item).
  6. Reproduce the six-event example: IPS 1.72, SNIPS 0.84, effective sample size about 3.4.

What to look for. The naive estimates should correlate with the old ranker's order as much as with true relevance, and items the old ranker buried should be underestimated. IPW should correlate better with the truth but be noisier for items mostly shown low. Without exploration, some items never appear; with 5% exploration, every item gets data. IPS on the exploration traffic should be close to the truth on average but vary from run to run; SNIPS should vary less.
recap: A recommender learns from data it produced itself: what it showed, where, and to whom, so its training data is biased by its own past decisions.
Position bias means users examine top positions more; the examination model says P(click) = P(examined at that position) × P(clicked | examined), and only the second factor reflects relevance.

Inverse propensity weighting divides each click by the probability that its position was examined; in the worked example, an item with 8% raw click rate at position 1 has an estimated 8% relevance-driven rate while one with 3% at position 4 (propensity 0.3) has 10%.

Propensities are estimated by randomised interventions, such as swapping the top result with a random lower position, or from naturally occurring variation, and they decline with rank (Joachims et al. found the smallest around 0.12 by rank 21).
Unbiased learning to rank trains rankers on clicks weighted by inverse propensities, which makes the training objective an unbiased estimate of the one with true relevance labels.
Selection or exposure bias means items never shown have no labels; propensities of exposure, exploration traffic and care in evaluation address it.
Popularity bias and feedback loops concentrate exposure on already-popular items; monitoring concentration and adding exploration and re-ranking counteract it.

Counterfactual evaluation estimates how a new policy would have performed from logged data: IPS averages reward × 1[new policy agrees] / logging propensity; it is unbiased but high-variance, and self-normalised IPS or clipping tame it.
In the six-event example, plain IPS gives an impossible click rate of 1.72 while self-normalised IPS gives 0.84, against 0.67 for the logging policy.
glossary: Counterfactual evaluation
Estimating how a different policy would have performed using data logged under the current policy, by reweighting logged outcomes.
Doubly robust estimator
An off-policy estimator that combines a reward model's predictions with inverse propensity corrections, remaining accurate if either the model or the propensities are good.
Examination hypothesis
The assumption that a user clicks an item only if they examine it and find it relevant, so P(click) = P(examine) × P(relevant).
Exposure bias
Bias from items having very different chances of being shown, so the data contains many outcomes for some items and none for others.
Feedback loop
The cycle in which a system's recommendations shape user behaviour, which becomes training data that shapes the next recommendations.
Filter bubble
A hypothesised state in which personalisation narrows what a user sees to content similar to what they already consume.
Inverse propensity weighting (IPW)
Weighting each observation by one over the probability that it was observed, so under-observed cases count more and the weighted data mimics an unbiased sample.
IPS (inverse propensity scoring)
The off-policy estimator that averages logged reward × 1[new policy takes the logged action] / logging propensity of that action.
Logging policy
The policy (ranker or recommender) that generated the logged data, along with the probabilities with which it chose each action.
Missing not at random (MNAR)
Missing data whose missingness depends on the missing value itself, such as people rating mostly items they expected to like.
Popularity bias
The tendency of models trained on interaction data to over-recommend already-popular items beyond their true appeal.
Position bias
The effect of display position on engagement independent of relevance: higher positions get more attention and clicks.
Propensity
The probability that a given observation happened under the logging process, such as the probability that position 4 is examined or that an item was shown.
Randomisation intervention
Deliberately randomising part of the ranking (swaps, shuffles, random slots) on a small share of traffic to measure biases or collect unbiased data.
Self-normalised IPS (SNIPS)
IPS divided by the average importance weight instead of by the number of events, which reduces variance and keeps estimates within the reward range.
Unbiased learning to rank
Training rankers on biased click data with propensity corrections so that the objective is unbiased for true relevance.
drill:
Design: debiasing a job-recommendation ranker

A jobs marketplace shows 10 job listings per page to job seekers. Its ranker is trained on "applied" clicks from its own traffic. Recruiters complain that new listings get almost no applications for their first week; analysts find the top 2% of employers receive 40% of all impressions, up from 25% a year ago; and a new ranker that looked 6% better offline on nDCG lost its A/B test. Propose a plan covering data collection, training, evaluation and monitoring.

Answer

Diagnosis. Three loops. Position bias: applications concentrate on top slots, and the model learns that whatever the old ranker placed high is good. Exposure bias: new listings start with no data, are ranked low, get few impressions and therefore few applications, confirming the low score. Popularity concentration: large employers with many listings and strong brand pull dominate exposure, rising year on year. The failed launch is the rec8 pattern: offline nDCG on logged applications rewards imitating the old ranker.

Data collection. Run a swap intervention on 1-2% of traffic (top result swapped with a random position 1-10) for two weeks, per device and layout, to estimate position propensities. Add an exploration policy: one of the 10 slots, on 10% of page views, filled by sampling from relevant new or under-exposed listings with known probabilities. Log, for every impression, the position, the propensity of that position, and for exploration slots the sampling probability.

Training. Weight applications by 1/p(position), clipped at 10, in the ranker's loss (or add a position tower removed at serving and compare). Use a smoothed prior for new listings' engagement features so they are not judged on a handful of impressions.

Evaluation. Counterfactual estimates (SNIPS with effective sample size) of each candidate ranker on exploration and swap traffic; interleaving against production for fast directional checks; then an A/B test whose primary metric is applications that lead to a recruiter response (a quality signal less driven by position), with guardrails on new-listing applications in the first week and employer concentration.

Monitoring. Top-2% employer impression share and Gini, time to first 10 applications for new listings, CTR by position, propensity re-estimation after any layout change, and a three-month holdout on the old policy to measure long-term effects on job seekers' success and recruiter retention.
qa: E
What is position bias and why does it matter for training?

Users pay more attention to top positions, so items shown higher get more clicks regardless of quality. If a model is trained on clicks without accounting for position, it learns that items the old system placed on top are good, entrenching the old ranking and making evaluation optimistic for models that imitate it.
E
What is the examination hypothesis?

It says a click requires two things: the user examined the item, and having examined it, found it relevant. So P(click | item, position) = P(examined | position) × P(relevant | item). Position affects only the first factor; relevance only the second. Separating them is the basis of position-bias correction.
E
What is selection or exposure bias in recommender data?

We only observe outcomes for items that were shown, and what was shown was chosen by the system. Items never shown have no labels, popular items have many, and missingness depends on what the model believed. A model trained on this data cannot learn about items outside its old comfort zone.
M

Two items: A shown 10,000 times at position 1 with 800 clicks, B shown 10,000 times at position 4 with 300 clicks. Position 4's examination propensity relative to position 1 is 0.3. Which is more relevant?

Naively A (8% vs 3%). Correcting for examination: A's clicks per examination are 800 / (10,000 × 1.0) = 8%, B's are 300 / (10,000 × 0.3) = 10%. B is more relevant given that it is seen; it was handicapped by its position. Inverse propensity weighting does exactly this division for each click when training.

Follow-up: How confident are you? — Less for B: its estimate effectively rests on 3,000 examinations, and the propensity itself is estimated with error; the variance of IPW estimates grows as propensities shrink.
M
How do you estimate position propensities?

With a randomisation intervention: on a small share of traffic, swap the top result with one at a random position r and compare its click rate at r with its click rate at 1; the ratio estimates p_r / p_1, because the same item's relevance cancels. Joachims et al. did this for 7 days, swapping the top result with a uniformly random rank from 1 to 21. Alternatives use naturally occurring variation, where the same item appears at different positions across rankers or time, or fit click models to logs.
M
How does unbiased learning to rank work?

Train on clicks, but weight each clicked document's contribution to the loss by 1 / p(position it was shown at). Under the examination model, the expected weighted loss equals the loss you would get with true relevance labels, so minimising it learns a ranker for relevance rather than for the old positions. Joachims et al.'s propensity-weighted ranking SVM, trained on 21 days of clicks, beat the production ranker in live interleaving 87 wins to 48 (83 ties).
M
What is counterfactual (off-policy) evaluation?

Estimating how a new policy would have performed using data logged under the old one. If the old policy was stochastic and logged the probability of each action it took, inverse propensity scoring averages, over logged events, the reward times an indicator that the new policy would have taken the same action, divided by the logged probability. It is unbiased if the logged propensities are correct and every action the new policy might take had a non-zero chance under the old one.
M
Why does IPS have high variance and what do you do about it?

Events where the logging policy chose an action with small probability get large weights (1 / 0.01 = 100), so a handful of events dominate and the estimate swings, even outside the possible reward range. Fixes: clip weights at a maximum, self-normalise (divide by the sum of weights instead of the event count), use doubly robust estimators that add a reward model, and ensure the logging policy explores enough that propensities are not tiny.
H
Compute IPS and SNIPS for a new policy from six logged events.

Logged (action, propensity, reward): A 0.5 1; B 0.3 0; A 0.5 0; C 0.2 1; B 0.3 1; A 0.5 1. The new policy would choose A, A, A, C, B, B. Matches are events 1, 3, 4 and 5 with weights 2, 2, 5 and 3.33; reward-weighted sum 2 + 0 + 5 + 3.33 = 10.33. IPS = 10.33 / 6 = 1.72, an impossible click rate, showing the variance. SNIPS = 10.33 / (2 + 2 + 5 + 3.33) = 0.84. The logging policy's own average reward was 4 / 6 = 0.67, so the new policy looks better, but with six events neither estimate deserves much trust.

Follow-up: What else would you check? — Effective sample size (the squared sum of weights over the sum of squared weights), whether the new policy takes actions the logging policy rarely took, and a confidence interval by bootstrap.
H
How do feedback loops cause popularity bias, and how would you measure and mitigate it?

Popular items are shown more, so they get more interactions, so the next model scores them higher, so they are shown more. Exposure concentrates beyond what genuine preferences justify, and new or niche items never accumulate enough data. Measure exposure concentration (Gini of impressions, share to the top 1% of items), coverage, and new-item time to first meaningful exposure, over time. Mitigate with exploration traffic, propensity-weighted training, logQ correction in retrieval, normalised embeddings, re-ranking with exposure constraints, and holdouts that measure long-term effects.
H
Your team wants to train the next ranker only on clicks from the current ranker's traffic. What are the risks and what do you propose?

The data contains only items the current ranker chose, at the positions it chose; the next ranker learns to imitate it, position effects inflate its top choices, and items it never surfaced remain unknown. Propose: log propensities (the probability each item was shown at each position, which requires a stochastic component), reserve a small exploration share (randomised swaps or an exploration slot), train with inverse propensity weights or a position tower, evaluate candidates counterfactually and with interleaving before A/B tests, and monitor concentration metrics.
H
Is the filter-bubble concern real? How would you approach it as an engineer?

The research evidence is mixed: simulations show feedback loops can homogenise what users see, and some audits of specific platforms find narrowing, while other studies find algorithmic recommendations expose people to more variety than their own choices. As an engineer, I would not assume either answer: measure per-user diversity over time (category entropy of consumption and of recommendations), compare with a randomised holdout, track whether users' consumption narrows faster in treatment than control, and add calibration and diversity re-ranking (rec12) where narrowing appears.

A recommender learns from data it produced; items it never shows get no labels, and logged probabilities of random choices make unbiased learning and evaluation possible.
rec4
A two-tower item tower can embed a brand-new item from its content features, so it has a vector before anyone interacts with it.
rec3
Collaborative filtering needs interactions; a new user or item has none, which is the cold-start problem.
