why:
A music service adds 100,000 new tracks every day. Its recommender, trained on billions of past plays, is excellent at recommending tracks that already have plays. A new track has none. Its collaborative-filtering vector does not exist, its click-through rate is undefined, and the ranker, trained to predict engagement from engagement history, scores it with whatever its default features suggest, usually low. So the track is not recommended, so it gets no plays, so it stays unknown. Somewhere in that daily batch are the next season's hits, and the system is structurally unable to find them.

The same happens to people. A new user signs up and the system knows their country and their phone. Every model built on interaction history has nothing to say. If the first session is generic and dull, many new users never come back, and the system never learns anything about them. These are the two halves of the cold-start problem.

Underneath cold start sits a more general problem that applies even to established users and items: the system only learns about what it shows (rec10). If it always shows what it currently believes is best, it never discovers that something else is better. Every recommendation is therefore a small decision between exploiting current knowledge and exploring to improve it. Too little exploration and the system freezes around its early beliefs; too much and users get a worse product today. The mathematics of this trade-off is the multi-armed bandit problem, and its algorithms, ε-greedy, upper confidence bounds and Thompson sampling, are among the most practically useful tools in recommendation.

Interviewers love this area because it tests judgement. "How would you recommend to a brand-new user?" and "how would you give new items a fair chance?" have no single right answer, but strong answers share a shape: use every prior you have, explore deliberately rather than by accident, bound the cost, log the probabilities, and measure both the short-term price and the long-term benefit. The algorithms make that shape concrete.

This lesson starts with practical cold-start strategies for new items and new users, then builds bandits from scratch: regret, ε-greedy, UCB1 and Thompson sampling, worked over three arms for several rounds. It then adds context (contextual bandits and LinUCB), shows how to evaluate bandits offline without bias using random traffic, follows Yahoo!'s news-recommendation case, and finishes with how exploration is actually implemented in a large ranked feed: exploration slots, uncertainty-driven boosts and logged probabilities.
primer:
The name comes from a gambler facing a row of slot machines ("one-armed bandits"), each paying out with an unknown probability. Every pull earns a reward and reveals a little about that machine. The gambler wants to win as much as possible over an evening. Pulling only the machine that has paid best so far might mean missing a better one that had an unlucky first few pulls; pulling every machine equally wastes money on bad ones. A good strategy tries machines it is unsure about, especially ones that might be good, and gradually concentrates on the best.

A recommender faces the same choice every time it fills a slot. The arms are the candidate items (or layouts, or rows). The reward is a click, a play, a purchase. The gambler's uncertainty is the system's uncertainty about each item's appeal, which is large for new items and small for items with millions of impressions. A bandit algorithm turns that uncertainty into a decision rule.

Three rules capture most of the field. ε-greedy: usually play the best-looking arm, but with small probability ε play a random one. Upper confidence bound (UCB): play the arm whose optimistic estimate (its average plus a bonus for being little-tried) is highest; uncertainty is treated as potential. Thompson sampling: for each arm, imagine a plausible true value drawn from your current belief about it, and play the arm whose imagined value is highest; arms get played in proportion to the chance they are actually best.

The analogy breaks in ways that matter for recommenders. Slot machines have a fixed payout; items' appeal changes (news ages in hours, songs trend and fade). There are three machines in the story and millions of items in a catalogue, so pure bandits over all items are hopeless; bandits are applied over a few candidates the models already like, or over model-predicted values with uncertainty. And the gambler's choice affects only the gambler; a recommender's choices shape users' tastes and creators' incentives. Still, the core idea transfers intact: direct exploration to where uncertainty and potential are both high, and log what you did.

It is worth separating two questions that the word "exploration" mixes together. One is what to explore: which items or options are worth spending traffic on, which depends on uncertainty and on how good they might be. The other is how much to explore: what share of traffic, which positions, which users, which depends on the cost the product can bear. Bandit algorithms answer the first question well. The second is a product decision, settled by measuring the cost against long-term benefits, and no algorithm can make it for you.

Cold start is the most extreme case of that idea. A new item is an arm with no pulls; a new user is a context the models have never seen. The practical strategies in the first part of the lesson are about getting good priors, informed first guesses from content and context, so that exploration starts from a sensible place rather than from zero.
body:
1. Cold start for new items

A new item lacks three things: interaction counts (so engagement features are empty), a collaborative representation (no matrix-factorisation vector, no trained ID embedding) and the trust that comes from history. Each has a remedy.

Content-based representation. Everything known about the item at upload time can place it: title and description text through a text encoder, the thumbnail and frames through an image or video encoder, the audio through an audio model, the creator, category, language, duration and price. A two-tower item tower trained with these features (rec4) gives a new item a vector immediately, so retrieval can surface it to users whose vectors are nearby. Yi et al. assign never-seen IDs to shared hash buckets so the content features carry the vector until the ID embedding is learned.

Priors for engagement features. A new item's click rate is undefined; feeding 0 tells the ranker "nobody clicks this". Better: a smoothed rate with a prior from similar items, (clicks + α × prior) / (impressions + α) (rec6, rec9), where the prior comes from the creator's history ("this creator's videos average 6% CTR"), the category, or a model that predicts engagement from content. Add an explicit "impressions so far" feature so the ranker knows how much evidence stands behind the rate.

Guaranteed exploration. Even with good content features, a new item needs real interactions to confirm or correct the prior. Systems give each new item an exploration budget, for example its first 500 impressions to users predicted to match it, delivered through exploration slots or a temporary score boost. The budget ends when the item's estimates are confident (enough impressions for a narrow posterior) or it has clearly underperformed. hd3 described this for a video platform: new uploads inserted into the index within minutes, with an exploration budget.

Fast updates. The faster interaction counts and embeddings update (nearline counters, frequent retraining, rec9), the shorter the cold period. An item that gets 500 impressions in its first hour should be ranked on its own data by the second hour.

2. Cold start for new users

A new user is not a blank: the system knows the context of the signup. Country and language, device and operating system, the time, the acquisition channel (an ad for cooking videos, a link shared by a friend, an app-store search for "football highlights") and the first screen they land on are all informative. A model trained on new users' early sessions can predict their likely interests from this context alone.

Onboarding. Asking new users to pick a few interests (genres, artists, topics) gives a strong, explicit signal. It also costs friction: every extra step in signup loses some users. Common practice is a short, skippable selection whose choices seed the user vector (by averaging the embeddings of chosen artists, say) and the candidate sources.

A diverse first slate. The first page for a new user has two jobs: be good enough that they stay, and reveal their preferences. Ten popular items from the same category fail the second job; ten varied, broadly appealing items succeed at both. This is exploration at the user level: each click on the first page is far more informative than a click on the hundredth.

Fast fold-in. After the first interactions, update immediately: session features capture the last few actions within seconds (rec9), a user tower that reads recent history produces a new vector on the next request, and matrix-factorisation fold-in (rec3) solves the user's vector from their handful of interactions in microseconds. The weight on population priors should fall as personal evidence accumulates, which a model trained with "number of interactions so far" as a feature learns automatically.

3. The explore-exploit trade-off and regret

Formalise the problem. There are K options (arms). Each time step t, the system chooses one arm at and receives a reward rt (1 for a click, 0 otherwise) drawn from that arm's unknown distribution with mean μa. The goal is to maximise total reward over T steps. The best possible strategy, knowing all the μ, would always play the best arm with mean μ*. Regret is the reward lost by not doing so:

Regret(T) = T × μ*  −  Σ over t of μ(a_t)

A strategy that never explores can lock onto a suboptimal arm forever, so its regret grows linearly with T. A strategy that explores uniformly forever also has linear regret, because it keeps paying for bad arms. Good algorithms achieve regret that grows only logarithmically with T: they explore a lot early, then less and less, spending exploration mostly on arms that might still be best. Lai and Robbins showed in 1985 that logarithmic growth is the best achievable in general, which gives a benchmark for comparing algorithms.

Throughout this section, use a running example: three candidate headlines for a promoted article, arms A, B and C, after some traffic. A was shown 20 times with 2 clicks; B 50 times with 4 clicks; C only 5 times with 1 click. Total plays t = 75. Observed click rates: A 0.10, B 0.08, C 0.20.

4. ε-greedy

The simplest strategy: with probability 1 − ε, play the arm with the highest observed mean (exploit); with probability ε, play an arm chosen uniformly at random (explore). With ε = 0.1 on the example, 90% of the time the system plays C (highest mean 0.20, from five plays), and 10% of the time a random arm, so each arm gets about 3.3% of plays from exploration.

Its virtues are simplicity and robustness, which is why it is everywhere. Its weaknesses are clear in the example. The greedy choice rests on C's five plays; one more non-click drops C's mean to 0.17, and two drop it to 0.14, flipping the leader. Exploration is undirected: B, with fifty plays and a mean of 0.08, gets as much exploration as C, about which we know almost nothing. And with constant ε the system keeps exploring at the same rate forever, so regret grows linearly. Decaying ε (for example εt = min(1, c/t)) fixes the last issue but needs tuning. In recommender practice, ε-greedy survives mainly as a simple "random slot" policy whose uniform randomness is valuable for debiasing (rec10), even if it is not the most efficient learner.

5. UCB1: optimism in the face of uncertainty

The upper confidence bound idea is to act as if each arm is as good as it plausibly could be. For each arm, compute an upper confidence bound on its mean; play the arm with the highest bound. Arms with few plays have wide confidence intervals and therefore high bounds, so they get tried; as they are tried, their bounds shrink to their true means. Auer, Cesa-Bianchi and Fischer's UCB1 uses:

UCB(a) = mean(a) + sqrt( 2 ln t / n_a )

where na is the arm's plays and t the total. On the example, ln 75 = 4.317:

  • A: 0.10 + sqrt(8.63 / 20) = 0.10 + 0.657 = 0.757
  • B: 0.08 + sqrt(8.63 / 50) = 0.08 + 0.416 = 0.496
  • C: 0.20 + sqrt(8.63 / 5) = 0.20 + 1.314 = 1.514

UCB1 plays C. The bonus dominates: C's bound is high because it has been tried only five times, not because of its mean. Notice the scale: the bonuses (0.4-1.3) are far larger than the click rates (0.08-0.20). UCB1's bonus is derived for any reward in [0, 1] and does not know that click rates are small, so it explores very generously at these counts. Variance-aware variants (UCB-V, KL-UCB) use the observed variance or the Bernoulli structure and give much tighter bounds for low rates. UCB1 is deterministic given the history, which is a disadvantage when feedback is delayed or batched: every request between updates gets the same choice.

6. Thompson sampling, worked over several rounds

Thompson sampling (from William Thompson's 1933 paper, rediscovered in the 2000s) keeps a full probability distribution, a posterior, for each arm's mean, and makes decisions by sampling from it. For click-or-not rewards, the natural posterior is a Beta distribution. Start each arm at Beta(1, 1), which is uniform on 0 to 1 ("no idea"); after s clicks and f non-clicks, the posterior is Beta(1 + s, 1 + f). Its mean is (1 + s) / (2 + s + f) and its spread shrinks as s + f grows. The rule:

  1. For each arm, draw one random value from its posterior.
  2. Play the arm with the highest draw.
  3. Observe the reward and update that arm's posterior (add 1 to the first parameter for a click, to the second for no click).

On the example, the posteriors are A: Beta(3, 19), mean 0.136, standard deviation 0.072; B: Beta(5, 47), mean 0.096, SD 0.040; C: Beta(2, 5), mean 0.286, SD 0.160. Here are five rounds, with draws given (in a real system they come from a random number generator):

RoundDraws A / B / CPlayClick?Updated posterior (mean, SD)
10.11 / 0.09 / 0.31CnoC: Beta(2, 6) (0.250, 0.144)
20.16 / 0.10 / 0.12AyesA: Beta(4, 19) (0.174, 0.077)
30.14 / 0.12 / 0.35CyesC: Beta(3, 6) (0.333, 0.149)
40.13 / 0.08 / 0.21CnoC: Beta(3, 7) (0.300, 0.138)
50.17 / 0.11 / 0.15AnoA: Beta(4, 20) (0.167, 0.075)

Read the pattern. C, the least-tested arm, won three of five rounds, not because its mean was always highest but because its wide posterior often produced the highest draw. In round 2 its draw happened to be low (0.12), and A, whose posterior overlaps C's, won and got a click. B, well-tested and probably the worst, never won: its narrow posterior around 0.10 rarely produces a draw above the others. Each update narrows the played arm's posterior: C's SD went from 0.160 to 0.138 in three plays. Over hundreds of rounds, C's posterior will settle near its true rate; if that is high, C will win almost every draw; if low, it will lose almost every draw and stop being explored.

This is the key property: Thompson sampling plays each arm with probability equal to the posterior probability that it is the best arm. Exploration goes where it can change the decision, and fades automatically. It is also randomised, which helps with delayed feedback (requests between updates get varied choices) and gives every choice a probability that can be logged for later debiasing, though computing that probability exactly requires extra work (for example by simulation).

Chapelle and Li's 2011 empirical study compared Thompson sampling with UCB variants on simulations and on display-advertising and news-recommendation data and found it competitive with or better than the alternatives, while being simple to implement. Agrawal and Goyal later proved logarithmic regret bounds for it. It is the most common default bandit in industry.

7. Contextual bandits and LinUCB

The headline example ignored who the user is. In recommendation, the best arm depends on context: a cooking article for one user, a football one for another. A contextual bandit observes a feature vector x (user features, time, device, and arm features) before each choice, and an arm's expected reward is a function of x.

LinUCB (Li, Chu, Langford and Schapire, 2010) assumes each arm's expected reward is linear in the context: E[r | x, a] = θa · x. For each arm it keeps the matrix Aa = Daᵀ Da + I and the vector ba = Daᵀ ca, where Da stacks the contexts in which the arm was played and ca the rewards; the ridge-regression estimate is θa = Aa−1 ba (the same ridge solution as ALS in rec3). It plays the arm maximising:

θ_a · x  +  α × sqrt( xᵀ A_a⁻¹ x )

The second term is the standard deviation of the prediction in the direction of this context: large when the arm has rarely been played in contexts like x, small when it has been played often in similar contexts. α sets how optimistic to be. The structure is UCB, but the uncertainty is per context, so an article well tested on sports fans but never shown to cooking fans gets an exploration bonus only for cooking fans. A Thompson-sampling version draws θa from a Gaussian posterior with covariance proportional to Aa−1 instead of adding a bonus.

Modern systems generalise this: the reward model is a neural network (often the ranker itself), and uncertainty comes from an ensemble of models, dropout, a Bayesian last layer, or count-based estimates of how much data supports each prediction. The decision rule stays the same: score = predicted value + exploration bonus, or score = a sample from the predictive distribution.

8. Evaluating bandits offline with replay

How do you compare bandit algorithms without running each one on live users? Logs from a deterministic production system cannot answer it: whenever the candidate algorithm would choose differently from what was logged, the outcome is unknown (rec10). Li and colleagues' solution was to log a random bucket: a small share of traffic in which the article shown was chosen uniformly at random from the pool. Then replay the logged events in order: for each event, ask the candidate algorithm which arm it would choose given its history so far; if it matches the logged (random) arm, record the reward and let the algorithm learn from it; otherwise skip the event. Because the logged choice was uniform and independent of everything, the retained events are distributed exactly as if the algorithm had been running live; the estimate of its click rate is unbiased. The cost is data: with K arms, only about 1 in K events is retained.

The same paper used this method to evaluate LinUCB and baselines on Yahoo!'s front page, described below. When logging is random but not uniform, inverse propensity weighting with the logged probabilities generalises replay (rec10).

9. Exploration in a large ranked feed

Production recommenders rarely run a textbook bandit over the whole catalogue. Exploration is built into the funnel instead.

Exploration slots. Reserve one or two positions per page (or a probability per page) for exploration. Fill them from a candidate pool of uncertain items, new items, items with few impressions in this user's segment, or items from categories the user has not engaged with, chosen by Thompson sampling or UCB on the ranker's predicted value plus an uncertainty estimate. Place exploration where it is seen but costs little (positions 3-8 rather than position 1). Log the selection probability and position for every exploratory impression.

Score boosts. Instead of separate slots, add an exploration bonus to uncertain candidates' scores in the ranker or re-ranker (rec12), for example proportional to 1/sqrt(impressions), decaying as data accumulates. This is UCB inside a ranker. It is less transparent than slots and its probabilities are harder to log, so randomise a little and log what you can.

Budgets and caps. Limit how much of each user's feed is exploratory (no one should get a page of experiments) and how many impressions any item receives from exploration. Measure the cost with a holdout group that receives no exploration: the short-term engagement difference is the price, and the long-term difference (catalogue coverage, new-item success, retention) is the benefit.

Bandits at the top of the stack. True bandits remain the right tool for small, discrete, fast-changing decisions: which of five headlines or thumbnails to show for an article, which promotional banner to show, which of a dozen home-screen rows to place first. Spotify described a contextual bandit (BaRT) personalising which shelves and explanations appear on its home page, with exploration built into production serving.

10. Uncertainty estimates for a neural ranker

UCB and Thompson sampling need an uncertainty for each candidate's predicted value. With Beta counts that is free; with a deep ranker it must be estimated. Four practical approaches, from cheapest to most principled. Count-based: treat the number of impressions the item (or the user-segment × item pair) has received as a proxy, with uncertainty proportional to 1/sqrt(impressions + prior count); crude but robust and easy to explain. Ensembles: train several rankers with different random seeds or data subsets; the spread of their predictions is the uncertainty, and sampling one member per request is a form of Thompson sampling. Dropout at inference: keep dropout active at serving and run a few passes; the spread approximates uncertainty, at extra compute cost. Bayesian last layer: treat the final linear layer's weights as Gaussian, as LinUCB does for the whole model, and compute the predictive variance from the layer's input; cheap at serving and principled for the part of the model it covers.

Whatever the method, check that the uncertainty is meaningful: items with few impressions should have wider intervals, and predictions with wide intervals should be wrong more often. A miscalibrated uncertainty sends exploration to the wrong places just as a miscalibrated probability distorts a value model (rec6).
deep:
Why Thompson sampling explores the right amount

The probability that Thompson sampling plays arm a equals the posterior probability that a is the best arm. That is a principled allocation: an arm that is almost certainly worse than the leader is played almost never; an arm that has a 30% chance of being the best is played about 30% of the time. As evidence accumulates, these probabilities concentrate on the best arm and exploration fades. UCB achieves a similar effect deterministically through confidence bounds. Both achieve logarithmic regret, but Thompson sampling's randomisation makes it robust to delayed and batched feedback, which is the normal case in recommenders, where rewards arrive seconds to days later and model updates happen in batches.

Priors are where domain knowledge enters

Beta(1, 1) says "any click rate from 0 to 1 is equally likely", which is absurd for a feed where rates are 1-10%. A uniform prior makes every new arm look like a potential 50% winner and over-explores. A prior fitted to similar items, for example Beta(2, 38) for a category averaging 5% click rate, is equivalent to having already seen 40 impressions with 2 clicks, so a new item starts near the category average with moderate uncertainty. Priors from content models do the same per item. Getting priors right is the single biggest practical improvement to bandit performance in recommendation, and it is exactly the cold-start problem from the first section viewed through a Bayesian lens.

Non-stationarity

Bandit theory usually assumes fixed reward rates. News, trends and seasonal content violate this: an article's appeal decays over hours, a song's rises and falls over weeks. A posterior built on all history becomes overconfident and stops exploring an arm whose value changed. Remedies: discount old observations (multiply both Beta parameters by a factor below 1 each hour, which keeps the mean and widens the spread), sliding windows, change-point detection that resets an arm's posterior, or including time features (item age, time of day) in a contextual model. Yahoo!'s news setting, where articles enter and leave the pool constantly, is a case where the arm set itself changes, so new arms' priors matter as much as old arms' updates.

The value of information

A different way to think about exploration asks how much a single impression is worth as information. Showing a new item with an uncertain 2-12% click rate to one user produces an expected reward now (its mean, say 7%) and a reduction in uncertainty that improves all future decisions about that item, for every user who might see it. The more future traffic the item could receive, the more that information is worth. This explains several practical rules: explore items with large potential audiences more than niche ones, explore early in an item's life (when there is the most future to benefit), and explore less near the end of an item's life (news a day old, a seasonal product after the season). Formal "knowledge gradient" and Gittins-index methods compute this trade-off directly; in practice, horizon-aware budgets approximate it.

Exploration has users on the other end

Exploration means showing some users something the system believes is worse. That has ethical and product dimensions. Caps per user, avoiding exploration in sensitive contexts (health, finance, children's surfaces), and excluding items that fail integrity checks from exploration pools are standard. The flip side is also ethical: without exploration, new creators and niche content are structurally excluded, and the system's early biases become permanent (rec10). Teams should be able to state their exploration budget and its measured cost.

Bandits and A/B tests are complements

A/B tests fix allocation in advance to estimate an effect with controlled error; bandits change allocation adaptively to maximise reward. Adaptive allocation breaks the assumptions of standard significance tests (the sample sizes depend on the results), so bandit results should not be read as A/B test results. A common combination: use a bandit to allocate traffic among many short-lived variants (headlines), and A/B tests for lasting decisions about algorithms and policies, including the decision to use the bandit itself (math7 discusses bandits versus A/B tests from the statistics side).

Exploration in retrieval, not just ranking

An item that retrieval never returns cannot be explored by the ranker. Dedicated candidate sources for fresh and under-exposed items (rec1), random sampling of a few candidates from the eligible pool, and retrieval with perturbed user vectors (adding noise to the query embedding, a form of Thompson sampling in embedding space) push exploration down the funnel. Without them, ranker-level exploration only explores among items retrieval already likes.
prod:
The public case: LinUCB on Yahoo!'s Today Module

Li, Chu, Langford and Schapire's 2010 WWW paper is the classic production case for contextual bandits. The Today Module was the most prominent panel on Yahoo!'s front page, featuring news articles from a small, constantly changing pool chosen by editors. Collaborative filtering was a poor fit: articles live for hours, so there is never much history per article, and the pool changes too quickly. The authors framed article selection as a contextual bandit: arms are the articles in the pool; the context is a feature vector built from user features (demographics, behavioural categories, reduced by clustering) and article features; the reward is a click.

The evaluation is as important as the algorithm. Yahoo! ran a random bucket: a small fraction of front-page traffic in which the featured article was chosen uniformly at random from the pool. The authors collected events from this random bucket in May 2009, over 33 million events in total, using the first day's roughly 4.7 million events to tune parameters and the rest for evaluation. Using the replay method (keep only events where the algorithm's choice matches the random logged article), which they proved unbiased, they compared LinUCB with context-free bandits (ε-greedy, UCB) and with variants that used context in other ways. The abstract reports a 12.5% click lift for their approach compared with a standard context-free bandit, with the advantage growing when data was scarcer, the cold-start regime where context matters most.

The case shows three ideas working together: context-aware exploration (LinUCB's per-context uncertainty bonus), a deliberately randomised logging policy that made unbiased offline evaluation possible, and the value of evaluating exploration algorithms on the metric that matters (clicks over time) rather than on prediction accuracy.

How exploration fails in production

Exploration without logging. A team adds random slots but does not log which impressions were exploratory or their probabilities. The traffic is spent; its value for debiasing is lost. Log the probability with every exploratory decision from day one.

Uniform priors. A Beta(1, 1) prior on every new item over-explores obviously weak items and floods exploration slots with them; users notice the quality drop. Use priors from content or category.

Exploration that never ends. An item that has had 10,000 exploratory impressions with a clearly poor click rate is still being explored because its pool membership was based on age, not on uncertainty. Exit rules based on posterior confidence fix it.

Stale posteriors. Trending content's posteriors, built over a week, stop the system from noticing that an item's appeal collapsed this morning. Discount old evidence.

Hidden cost. Exploration's short-term cost is never measured, so it is cut during the next engagement push. Keep a no-exploration holdout and report both the cost and the long-term benefit (new-item success, catalogue coverage, retention).

What to monitor

Share of impressions that are exploratory, per surface and per user; engagement on exploratory versus exploitative impressions; time from item upload to first 100 impressions and to a confident estimate; share of new items that "graduate" to normal ranking; posterior widths for active items; for bandit-controlled decisions, traffic allocation per arm over time and replay estimates on random buckets; and the holdout comparison of long-term metrics.
myths: Exploration is a cost you pay to be fair to new items.

Exploration is how the system learns what it does not know, which is mostly in the system's own interest: a new item that would be a hit can only be discovered by showing it, and a model that never sees outcomes outside its comfort zone cannot improve there. It costs a little short-term engagement and repays it with better long-term models, catalogue health and user satisfaction.
ε-greedy is good enough for any bandit problem.

ε-greedy explores blindly: it spends the same share of traffic on arms it already knows are bad as on promising uncertain ones, and it never stops exploring even when it is sure. UCB and Thompson sampling direct exploration to arms whose value is uncertain and could be high, and explore less as evidence accumulates. In practice Thompson sampling is usually the strongest simple choice.
Cold start is solved by recommending the most popular items.

Popularity is a reasonable first answer for a new user, but it is the same answer for everyone, reinforces popularity bias and teaches little about the person. Good cold-start strategies use every signal available (context, signup source, device, region, onboarding choices), present diverse options that reveal preferences quickly, and adapt after each interaction. For new items, popularity is useless by definition; content features and exploration are needed.
A bandit replaces the ranking model.

Bandits decide how to allocate uncertain choices; in a large recommender they usually sit on top of or beside learned models, deciding which uncertain candidates get exploration slots, or tuning a few discrete choices (layouts, a small set of rows). A full ranker over millions of items is not a bandit with millions of arms; it is a model whose uncertainty can be used to guide exploration.
You can evaluate a bandit algorithm by replaying normal logged traffic.

Normal logs come from a deterministic or near-deterministic policy, so most of the bandit's choices have no logged outcome. Li et al.'s replay method works because they logged a random bucket in which articles were chosen uniformly; then any event where the bandit's choice matches the logged one is an unbiased sample. Without logged randomness, offline bandit evaluation is biased (rec10).

Goal: implement ε-greedy, UCB1 and Thompson sampling, reproduce the worked rounds, and compare regret in simulation, including a non-stationary arm. Python 3.12, standard library only (random.betavariate samples a Beta distribution).

  1. Create rec11_lab.py. Write ucb1(counts, clicks, t) and check it returns C with bounds 0.757, 0.496, 1.514 for the example.
  2. Reproduce the Thompson table: starting from A (2/20), B (4/50), C (1/5), apply the five rounds with the given draws and outcomes and print each updated posterior's mean and standard deviation (mean a/(a+b), SD sqrt(ab/((a+b)²(a+b+1)))).
  3. Simulate three arms with true click rates 0.04, 0.05 and 0.07 for 20,000 rounds. Run greedy (ε = 0), ε-greedy (ε = 0.1), UCB1 and Thompson sampling with Beta(1, 1) priors. Record cumulative regret (0.07 minus the chosen arm's true rate, summed). Average over 20 seeds and print regret at rounds 1,000, 5,000 and 20,000.
  4. Repeat Thompson sampling with an informed prior Beta(1, 19) on every arm (prior mean 5%) and compare early regret.
  5. Make the problem non-stationary: at round 10,000, swap the best and worst arms' true rates. Compare plain Thompson sampling with a discounted version that multiplies all Beta parameters by 0.999 each round (keeping them at least 1).
  6. Replay evaluation: generate a log of 30,000 events where the arm is uniform random and the reward is drawn from the true rates; evaluate Thompson sampling by replay and compare its estimated click rate with the online simulation from step 3.

What to look for. Greedy should sometimes lock onto a worse arm (high variance across seeds). ε-greedy's regret should keep growing linearly. UCB1 should explore heavily at first (its bonus is large for small click rates) and then flatten; Thompson sampling should usually have the lowest regret, and the informed prior should reduce early regret. After the swap, plain Thompson sampling should take a long time to notice; the discounted version should recover faster. The replay estimate should be close to the online result, using about one third of the logged events.
recap: Cold start means having no interaction data for a new user or item; collaborative signals are missing, so content, context and exploration must fill in.

For new items, an item tower or content model places them by their features, and guaranteed exploration impressions collect the first interactions; for new users, context, onboarding and fast fold-in of early actions shape the first sessions.

Every recommendation trades exploitation (show what is believed best) against exploration (show something uncertain to learn); regret measures the reward lost relative to always choosing the best option.
ε-greedy explores a fixed fraction of the time uniformly at random; it is simple but wastes exploration on known-bad arms and never stops.
UCB1 picks the arm with the highest mean plus sqrt(2 ln t / n), an optimism bonus that shrinks as an arm is tried more.

Thompson sampling keeps a posterior per arm, such as Beta(1 + clicks, 1 + non-clicks), draws one sample from each and plays the arm with the highest draw, so arms are chosen in proportion to the probability they are best.
In the worked example, an arm with only 5 trials keeps getting chosen because its wide posterior often produces the highest draw, until data narrows it.

Contextual bandits condition on user and item features; LinUCB fits a linear model per arm and adds an uncertainty bonus from the feature covariance, and gave a 12.5% click lift over a context-free bandit on Yahoo!'s front page.
Bandit algorithms can be evaluated offline without bias by replaying events logged under a uniformly random policy and keeping only those where the algorithm's choice matches the logged one.
In large recommenders, exploration is usually implemented as exploration slots or score boosts for uncertain candidates, with the probabilities logged for later debiasing.
glossary: Arm
One of the options a bandit can choose, such as an article, a layout or a candidate item.
Bandit feedback
Feedback only for the option that was chosen; the outcomes of other options remain unknown.
Beta distribution
A distribution over probabilities between 0 and 1, described by two counts; Beta(1 + successes, 1 + failures) is the posterior for a click rate after starting from a uniform prior.
Cold start
The situation where a user or item has too little interaction history for collaborative methods to work.
Context-free bandit
A bandit whose arms' values are the same for every user and moment.
Contextual bandit
A bandit that observes features (the context) before choosing and whose arms' values depend on those features.
ε-greedy
A policy that chooses the best-looking arm with probability 1 − ε and a uniformly random arm with probability ε.
Exploration slot
A position in a ranked list reserved for an item chosen to gather information, typically an uncertain or new candidate.
Exploit
Choose the option currently believed to be best.
Explore
Choose an option to learn more about it, accepting a possible short-term loss.
LinUCB
A contextual bandit algorithm that predicts each arm's reward with a linear model of the context and adds a bonus proportional to the prediction's uncertainty.
Onboarding
The first-run flow in which a new user states preferences or makes choices that seed recommendations.
Regret
The cumulative difference between the reward of the best possible choice and the reward of the choices actually made.
Replay evaluation
Offline evaluation of a bandit policy on events logged under uniformly random choice, counting only events where the policy's choice matches the logged one.
Thompson sampling
A bandit policy that samples a plausible value for each arm from its posterior and plays the arm with the highest sample.
UCB (upper confidence bound)
A family of bandit policies that choose the arm with the highest optimistic estimate: its mean plus a bonus that is larger for less-tried arms.
drill:
Design: cold start and exploration for a podcast app

A podcast app has 3 million monthly listeners, 400,000 shows, and 2,000 new shows per day. New shows get almost no listens in their first month; 70% of listening goes to the top 1,000 shows. New users churn at 55% within their first week. Product asks for a plan to help new shows and new users without hurting overall listening by more than 1%. Propose the strategies, the exploration mechanism, and how you will measure cost and benefit.

Answer

New shows. Embed each new show at ingest from its description, episode titles and transcripts (speech-to-text plus a text encoder), category, language and host's previous shows, using the item tower so retrieval can match it to listeners with nearby vectors. Set engagement priors from category and host history (for example Beta(2, 18) on "listened over 10 minutes" for a category averaging 10%). Give each new show an exploration budget of, say, 300 impressions to well-matched listeners in its language, delivered through one exploration slot on the home page's "new for you" row, selected by Thompson sampling over the ranker's predicted value with posterior uncertainty from impression counts. Shows graduate when their posterior SD falls below a threshold or after the budget; underperformers exit early.

New users. Use signup context (country, language, acquisition campaign, device) to predict initial interests; offer a skippable pick-three-topics screen; show a diverse first home page (several categories, a mix of popular and well-reviewed niche shows); fold in each listen within seconds via session features and re-rank. Measure the first-week funnel: first listen, second-day return, seventh-day return.

Exploration mechanics. At most one exploratory item per row and two per page; only items passing quality and policy checks; log selection probabilities and positions. Use the exploratory impressions for propensity-weighted training (rec10) and to update new shows' statistics nearline.

Measuring cost and benefit. A/B test with three arms: control (no exploration slots), exploration at 1 slot per page, exploration at 2. Primary metric: listening minutes per user over four weeks (cost must stay above −1%). Secondary: new shows reaching 100 listeners within 14 days, share of listening outside the top 1,000 shows, first-week retention of new users. Keep a small long-term holdout without exploration for three months to measure ecosystem effects (new-show creator retention, catalogue coverage).
qa: E
What is the cold-start problem and why can't collaborative filtering solve it?

A new user has no history and a new item has no interactions, so methods that learn from co-engagement have nothing to work with: there is no row or column to factorise and no neighbours to compare. Solutions use other information (content features, context, onboarding answers) and deliberately gather the first interactions through exploration.
E
What is the explore-exploit trade-off?

Exploiting means showing what you currently believe is best, which maximises immediate reward. Exploring means showing something uncertain, which may be worse now but teaches you whether it is better. Too little exploration locks the system into its early beliefs; too much wastes traffic on bad options. Bandit algorithms manage the trade-off, and regret measures how much reward it costs.
E
Explain ε-greedy and its weakness.

With probability 1 − ε, show the arm with the highest estimated reward; with probability ε, show a uniformly random arm. It is simple and guarantees every arm is tried. Its weakness is that exploration is undirected: it keeps trying arms it is confident are poor, at the same rate forever, and treats a barely tried promising arm the same as a thoroughly tested bad one. Decaying ε over time helps but must be tuned.
M
How does UCB1 decide which arm to play? Compute it for three arms.

It plays the arm maximising mean + sqrt(2 ln t / n), where t is total plays and n the arm's plays. With t = 75: arm A, 2 clicks in 20 plays, 0.10 + sqrt(2 × 4.32 / 20) = 0.10 + 0.66 = 0.76; arm B, 4 in 50, 0.08 + 0.42 = 0.50; arm C, 1 in 5, 0.20 + 1.31 = 1.51. C wins because it is barely tried: optimism in the face of uncertainty. The bonus shrinks as n grows, so well-tested arms compete on their means.

Follow-up: Why are these bonuses so large compared with click rates? — UCB1's bonus is designed for rewards in [0, 1] without assuming small rates; for click rates of a few percent, variance-aware versions (UCB-V, KL-UCB) or Thompson sampling with Beta posteriors explore far more efficiently.
M
Walk through Thompson sampling for three arms.

Keep a Beta(1 + clicks, 1 + non-clicks) posterior per arm: A Beta(3, 19), B Beta(5, 47), C Beta(2, 5). Each round, draw one value from each posterior and show the arm with the highest draw. If draws are A 0.11, B 0.09, C 0.31, show C; no click updates C to Beta(2, 6). Next draws A 0.16, B 0.10, C 0.12: show A; a click updates A to Beta(4, 19). The poorly known arm C keeps winning some draws because its posterior is wide; as data accumulates the posteriors narrow and the best arm wins most draws.
M
Why is Thompson sampling often preferred in practice?

It explores in proportion to the probability that each arm is the best, so it naturally spends little on clearly bad arms and more on uncertain promising ones; it has strong theoretical regret guarantees and in empirical comparisons (for example Chapelle and Li, 2011) it matches or beats UCB variants. It handles delayed feedback and batched updates gracefully because randomisation keeps choices diverse between updates, and it extends naturally to contextual models through posterior sampling.
M
How would you handle cold start for new items in a video feed?

Embed them immediately from content (title text, visual and audio embeddings, creator, category) with the item tower so they can be retrieved for users with matching tastes; give each new item a guaranteed exploration budget, a number of impressions to well-matched users, served through an exploration slot or a score boost with logged probabilities; use the creator's history as a prior for its engagement rates; and update the item's statistics and ID embedding quickly (nearline counters, frequent retraining). Stop exploring an item once its estimates are confident.
M
How would you handle cold start for new users?

Use the context you have: country, language, device, signup source, time, and anything from the referral (an ad for cooking videos). Offer a short onboarding choice of interests, but keep it optional. Start with a diverse slate of popular items within that context, chosen to reveal preferences quickly (different categories, not ten similar items). Fold in each interaction immediately (session features, rec9) so the second page already adapts. Shift from population priors to personal signals as evidence accumulates.
M
What is a contextual bandit and how does LinUCB work?

A contextual bandit sees features of the user and arms before choosing, and the best arm depends on them. LinUCB assumes each arm's expected reward is linear in the context, θ_a · x; it fits θ_a by ridge regression on the arm's past contexts and rewards (A_a = Dᵀ D + I, b_a = Dᵀ c, θ_a = A_a⁻¹ b_a) and chooses the arm maximising θ_a · x + α sqrt(xᵀ A_a⁻¹ x), where the square-root term is the uncertainty of the prediction in this context's direction. On Yahoo!'s Today Module it gave a 12.5% click lift over a context-free bandit.
H
How do you evaluate a bandit algorithm offline?

Log a stream of events where the arm was chosen uniformly at random (a random bucket). Replay the stream: for each event, ask the algorithm which arm it would choose given its history so far; if it matches the logged arm, record the reward and let the algorithm update; otherwise skip the event. Li et al. proved this gives an unbiased estimate of the algorithm's performance, using about K times as many logged events as evaluated ones for K arms. With non-uniform logging, use inverse propensity weighting with logged probabilities (rec10).

Follow-up: What breaks replay evaluation? — Arms or contexts in the evaluation period that were not in the random bucket, a random bucket too small for the number of arms, and interactions between users and the policy that a static log cannot reproduce.
H
Design exploration for a home feed of 20 items per page.

Reserve one or two slots per page (or a probability per page) for exploration. Fill them with candidates whose value is uncertain but plausibly high: new items with content-based scores near the top, items with few impressions in this user's segment, chosen by Thompson sampling over the ranker's predicted value with an uncertainty estimate (for example from count-based variance or an ensemble). Place exploration slots at positions where the cost is modest but users still see them (say positions 4-8), log the selection probability and position, cap per-user exploration so no one gets a degraded feed, and measure the cost with a holdout that has no exploration slots. Use the data for propensity-weighted training and new-item estimates.
H
How do bandits handle non-stationarity, such as news articles whose appeal decays within hours?

Stationary posteriors become overconfident and stop exploring arms whose value has changed. Fixes: discount old observations (multiply counts by a factor such as 0.99 per hour, or use a sliding window), reset or widen priors periodically, include time features (article age) in a contextual model, and keep a floor of exploration. News-style systems also add new arms constantly, so priors for new arms should come from content features or from similar past articles rather than a flat Beta(1, 1).
H
When should you use a bandit instead of an A/B test?

An A/B test is for learning which variant is better with a controlled error rate, holding traffic fixed until the end; it is right for decisions with lasting consequences and multiple metrics. A bandit is for maximising reward while learning, shifting traffic towards winners as evidence arrives; it is right when there are many short-lived options (headlines, news articles, promotions), when the cost of showing losers is high, or when the best option changes over time. Bandits make classical significance testing awkward because allocation is adaptive, so use them for allocation and A/B tests for decisions.

why:
A sports fan opens a video app the evening after a big match. The ranker has done its job well: for this user, every highlight clip of the match has a predicted watch probability above 90%. So the top of the feed is: the official highlights, a fan's re-upload of the official highlights, the five best goals, the post-match interview, the manager's press conference, another re-upload, a tactical breakdown, two more goal compilations. Each item, judged alone, is an excellent recommendation. As a page it is poor. The user watches one or two and scrolls past the rest, and the cooking channel they also love, and the comedy special released that afternoon, are nowhere to be seen.

The ranker cannot fix this, because it scores items one at a time. It does not know that the second clip is a copy of the first, or that interest in the fifth clip about one match is far lower than in the first, or that the business has promised every new creator a chance, or that an ad must appear in slot 5, or that the same seller should not fill the first three rows of a marketplace. Those are properties of the page, not of items, and they are the job of the re-ranking stage and the business logic that runs with it (rec1).

Re-ranking is easy to under-design. Many systems start with a few heuristic rules ("no more than two items per creator", "remove items with identical titles"), add more over time, and end up with an unexplained tangle of rules that fight each other and the model. YouTube's 2018 paper on diversification gives a striking illustration: three reasonable heuristics, fuzzy deduplication, a sliding-window rule and a smooth score penalty, each reduced their key user-satisfaction metric in live tests, while a principled model of diversity increased it and raised watch time by about half a percent.

In interviews, re-ranking is where a design shows maturity. Weak answers end at "sort by the ranker's score"; strong ones say what the page must also achieve (variety, freshness, fairness, ads, rules), how each is expressed (penalties, boosts, constraints), in which order they run, what each costs in relevance, and how the trade-off will be measured online. Being able to compute an MMR step or an exposure share on the whiteboard makes those claims concrete.

This lesson builds the re-ranking stage properly: greedy page construction; maximal marginal relevance worked by hand on six videos; determinantal point processes and YouTube's results; freshness; near-duplicate removal; fairness of exposure, computed for two groups of sellers with position weights; calibrated re-ranking; blending ads and other content types; and how to manage several objectives at once with weights, constraints and trade-off curves.
primer:
Think of putting together a dinner party menu. Each dish on its own has a score: how much the guests will enjoy it. The five highest-scoring dishes might be five rich pasta dishes, each excellent, together a disaster. A good host picks the best dish first, then asks "given what's already on the menu, what adds the most?", and continues. A light salad scores lower than a third pasta dish in isolation, but adds far more to this particular menu. The host also has rules that override taste: one guest is vegetarian, the budget is fixed, the sponsor's wine must be served.

Re-ranking is that host. It receives the ranker's scored candidates and builds the page one slot at a time, asking at each step which remaining candidate adds most to the page as it stands, after accounting for similarity to what is already there, freshness, fairness and constraints. The general pattern is greedy page building:

page = []
while page not full:
    for each remaining candidate c:
        adjusted(c) = score(c) − redundancy(c, page) + boosts(c) − costs(c)
    add the candidate with the highest adjusted score that satisfies all rules

Read the loop as a recipe with four ingredients. The score is what the ranker believes the item is worth on its own. The redundancy term subtracts value the page already provides: the more the candidate resembles items already placed, the less it adds. The boosts add value the ranker does not see, such as freshness, exploration of an uncertain new item, or a promotion the business has committed to. The costs subtract value the page would lose, such as the user-experience cost of an ad. Rules then act as filters on the choice: a candidate that would break a cap or a spacing rule is skipped for this slot even if its adjusted score is highest. Almost every technique in this lesson is a way to define one of those four terms or one of those rules well.

Because the loop runs over a few hundred candidates and about twenty slots, it is cheap: a few thousand similarity computations per request, well under ten milliseconds. Its cost is not compute but design: deciding the terms, their weights, and the rules, and keeping them coherent as the product grows.

The analogy breaks in two helpful ways. A host knows the guests; re-ranking must estimate how much similar items reduce each other's value, and that estimate is a model to be learned and tested, not a fixed fact. And a dinner party happens once; a feed is refreshed many times a day, so re-ranking also shapes what users learn to expect and what data the next model is trained on (rec10). A page that always shows one interest teaches the model that the user has one interest.

A good mental division: the ranker answers "how good is each item for this person now?", re-ranking answers "what is the best page made of these items, given everything else we care about?". The second question involves the first, plus redundancy, freshness, fairness, ads and rules. Keeping the two separate lets each be measured and tuned on its own.
body:
1. Why the page is not the sum of its items

The ranker's score for an item estimates its value if shown, assuming the rest of the page does not matter. That assumption fails in predictable ways. Redundancy: two near-identical items split the user's interest; seeing one makes the other almost worthless. Satiation: interest in a topic declines with each additional item about it on the same page. Coverage: users often have several current interests, and a page that serves only one misses value. Position interactions: an item's value depends on where it lands and what is above it. Each of these means the value of a page is less than the sum of its items' scores when items are similar, which is exactly what diversity-aware re-ranking corrects.

In principle, one could rank whole pages: score every possible page and pick the best. With 300 candidates and 20 slots that is astronomically many pages. In practice, re-ranking uses greedy construction (add the best next item given the page so far), which is fast and, for objectives with diminishing returns (the technical term is submodular), provably close to optimal. All the methods below are variations on greedy construction with different definitions of "best next item".

2. Maximal marginal relevance, worked

Maximal marginal relevance (MMR), introduced by Carbonell and Goldstein in 1998 for search results and summarisation, is the simplest principled diversity rule. At each step, every remaining candidate c gets:

MMR(c) = λ × rel(c)  −  (1 − λ) × max over selected s of sim(c, s)

and the highest is added. λ between 0 and 1 sets the trade-off: λ = 1 is plain ranking by relevance; λ = 0.5 weighs novelty equally with relevance. The similarity function can be the cosine of item embeddings, shared categories, shared creators or any combination.

Worked example. Six candidate videos with relevance scores from the ranker: v1 football 0.95, v2 football 0.93 (a re-upload of v1), v3 football 0.90, v4 cooking 0.85, v5 comedy 0.80, v6 cooking 0.78. Similarities: v1 and v2 are near-duplicates, 0.95; other pairs on the same topic 0.8; pairs on different topics 0.1. Use λ = 0.7 and build four slots.

  • Slot 1 (nothing selected, so no penalty): scores are 0.7 × relevance: v1 0.665, v2 0.651, v3 0.630, v4 0.595, v5 0.560, v6 0.546. Pick v1.
  • Slot 2: v2 = 0.7 × 0.93 − 0.3 × 0.95 = 0.651 − 0.285 = 0.366; v3 = 0.630 − 0.3 × 0.8 = 0.390; v4 = 0.595 − 0.3 × 0.1 = 0.565; v5 = 0.560 − 0.03 = 0.530; v6 = 0.546 − 0.03 = 0.516. Pick v4 (cooking).
  • Slot 3: each candidate's penalty is now its maximum similarity to v1 or v4. v2 0.366, v3 0.390 (closest to v1), v5 0.530, v6 = 0.546 − 0.3 × 0.8 = 0.306 (close to v4). Pick v5 (comedy).
  • Slot 4: v2 0.366, v3 0.390, v6 0.306. Pick v3.

The page is v1, v4, v5, v3 instead of v1, v2, v3, v4. The near-duplicate never appears; three interests are covered in the first three slots. The sum of raw relevance on the page drops from 3.63 to 3.50 (about 4%), which is the "price" of diversity if one believes the ranker's isolated scores; whether users actually prefer the diverse page is measured online.

MMR's weaknesses: the penalty considers only the single most similar selected item, not how many similar items are already there; λ is a hand-tuned global constant; and similarity must be defined well, or the penalty pushes in irrelevant items. It remains a strong, easy baseline, and is widely used in RAG to diversify retrieved chunks (lm9).

3. Determinantal point processes

A determinantal point process (DPP) gives a principled score to a whole set. Build an N × N kernel matrix L for the N candidates: the diagonal entry Lii encodes item i's quality (for example its score squared), and the off-diagonal Lij encodes quality times similarity. The DPP assigns each subset Y of candidates a probability proportional to the determinant of the submatrix LY. Determinants have the right behaviour: for two items with qualities q1, q2 and similarity s, the submatrix is [[q1², q1q2s], [q1q2s, q2²]] and its determinant is q1²q2²(1 − s²): large when both are high quality and dissimilar, near zero when s approaches 1 (near-copies). Unlike MMR, the determinant accounts for all pairwise similarities in the set at once.

Finding the highest-probability set of size k is NP-hard in general, but a greedy algorithm (add the item that most increases the determinant) works well, and efficient implementations exist (Chen, Zhang and Zhou, 2018). The kernel's parameters can be learned from data: choose them to maximise the probability of the sets users actually engaged with.

YouTube's version. Wilhelm and colleagues (CIKM 2018) placed DPP re-ranking late in YouTube's pipeline, with a typical input of N = 100 videos, each with a personalised quality score q from the ranker and a sparse embedding from the video's topical content. Their kernel was Lii = qi² and Lij = α qiqj exp(−Dij / 2σ²), with Dij a distance between embeddings (Jaccard distance over sparse topic tokens worked best) and α, σ learned by grid search on homepage data: α scales all similarities up or down. To order a feed of several hundred videos, they repeatedly asked the DPP for a high-probability set of about a dozen videos, placed those next, and continued with the rest, because similarity between items far apart in the feed matters less than between neighbours.

The live results (about one week of experiments on the mobile homepage) are the public case below: every heuristic they tried lowered "satisfied homepage watchers", while DPPs raised it by 0.63% and overall watch time by 0.52%.

4. Freshness

Freshness matters differently by surface: crucial for news, live events and social feeds, modest for films, irrelevant for reference documentation. Three layers handle it.

In the ranker: age features (hours since publication, with interactions) let the model learn how much users value recency in each context. YouTube's 2016 paper's "example age" feature was a version of this for training (rec4).

In re-ranking: an explicit boost that decays with age, such as score × (1 + β × e−age/τ). With β = 0.3 and τ = 6 hours, a video an hour old gets a 25% boost, a 6-hour-old video 11%, a day-old video 0.5%. Explicit boosts are useful when product goals (keeping the feed feeling alive, supporting new uploads) exceed what engagement-trained models learn, and because they are transparent and easy to tune. They must be tested, since a strong boost floods the feed with new but weak content.

In supply: a fresh-content retrieval source (rec1) and sometimes a reserved slot, because no boost can promote an item that retrieval never returned. Exploration (rec11) overlaps here: new items are both fresh and uncertain.

5. Near-duplicate removal

Duplicates come from re-uploads, cross-posts, the same product listed by several sellers, syndicated news articles and template content. They waste slots and make a page look broken. Detection uses content fingerprints (perceptual hashes for images and video frames that change little under resizing and re-encoding; MinHash signatures over word shingles for text, ev11), embedding similarity above a threshold, and metadata (same product identifier, canonical URL, source ID). Candidates are clustered, and only the best member of each cluster is placed, ideally with the others linked ("also sold by 3 other sellers").

Order matters. Deduplicate after ranking, so the best representative is chosen with full information; and before diversity re-ranking, so diversity penalties are not spent on copies. Overly aggressive "fuzzy" deduplication can remove items that are related but distinct (two different goals from the same match), which is one reason YouTube's fuzzy-dedup heuristic slightly hurt their metric.

6. Fairness of exposure

Rankings allocate attention, and attention is valuable to whoever is ranked: sellers, creators, job seekers, news outlets. Because attention falls steeply with position (rec10), small score differences become large exposure differences. Singh and Joachims (KDD 2018) formalised fairness of exposure: define each position's exposure weight (for example 1/log2(rank + 1), or measured examination propensities); a group's exposure is the sum of the weights of the positions its items occupy; fairness can then require exposure proportional to the group's merit (relevance) rather than to whatever the sort order happens to produce.

Worked example. A marketplace ranks 10 listings: five from large sellers (group A, average relevance 0.84) and five from small sellers (group B, average 0.80). Sorting by relevance puts all of A at ranks 1-5 and B at 6-10. Exposure weights 1/log2(rank + 1) are 1.000, 0.631, 0.500, 0.431, 0.387 for ranks 1-5 (sum 2.948) and 0.356, 0.333, 0.315, 0.301, 0.289 for ranks 6-10 (sum 1.595). Group A gets 2.948 / 4.543 = 65% of exposure while holding 4.2 / 8.2 = 51% of the total relevance. A 5% relevance gap became a 30-point exposure gap.

Alternating the groups (A at ranks 1, 3, 5, 7, 9; B at 2, 4, 6, 8, 10) gives A 1 + 0.5 + 0.387 + 0.333 + 0.301 = 2.521 and B 0.631 + 0.431 + 0.356 + 0.315 + 0.289 = 2.022: shares of 55.5% and 44.5%, much closer to the relevance split, at the cost of moving some slightly better items down. Practical systems implement this as a constraint in greedy re-ranking ("if group B's running exposure share falls below 0.9 × its merit share, place the best B item next") or by amortising over time (fair on average across many requests rather than within each page).

Two cautions. Merit is usually the model's predicted relevance, which may itself be biased by feedback loops (rec10): small sellers may be under-scored because they were under-shown. Exposure fairness should therefore be paired with exploration. And groups must be defined carefully and legally; fairness work involving protected attributes needs legal and policy review, not just engineering.

7. Calibrated re-ranking

rec8 defined calibration of a list: whether its mix of categories matches the user's interests. Steck's method re-ranks greedily to maximise (1 − λ) × total relevance − λ × KL(user's category mix ∥ list's category mix). For a user with 70% romance and 30% action history, it keeps adding romance while romance is under-represented relative to 70% and switches to action once action falls below 30%. It is the targeted form of diversity: not "as varied as possible" but "as varied as this user is". It particularly protects minority interests, which plain relevance ranking tends to crowd out.

8. Blending ads and other content types

Many feeds mix several kinds of items: organic posts, ads, recommended accounts, short videos, promotional modules. Each comes from its own pipeline with its own scores, which are not on a common scale. Blending decides which goes where.

The simplest approach is fixed slots: an ad at positions 5, 12, 19. It is predictable and easy to sell, but ignores context: an irrelevant ad at position 5 costs the user experience more than a relevant one. The principled approach puts everything into one currency. For each ad, the value is its expected revenue (bid × predicted click or conversion probability, from a calibrated model, rec6). The cost is the expected loss in user value from displacing the organic item that would otherwise occupy that slot, plus any long-term effect (users who see more ads return slightly less often). An ad is inserted where value exceeds cost by a margin, subject to constraints: maximum ad load per page, minimum spacing between ads, no ad in the first slot, per-advertiser frequency caps. The exchange rate between revenue and user value is a business decision, informed by long-running experiments that vary ad load and measure retention.

The same logic applies to non-ad modules ("people you may know", promotions): each needs a value estimate and a cost, or it ends up placed by politics rather than evidence.

9. Several objectives at once

By now the page serves many goals: engagement, satisfaction, diversity, freshness, creator fairness, revenue, safety. There are three standard ways to combine them.

Scalarisation: one weighted score, as in the value model (rec6) plus re-ranking terms. Simple and fast, but the weights are hard to interpret and must be retuned when models or content change.

Constraints: optimise the main objective subject to floors and caps for the others ("maximise expected engagement subject to at least 30% of exposure for small creators, at most 15% ad load, at least three categories in the top ten"). Constraints are easier to explain and to guarantee, and greedy re-ranking enforces them naturally. They can be infeasible on some requests (not enough small-creator candidates), so define fallbacks.

Pareto analysis: run several settings (say five values of a diversity weight) and plot each objective against the others. The Pareto frontier is the set of settings where no objective can improve without another getting worse; choosing a point on it is a product decision, made with the curve in view rather than one number. Experiments can map the frontier online with a few arms.

In all three, the metrics that define success should include long-term outcomes (rec13): many re-ranking goals, such as diversity, freshness and fairness, show their value over weeks in retention and ecosystem health, not in the next click.

10. Search results versus feeds

Re-ranking looks different on a search results page. The query states a specific intent, so diversity is mostly about ambiguity: for "jaguar", show the car, the animal and the guitar if the query-understanding model (rec5) is unsure, a practice called intent-aware diversification, which allocates top slots in proportion to the probability of each interpretation. For a clear query ("jaguar f-type price"), diversity should be minimal, and deduplication matters more (several dealers listing the same car). Freshness matters for news-like queries and hardly at all for reference ones. Seller caps and exposure fairness apply as in feeds, but the cost of moving a highly relevant result down is higher, because the user asked for it.

Feeds, by contrast, have no stated intent, are scrolled through, and are visited many times a day, so variety across the page and across visits matters more, and satiation across sessions becomes relevant (do not show the same article a user scrolled past this morning). Many feeds therefore track recently shown items per user and penalise or exclude them, a form of cross-request diversity that per-page methods cannot express.

11. Evaluating re-ranking changes

Re-ranking changes are notoriously hard to evaluate offline. Logged data contains engagement only with pages the old re-ranker built; a new page with different items and order has no labels for its new parts (rec10's selection problem), and the value of diversity shows up in session length and return visits, not in per-item clicks. Offline, report the page-level metrics (distinct topics and creators, duplicate rate, exposure shares, freshness share, calibration KL) and the relevance cost (sum or nDCG of ranker scores on the page), which together trace the trade-off curve. Then rely on online experiments with session and long-term metrics, using several arms to map the curve, and keep long-running holdouts for settings like ad load whose effects accumulate slowly.
deep:
Submodularity: why greedy works

Many page-quality objectives have diminishing returns: adding an item to a page that already covers its topic adds less than adding it to a page that does not. Functions with this property are called submodular. For monotone submodular objectives under a size constraint, the greedy algorithm (always add the item with the largest marginal gain) is guaranteed to reach at least 1 − 1/e ≈ 63% of the optimum, and in practice usually much more. Coverage-style objectives (how many of the user's interests are represented, weighted by their strength) are submodular, and the log-determinant of a DPP kernel is submodular too, which is why greedy DPP inference performs well. MMR is a heuristic with similar spirit but without the guarantee.

Learning the diversity trade-off

Hand-tuned λ values and penalties are brittle. Better approaches learn them. DPP kernel parameters can be fitted to the sets users engaged with, as YouTube did by grid search and later with "deep Gramian" kernels learned by a neural network (which looked strong on their metric but changed the ranking enough to disturb secondary business metrics, so it was not yet deployed). Another approach makes the ranker itself list-aware: features about the page so far (how many items from this topic are already above) let the model learn satiation directly, at the cost of scoring sequentially. Slate-level models (rec14 mentions generative approaches) predict the value of whole pages and are an active research area.

Exposure fairness over time, not per page

Enforcing fairness constraints on every single page is costly: some requests have few good candidates from the protected group. Amortised fairness relaxes it: across many requests (per day, per query type), each group's cumulative exposure should track its cumulative merit. The re-ranker keeps running totals and nudges harder when a group falls behind, which costs much less relevance than strict per-page balance. Singh and Joachims discuss both per-ranking and amortised formulations; production systems usually prefer amortised ones.

Diversity across time, not only within a page

Users see many pages a day. A page can be perfectly varied while the day's feed is not: the same three topics rotate through every refresh, or an article the user scrolled past at breakfast reappears at lunch. Cross-request diversity uses per-user memory of recent impressions: penalise items shown recently without engagement, cap how often a topic or creator appears per day, and decay these penalties over hours. It costs a fast per-user store of recent impressions (often the same session store that feeds the ranker, rec9) and it matters most on surfaces users open many times a day.

Rules as code with owners

Business rules accumulate. A rule added for a launch, a legal requirement in one country, a partner contract, an incident fix: years later, nobody knows why "no more than one item from category 47 above position 8" exists. Treat rules as code: each has an owner, a reason, a creation date, a test, a metric for how often it fires and what it changes, and a review date. Log for every response which rules fired. Many teams discover that a third of their rules no longer fire at all and another third conflict with newer ones.

Position-aware placement

Greedy construction fills slots in order, implicitly assuming the most valuable slot is first. On many layouts that is false: grid layouts put two or three items in the first row; carousels hide items beyond the first few; autoplay makes the first video dominant. Placement can use measured position propensities (rec10) as slot values: the best item goes to the slot with the highest examination probability, and constraints such as "no ad in the most-viewed slot" refer to measured attention rather than index numbers. When the layout changes, the re-ranker's notion of "top" must change with it, or carefully tuned diversity and fairness constraints act on the wrong positions.

The order of operations is a design decision

Filters, deduplication, diversity, freshness, fairness, ads and rules interact, and their order changes the result. A useful default: hard eligibility filters first (they define the candidate set); deduplication next (one representative per cluster); then a single greedy pass that combines the value score with diversity, freshness and exploration terms while enforcing constraints (per-seller caps, fairness floors, ad spacing); then final validation (nothing ineligible, page length met). Doing these as separate passes, each re-sorting the list, is how rule tangles start: a later pass silently undoes an earlier one.
prod:
The public case: DPPs on YouTube's homepage

Wilhelm, Ramanathan, Bonomo, Jain, Chi and Gillenwater's CIKM 2018 paper describes diversifying recommendations on the YouTube mobile homepage feed, where the system must order a few hundred videos for each user. Before DPPs, diversity was handled by heuristics in the serving layer. The authors explain why that is fragile: heuristics are "impoverished models" of diversity, the retrieval and ranking layers are unaware of them, and tuning many interacting heuristics requires repeated, exponentially growing searches over their parameters.

They ran live experiments of about one week each, measuring "satisfied homepage watchers", a metric counting sessions that originate from the homepage and last a significant time. The heuristics all lost: fuzzy deduplication −0.05%, a sliding-window rule −0.26%, and a smooth score penalty (decaying each video's score by its similarity to previously placed ones) −0.41%. The DPP re-ranker, with the RBF-style kernel over ranker quality scores and Jaccard distances between sparse topic-token embeddings, applied in windows of about a dozen videos over an input of around 100 candidates in the base version, gained +0.63% on the same metric and +0.52% in overall watch time, which the authors call "quite a significant jump over the baseline". After the mobile success, DPP diversification was deployed on all surfaces, including TV, desktop and Live. A learned "deep Gramian" kernel scored +1.72% on the satisfaction metric in experiments but changed rankings enough to affect secondary business metrics and had not been deployed at the time of writing.

One more detail is instructive: for some parameter settings, direct interactions on the homepage fell, yet site-wide engagement rose, with more activity in the related-videos panel and longer sessions starting from the homepage. Diversity's value showed up downstream, not in homepage clicks, which is why re-ranking must be judged on session and long-term metrics.

How re-ranking fails in production

Rule tangles. Dozens of heuristic rules, applied in sequence, undo each other and make the page's behaviour inexplicable. Consolidate into one greedy pass with explicit terms and constraints, log rule firings, and delete dead rules.

Over-diversification. A strong penalty with a coarse similarity function pushes in irrelevant items; engagement drops; the team concludes diversity is bad. Map the trade-off curve before deciding, and use fine-grained similarity.

Fresh-content floods. A freshness boost tuned during a busy news week overwhelms the feed during a quiet one with weak new items. Make boosts depend on the quality of fresh candidates, not just their age.

Ad-load creep. Each quarter's revenue target nudges ad load up by a small, individually acceptable amount; retention slowly erodes. A long-term ad-load holdout and a ceiling owned by the product, not the revenue team, prevent it.

Infeasible constraints. A fairness floor cannot be met on requests with few eligible items from the group; the re-ranker fills slots with poor items or times out. Define what happens when constraints are infeasible (relax, amortise, or skip) and monitor how often it occurs.

Who owns the page

Re-ranking is where many teams' interests meet: ranking wants engagement, ads wants revenue, creator and seller teams want fair exposure, trust and safety wants guarantees, product wants freshness and variety, partnerships want contractual placements. Without an explicit owner and a shared objective, each team adds its own rule and the page becomes a negotiated settlement nobody can reason about. Mature organisations make one team own the re-ranking stage, express every request as a term or constraint in one framework, require an experiment for every change to it, and publish a regular report of the trade-offs being made, so that decisions like "one more ad slot" are made with their measured cost in view.

What to monitor

Per page: number of distinct topics, creators and sellers in the top N; duplicate rate; share of fresh items; ad load and spacing violations; how often each rule and constraint fired. Over time: exposure shares by group versus merit shares, catalogue coverage, calibration KL (rec8). Effect: engagement, session length and return rate for re-ranking changes, with long-term holdouts for ad load and diversity settings. Latency: re-ranking time per request (should be a few milliseconds for a few hundred candidates).
myths: If the ranker is good enough, re-ranking is unnecessary.

The ranker scores each item as if it were the only one on the page. It cannot know that the second-best item is a near-copy of the best, or that the top ten are all from one creator.
