Page-level properties need page-level logic. YouTube's DPP work found that diversifying the homepage feed increased satisfied sessions and watch time, gains no per-item model was delivering.
Diversity always costs engagement.

Diversity lowers the sum of item scores on the page, but those scores overestimate the value of similar items shown together (interest in the fifth clip of the same match is much lower than the model predicts in isolation). Well-tuned diversification often raises engagement, as YouTube reported, while badly tuned heuristics lower it: in the same paper, fuzzy deduplication, a sliding-window rule and a smooth score penalty all reduced the target metric.
Fairness means giving every item or creator equal exposure.

Equal exposure regardless of relevance would show users poor results. The common fairness definitions instead ask that exposure be proportional to merit (relevance) across groups, or that no group be systematically under-exposed relative to its relevance. Position weights make this concrete: a group with half the relevance but a fifth of the exposure is being disadvantaged by ranking, not by quality.
Ads blending is just inserting an ad every five items.

Fixed ad slots are simple but ignore the trade-off: an irrelevant ad in slot 3 costs user engagement, while a highly relevant one barely does. Mature systems price the user-experience cost of each ad placement and compare it with the ad's expected revenue, varying ad load and position by user and context, under constraints on minimum spacing and maximum load.
Multi-objective optimisation means finding the right weights once.

Weights depend on the product's priorities, the models' calibration and the current mix of content, all of which change. A weight that balanced engagement and diversity last quarter may over- or under-shoot after a model update. Teams retune with experiments, track the trade-off curve (Pareto frontier) rather than a single point, and often express some objectives as constraints with guaranteed floors instead of weights.
lab:
Goal: implement MMR, a greedy DPP, exposure accounting and a fairness constraint, and see their trade-offs. Python 3.12, standard library only.

  1. Create rec12_lab.py. Encode the six-video example and implement mmr(candidates, rel, sim, lam, k). Check the order v1, v4, v5, v3 at λ = 0.7 and print the order at λ = 1.0, 0.5 and 0.3.
  2. Implement a 2×2 and 3×3 determinant by hand and a greedy DPP selector: start empty, and at each step add the candidate that maximises det(LY ∪ {c}) with Lii = qi², Lij = qiqj × sim(i, j). (For up to 4 items you can compute determinants by cofactor expansion.) Compare its top four with MMR's.
  3. Generate 200 candidates: random topic among 8, random relevance in [0.5, 1.0], similarity 0.8 within topic and 0.1 across. For λ in 1.0, 0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.5, 0.3, build a 20-item page with MMR and print the sum of relevance and the number of distinct topics. This is your trade-off curve.
  4. Exposure: implement exposure(page, groups) with weights 1/log2(rank + 1). Reproduce the lesson's 65% versus 51% and the 55.5% alternating result.
  5. Add a greedy fairness constraint: while building a 10-item page by relevance, if group B's running exposure share is below 0.9 × its relevance share, place the best remaining B item. Report relevance lost and exposure shares.
  6. Add a freshness boost score × (1 + 0.3 × e−age/6) with random ages from 0 to 72 hours, and report how many top-20 items are under 6 hours old with and without it.

What to look for. MMR should drop the near-duplicate at any λ below about 0.9 and spread topics more as λ falls; the trade-off curve should show diversity rising quickly at first for a small relevance loss, then the relevance loss accelerating. The DPP should also avoid the near-duplicate. The fairness constraint should move group B's exposure share up by many points at a small relevance cost. The freshness boost should noticeably raise the share of very new items in the top 20.
recap: Re-ranking optimises the page as a set: diversity, freshness, deduplication, fairness of exposure, blending of content types and ads, and rules that must always hold.
Greedy page building picks, at each slot, the candidate with the best score after penalties for its relation to items already placed.

Maximal marginal relevance scores each candidate as λ × relevance − (1 − λ) × its maximum similarity to already selected items; in the worked example with λ = 0.7 it replaces the near-duplicate and second football clip with cooking and comedy.

Determinantal point processes score a whole set by the determinant of a kernel combining quality and similarity, which rewards high-quality, mutually dissimilar sets; YouTube's live test reported +0.63% satisfied homepage watchers and +0.52% watch time.
Freshness is handled with age features in the ranker, explicit boosts that decay with age, and reserved slots or sources for new content.
Near-duplicate removal compares candidates by content hashes or embedding similarity and keeps one representative per cluster.

Fairness of exposure compares each group's share of position-weighted exposure with its share of relevance; in the worked example, sorting by relevance gives big sellers 65% of exposure for 51% of relevance, and interleaving brings it to 56%.
Ads and other content types are blended by comparing each insertion's expected value with its estimated cost to user experience, under load and spacing constraints.
Several objectives are combined by weighted scores, by constraints with floors and caps, or by exploring the Pareto frontier, and all weights are tuned with online experiments.
glossary: Ad load
The share of positions in a feed occupied by ads.
Calibrated re-ranking
Re-ranking that makes the mix of categories in a list match the mix in the user's history, measured by KL divergence (rec8).
Determinant
A number computed from a square matrix; for a kernel of quality and similarity, it is large when items are high quality and dissimilar, and near zero when two items are near-copies.
Determinantal point process (DPP)
A probability model over sets in which the probability of a set is proportional to the determinant of its kernel submatrix, so sets of similar items are unlikely.
Exposure
The attention an item or group receives from being ranked, usually estimated as the sum of position weights of the positions it occupies.
Fairness of exposure
A criterion requiring that groups receive exposure in proportion to their merit or relevance, rather than disproportionately less.
Freshness boost
An increase to a recent item's score that decays as the item ages.
Greedy re-ranking
Building the page one slot at a time, at each step choosing the candidate with the best adjusted score given what is already on the page.
Kernel matrix
A matrix whose entries measure the quality of each item (diagonal) and the similarity between pairs (off-diagonal).
Maximal marginal relevance (MMR)
A greedy re-ranking rule that trades off relevance against similarity to items already selected, with weight λ.
Multi-objective optimisation
Choosing rankings that balance several goals, such as engagement, diversity, revenue and fairness.
Near-duplicate
An item that is almost the same as another, such as a re-upload, a re-post or the same product from two sellers.
Pareto frontier
The set of solutions where no objective can be improved without worsening another.
Scalarisation
Turning several objectives into one by a weighted sum.
Spacing rule
A constraint on how close certain items may appear, such as at least four organic items between ads or no two items from one seller adjacent.
drill:
Design: the re-ranking stage for a news app

A news app's ranker orders 400 candidate articles per request for a feed of 30. Complaints: the same story appears five times from different outlets; small local publishers get almost no traffic; breaking news takes 20 minutes to appear; the ad team wants an ad every 4 items instead of every 6. Design the re-ranking stage, its order of operations, and how you will tune and evaluate it.

Answer

Order of operations. (1) Eligibility and safety filters (licensing, user blocks, misinformation labels). (2) Story clustering: group articles about the same event using text embeddings and named-entity overlap within a time window; keep the best article per cluster for the main feed (choosing by ranker score with a bonus for the outlet the user prefers), and attach the others as "more coverage". (3) One greedy pass building 30 slots with adjusted score = value score − MMR-style penalty on topic similarity (λ tuned) + freshness boost decaying over hours (stronger for clusters with a sharp recent rise in articles, a breaking-news signal) + small exploration bonus for uncertain new articles. Constraints during the pass: at most two articles per outlet in the top 15; an amortised exposure floor for local publishers relative to their predicted relevance; ads by value versus cost with minimum spacing.

Breaking news latency. The 20-minute delay is a supply problem: add a streaming fresh-articles retrieval source that indexes new articles within a minute, nearline engagement counters, and the freshness boost; re-ranking alone cannot place articles retrieval never returns.

Ads. Do not move to fixed every-4; estimate each ad's value and its cost to user experience from an ad-load experiment (arms at every 4, 5 and 6, plus value-based placement), measuring revenue, session length and 4-week retention. Choose the point on the revenue-retention frontier with the business, and set a hard maximum load.

Evaluation. Offline: duplicate-story rate, distinct stories and outlets per page, local-publisher exposure share versus relevance share, share of articles under one hour old. Online A/B with arms for λ and fairness floor settings: primary metric daily active reading time; guardrails on click-through, 4-week retention and complaint rate; ecosystem metrics for local publishers. Keep a long-term holdout for ad load.
qa: E
Why does a ranked list of the individually highest-scoring items often make a bad page?

Because the ranker scores each item independently, as if it were alone. Items that are near-duplicates or very similar have correlated appeal: once the user has seen one, the next is worth much less than its score says. A page of ten clips of the same match or ten items from one seller wastes slots and narrows choice. Re-ranking accounts for these interactions by building the page as a set.
E
What does maximal marginal relevance do?

It builds a list greedily. At each step, every remaining candidate gets a score λ × relevance − (1 − λ) × its highest similarity to anything already selected, and the best is added. λ = 1 is pure relevance; smaller λ trades relevance for novelty relative to what is already on the list. It is simple, fast on a few hundred candidates, and needs only a relevance score and a similarity function.
E
Name three kinds of business rules in a re-ranking stage.

Eligibility and safety (remove items not licensed in the user's country, blocked creators, content failing integrity checks); spacing and caps (at most two items per creator per page, no two ads adjacent, at least four organic items between ads); and guarantees (reserved slots for fresh content, an exploration slot, a contractual promotion). Rules must be logged so their effect on the page can be measured.
M

Run MMR with λ = 0.7 on six videos: three football clips (relevance 0.95, 0.93, 0.90; the first two near-duplicates with similarity 0.95, other same-topic pairs 0.8), two cooking (0.85, 0.78) and one comedy (0.80); cross-topic similarity 0.1.

Step 1: v1 (football, 0.665). Step 2: the near-duplicate v2 scores 0.7 × 0.93 − 0.3 × 0.95 = 0.366, the other football 0.39, cooking v4 0.7 × 0.85 − 0.3 × 0.1 = 0.565: pick v4. Step 3: comedy v5 0.53 beats the second cooking (0.306) and football (0.39). Step 4: football v3 0.39. Final top four: v1, v4, v5, v3, versus v1, v2, v3, v4 by relevance. The near-duplicate never makes it.
M
What is a DPP and why might it beat MMR?

A determinantal point process scores a whole set by the determinant of its kernel submatrix, where the diagonal holds squared quality and the off-diagonals hold scaled similarity times quality. The determinant is large for high-quality, mutually dissimilar sets and collapses when two items are near-copies. Unlike MMR's single nearest-item penalty, it accounts for all pairwise similarities jointly, and its parameters can be fitted to data on which sets users engaged with. YouTube found DPP-based re-ranking improved satisfied homepage sessions where heuristic rules hurt them.
M
How do you handle freshness in a feed?

Three layers. Give the ranker age features (hours since upload, and interactions with age) so it learns how much users value recency per context. Add an explicit freshness boost in re-ranking that decays with age, for example multiplying the score by 1 + β × exp(−age / τ), for surfaces where recency matters more than the model has learned (news, live events). Guarantee supply with a fresh-content candidate source and, if needed, a reserved slot. Measure the share of impressions on content under 24 hours old and its engagement.
M
How would you remove near-duplicates from a page?

Detect them with content fingerprints (perceptual hashes for images and video, MinHash for text, ev11) and embedding similarity above a threshold, plus metadata (same product ID across sellers, same canonical URL). Cluster candidates and keep the highest-scoring member of each cluster on the page, optionally linking the others ('also from 3 other sellers'). Do it after ranking so the best representative is chosen with full information, and before diversity re-ranking so diversity is not wasted on copies.
M
Compute the exposure share of two seller groups in a top-10 sorted by relevance.

Use position weights 1/log2(rank + 1): 1, 0.631, 0.5, 0.431, 0.387 for ranks 1-5 (sum 2.948) and 0.356, 0.333, 0.315, 0.301, 0.289 for ranks 6-10 (sum 1.595). If big sellers hold ranks 1-5 with average relevance 0.84 and small sellers 6-10 with 0.80, big sellers get 2.948 / 4.543 = 65% of exposure for 4.2 / 8.2 = 51% of relevance. Alternating the groups gives 2.521 versus 2.022, 55.5% versus 44.5%, much closer to the relevance shares at a small cost in ranking quality.
M
How are ads blended into an organic feed?

Each candidate ad has an expected value (bid × predicted click or conversion probability) and an estimated cost: the predicted loss of organic engagement or long-term retention from showing it in a given slot. Insert an ad where its value exceeds its cost, subject to constraints: maximum ad load per page, minimum spacing between ads, no ads in the first slot, frequency caps per advertiser. The cost model is trained on experiments that vary ad load and measure organic engagement and return visits; the exchange rate between revenue and user cost is a business decision.
H
Design the re-ranking stage for a marketplace home feed, including the order of operations.

Input: the ranker's top 300 with value scores and calibrated heads. Order: (1) hard filters and safety checks (eligibility, blocked sellers, policy); (2) near-duplicate clustering, keeping the best listing per cluster; (3) greedy page building with a combined objective: value score, minus an MMR or DPP-style similarity penalty, plus a decaying freshness boost and an exploration bonus for uncertain new listings; (4) constraints during the greedy pass: at most two listings per seller in the top 20, a minimum share of small sellers (exposure fairness floor), ads at positions chosen by value versus cost with spacing; (5) final validation (no sold items, page length met); (6) log every rule's effect. Tune λ, boosts and floors with A/B tests on long-term metrics.

Follow-up: How do you keep it fast? — Everything is greedy over a few hundred candidates with precomputed embeddings; similarity against already-placed items is at most a few thousand dot products, well under 10 ms.
H
Your diversity re-ranker raised intra-list diversity 20% but engagement fell 1.5%. What do you do?

Check how diversity is measured and penalised: similarity defined on the wrong signal (for example coarse categories, so two very different football videos count as duplicates) forces irrelevant items in. Check the trade-off parameter: plot engagement against diversity for several λ values to see whether a gentler setting gets most of the diversity at little cost. Check whether the loss is short-term only: diversity often helps session length and return rate more than immediate clicks, as YouTube observed when homepage interactions dipped for some settings while site-wide watch time rose. Then consider a learned approach (DPP with fitted parameters, or the ranker trained with list-level features) instead of a fixed heuristic.
H
How would you formalise and enforce exposure fairness for small creators without hurting users much?

Define groups (small creators by follower count), a merit measure (calibrated predicted value) and an exposure model (position weights from rec10's propensities). Compute, per period, each group's exposure share and merit share. Enforce a constraint in re-ranking such as 'small creators' exposure share ≥ 0.9 × their merit share' by greedily swapping in the best small-creator item when the running share falls below target, which is cheap and keeps relevance high. Measure the user cost with an A/B test and the creator benefit with small-creator impressions, follower growth and retention. Revisit the merit measure: if the ranker under-scores small creators because of feedback loops, proportional-to-merit fairness inherits that bias, which argues for exploration as well.
refs: Practical Diversified Recommendations on YouTube with Determinantal Point Processes (Wilhelm et al., CIKM 2018)

The public case: DPP re-ranking over about 100 candidates on YouTube's mobile homepage; heuristics (fuzzy dedup −0.05%, sliding window −0.26%, smooth penalty −0.41%) versus DPPs (+0.63% satisfied homepage watchers, +0.52% watch time).
The Use of MMR, Diversity-Based Reranking for Reordering Documents and Producing Summaries (Carbonell and Goldstein, SIGIR 1998)
The original maximal marginal relevance formula.
Fairness of Exposure in Rankings (Singh and Joachims, KDD 2018)
Exposure defined with position weights, fairness constraints proportional to merit, and how to compute fair ranking policies.
Re-ranking a list so its genre mix matches the user's history, trading a little accuracy for calibration.
Fast Greedy MAP Inference for Determinantal Point Process to Improve Recommendation Diversity (Chen, Zhang, Zhou, NeurIPS 2018)
An efficient greedy algorithm for selecting a high-probability DPP subset, used for diversified recommendation.

t: Online experimentation for ranking: A/B tests, interleaving, novelty effects, long-term holdouts and network effects
sum: How ranking changes are tested on live traffic: why ranking A/B tests need millions of users (3 million per arm to detect a 1% relative lift on a 5% click rate), team-draft interleaving worked step by step and Netflix's finding that it needs over 100 times fewer subscribers, choosing primary and guardrail metrics, novelty and learning effects, long-term holdouts and Google's ads-blindness study, and interference in marketplaces and social products with cluster, switchback and two-sided designs.
prereq: ml16
An A/B test randomises users to control and treatment, measures a metric in each and tests the difference; sample-ratio mismatch, peeking and novelty effects are classic traps.
math7
Sample size for a proportion grows with the variance p(1 − p) and with one over the squared minimum detectable effect; CUPED and sequential tests make experiments cheaper and safer to monitor.
rec8
Offline ranking metrics are proxies computed on logged data and often disagree with online results.
rec10
Position bias makes click comparisons across different rankings unfair unless the comparison controls for position.
why:
A recommendation team has a new ranker. Offline it is 3% better on nDCG@10 (rec8). The team runs an A/B test on 1% of users for two weeks, and the result is +0.3% in watch time with a confidence interval of ±0.5%: inconclusive. They run it for two more weeks at 5% of users: +0.15% ± 0.2%, still inconclusive. Meanwhile four other promising rankers wait in the queue, each needing a month of a large share of traffic. At this pace the team can evaluate about ten ideas a year, most results are ambiguous, and nobody knows whether the slow trickle of launches is helping users in the long run.

This is the normal state of ranking experimentation in a mature product. Effects of a single ranking change are small (a fraction of a percent on the metrics that matter) compared with the natural variation between users, so A/B tests need millions of users and weeks of time. Effects also change over time: users react to novelty, adapt to better or worse recommendations, and the system's own feedback loops (rec10) play out over months. In marketplaces and social products, treated and untreated users affect each other, which breaks the basic assumption of an A/B test.

The tools to cope are well established, and this lesson covers them in the order a team uses them. First, the arithmetic of A/B tests for ranking, so you know how much traffic a question costs (ml16 and math7 cover the statistics; here we apply them). Then interleaving, which compares two rankers within the same result list and, in Netflix's measurements, needed over 100 times fewer subscribers than their most sensitive A/B metric to find the better ranker. Then metric choice: primary, secondary and guardrail metrics that do not reward clickbait. Then time: novelty and learning effects, and the long-term holdouts that revealed, in a well-known Google study, that low-quality ads gradually teach users to ignore ads. Finally interference: what goes wrong when users share inventory or influence each other, and the cluster, switchback and two-sided designs that address it.

Interview questions here are rarely about formulas alone. "How would you test this new ranker?" invites a design: which stage first, which unit to randomise, which metric decides, which guardrails block, how long to run, how to recognise novelty, and what changes in a marketplace. Being able to estimate the sample size on the spot and to walk through an interleaved list by hand turns a generic answer into a credible one.

The aim is a practical experimentation programme for a ranking team: fast pruning of many ideas, careful measurement of a few, and a long-term view that keeps short-term wins from accumulating into long-term losses.
primer:
Imagine a wine shop deciding between two suppliers. One way is to give half the customers wine from supplier A and the other half wine from supplier B for a month, then compare how much each half bought. Customers differ enormously (some buy a bottle a year, some a case a week), so the difference between suppliers is buried in the difference between customers, and you need a lot of customers to see it. Another way is a blind tasting: give each customer one glass from each supplier, side by side, and ask which they prefer. Each customer compares the two directly, so their personal taste for wine in general cancels out, and a few dozen tastings may settle the question. But a tasting only tells you which wine people prefer in the moment; it cannot tell you whether customers will buy more wine over the year, or keep coming back.

That is the difference between an A/B test and interleaving for rankers. The A/B test gives each user one ranker and compares groups of users: unbiased and able to measure anything, including long-term behaviour, but noisy because users differ. Interleaving gives each user one list that mixes both rankers' results and sees which ranker's items the user engages with: very sensitive, because each user compares both, but limited to relative preference in the moment.

The analogy breaks in two places that matter. In a tasting, both glasses are poured side by side; in a ranked list, items occupy different positions, and position strongly affects engagement (rec10). Interleaving methods must therefore make sure each ranker is equally likely to supply each position, which is what the coin flips in team-draft interleaving do. And wine customers do not affect each other's choices much; users of a marketplace or a social network do, which is the interference problem at the end of the lesson.

A second useful distinction is between what a test can detect and what a launch will do. A test detects the difference between arms during the test, among the users in it, with everyone else unchanged. A launch changes the experience for everyone, permanently. The two coincide only when users do not affect each other, behaviour does not change with time, and the test population represents everyone. Much of this lesson is about the cases where they do not coincide, and about designs that bring the test closer to the launch.

One more contrast is worth holding: an A/B test answers "what happens if we launch?" and interleaving answers "which ranker do users prefer when both are available?". The first question is the one the business must answer; the second is cheaper and, for rankers, usually points the same way. Using the cheap question to choose which expensive question to ask is the central idea of the staged approach.

The overall picture used by mature teams is a staged funnel of evidence, much like the ranking funnel of rec1: cheap offline metrics prune many ideas; interleaving prunes the survivors quickly on small traffic; A/B tests measure the few best carefully on the metrics that matter; and long-term holdouts check that the sum of many small launches is actually good.
body:
1. The A/B test for a ranking change, and what it costs

The basic design (ml16): randomly assign users (not requests, so each user has a consistent experience) to control (current ranker) or treatment (new ranker); run for a fixed period; compare a pre-chosen metric between arms with a statistical test; check that the split is the expected 50/50 (a sample ratio mismatch means the assignment or logging is broken and the result cannot be trusted).

The cost is set by variance. For a proportion metric such as click-through rate p, a widely used rule of thumb for 80% power at a two-sided 5% significance level is n per arm ≈ 16 σ² / δ², where σ² = p(1 − p) and δ is the absolute effect to detect (math7 derives the exact version). Take a feed with a 5% click rate and a target of detecting a 1% relative lift, so δ = 0.0005: n ≈ 16 × 0.05 × 0.95 / 0.0005² = 16 × 0.0475 / 0.00000025 ≈ 3.0 million users per arm. For a 0.5% relative lift, four times as many: 12 million per arm. Ranking changes on mature products often have true effects of this size, which is why teams run tests on large shares of traffic for weeks.

Three things make it cheaper. Variance reduction: CUPED (math7) uses each user's pre-experiment value of the metric as a covariate, removing the part of the variance explained by who the user is; reductions of a third or more in required sample size are common for engagement metrics. More sensitive metrics: metrics closer to the change (engagement with the ranked surface) are less noisy than site-wide metrics, though less directly tied to value. Interleaving, below, for comparing rankers.

Two design details matter for ranking specifically. Randomise by user, and keep users in their arm for the whole test, because rankers have memory effects (yesterday's recommendations shape today's behaviour). And make sure the whole pipeline is consistent per arm: if the new ranker changes candidates, the re-ranker and logging must handle both, and caches keyed by user must not leak one arm's results into the other.

2. Interleaving, worked

Interleaving puts both rankers in front of the same user at the same time. The design challenge is fairness with respect to position: if ranker A always supplied the top item, A would win because of position bias, not quality. Team-draft interleaving (Radlinski and colleagues) solves it like picking teams for a game: in each round, a coin flip decides which ranker picks first; each ranker then adds its highest-ranked item not already in the list; repeat until the list is full. Each item is labelled with the "team" that picked it.

Worked example. Ranker A's list: a, b, c, d, e. Ranker B's list: b, f, a, g, c. Build six slots.

  • Round 1, coin says A first. A picks its top item, a (team A). B picks its highest not yet chosen: its top is b, so b (team B).
  • Round 2, coin says B first. B's highest unchosen: b is taken, so f (team B). A's highest unchosen: a and b are taken, so c (team A).
  • Round 3, coin says A first. A picks d (team A). B's highest unchosen: b, f, a are taken, so g (team B).

The user sees a, b, f, c, d, g with teams A, B, B, A, A, B. Each team has three items, and across many users each position is equally likely to belong to either team, so position bias cancels in expectation. If this user plays b and d, each team gets one credit: a tie for this user. Another user who plays only f gives B the win. For each user, the ranker with more credited engagement wins; ties are recorded.

Aggregate across users. Suppose 1,000 users engaged: A won for 520, B for 430, and 50 tied. A simple preference measure is (A wins − B wins) / users = (520 − 430) / 1,000 = 0.09. A sign test on the non-tied users treats each as a coin flip under the null hypothesis of no preference: z = (520 − 430) / √(520 + 430) = 90 / 30.8 ≈ 2.9, significant at the 1% level. A thousand engaged users can be enough, where the equivalent A/B test might need millions, because each user's general activity level cancels out of their own comparison.

Netflix's 2017 engineering post describes using a variant of team-draft interleaving for rows of titles on the homepage, with preference measured as which ranker produced the greater share of hours viewed within the interleaved row. Comparing interleaving with A/B tests on the same pairs of rankers using bootstrap subsampling, they found interleaving "can require >100× fewer subscribers to correctly determine ranker preference even compared to the most sensitive A/B metric", and that the interleaving preference correlated strongly with their most sensitive A/B metric across many rankers tested against production.

Variants exist: balanced interleaving (an older method, used in Joachims's unbiased-LTR evaluation, rec10), probabilistic interleaving, and multileaving, which compares more than two rankers in one list. All share the same strengths and limits.

3. What interleaving cannot do

Netflix's post lists the limits plainly. Interleaving is a relative measurement: it says users preferred A's items to B's in a merged list, not how much a launch of A would change retention, revenue or total viewing. Building it is engineering-heavy: the merged list must go through the same downstream logic, and business logic applied after ranking (deduplication, diversity re-ranking, rec12) can change which team's items survive and bias the comparison, requiring consistency checks. And it is short-term: it measures preference on the visits during the test, not learning effects over months. The standard answer is a two-stage process: interleaving to prune many candidates quickly, then an A/B test, now affordable at larger sample sizes per arm because there are fewer arms, to measure the absolute and longer-term effect of the best few.

4. Choosing metrics: primary, secondary, guardrails

An experiment's metrics should be chosen before it starts, in three tiers.

The primary metric (or overall evaluation criterion, OEC) is what the decision rests on. It should reflect user value, be sensitive enough for the test's size, and resist gaming. Click-through rate fails the last test: clickbait, larger thumbnails or moving items up all raise it. Better candidates: successful sessions (sessions containing at least one satisfying engagement such as a watch longer than a threshold), engagement from satisfied interactions, purchases or conversions, return visits within a week. Many teams validate their OEC historically: across past experiments, which short-term metric best predicted the long-term outcome they care about?

Secondary metrics explain the result: clicks, watch time, likes and hides per surface, distribution of engagement by content type, by user segment. They are not decision criteria; testing many of them invites false positives (math7's multiple-comparisons problem).

Guardrail metrics must not get worse beyond a threshold, regardless of the primary result: latency and errors; hides, reports and complaints; diversity and catalogue coverage (rec8); exposure for new creators or small sellers (rec12); ad revenue where the change should be neutral. Guardrails are often tested as non-inferiority: "we are confident the drop, if any, is smaller than 0.5%". A ranker that raises watch time by 1% and raises reports by 10% should not ship.

5. Time: novelty, learning and the long term

Users are not static. A visibly changed recommendation surface attracts exploration: people click new kinds of items out of curiosity, producing a novelty effect that fades. Conversely, some changes produce effects that grow: users gradually learn that a surface has become more useful and visit it more (or that it has become annoying and avoid it). These learning effects can take weeks or months.

Two practices detect them. Cohort analysis: plot the treatment effect not by calendar date but by days since each user first entered the experiment. A curve that starts high and decays is novelty; one that starts low and climbs is learning; a flat curve suggests the measured effect is stable. Longer tests and holdouts: when a curve has not flattened, the test is not done.

Google's 2015 KDD paper "Focusing on the Long-term: It's Good for Users and Business", by Hohnhold, O'Brien and Tang, is the classic demonstration that short-term results can mislead. Studying ads on Google search, they developed experiment designs to measure long-term user learning (described below) and found ads blindness and sightedness: users' propensity to click ads changes with the quality of ads they have previously seen. Showing more, lower-quality ads raised revenue in the short term but taught users to ignore ads, eroding it over time. Their applications included a change to the ads auction that increased the weight of ad quality, and a 50% reduction of the ad load on Google's mobile search interface.

6. Long-term holdouts and surrogate metrics

A team that ships 20 changes a year, each tested for two weeks, never measures their cumulative effect over a year. A long-term holdout keeps a small, random share of users (say 1-2%) on the system as it was at the start of a period, or without a class of features (no exploration slots, an older ad load), for many months. Comparing them with everyone else measures the cumulative long-term effect of everything launched, including learning effects and feedback loops (rec10), on retention and ecosystem metrics. The cost is real (those users get an older product), so holdouts are small, time-limited and refreshed.

Because long-term outcomes such as 6-month retention cannot be waited for in every test, teams build surrogate metrics: short-term metrics validated, on past experiments and holdouts, to predict the long-term outcome. Google's paper did exactly this, building a model that predicted long-term ad engagement from short-term measurements of ad quality. A surrogate is only as good as its validation; re-check it periodically against holdout results.

7. Interference: when users affect each other

The A/B test's core assumption is that one user's treatment does not affect another user's outcome (the stable unit treatment value assumption). Ranking systems break it in several ways.

Shared inventory. In a marketplace (rooms, rides, jobs, limited stock), if treatment users get better rankings, they book the best listings, leaving control users with worse ones. The treatment looks better partly because it took from control; launched to everyone, the effect would be smaller. The bias can even reverse the sign of the conclusion.

Supply-side reactions. Creators, sellers and hosts respond to the demand they see. A ranker that sends more traffic to new creators in the treatment arm changes those creators' behaviour (they upload more), which then affects control users who see the same creators.

Social spillovers. In social products, a treatment that makes treatment users share more changes what their friends, including control users, see.

Designs that reduce interference:

  • Cluster randomisation: randomise whole groups whose members interact mostly with each other (cities in a ride-hailing market, social clusters found by graph partitioning). Interference stays within an arm. Cost: far fewer independent units, hence much less power.
  • Switchback experiments: alternate an entire market between treatment and control over time slots (for example every hour, randomised), used when users cannot be separated, as in dispatch and pricing. Carry-over between adjacent slots must be handled, for example by discarding transition periods.
  • Two-sided randomisation: randomise both buyers and sellers, which allows estimating how large the interference bias is from the cells where treated buyers meet untreated sellers.
  • Budget or supply splitting: in ads and marketplaces, give each arm its own share of the limited resource (each advertiser's budget split between arms), so arms do not compete for it.

8. Running many experiments at once

A ranking organisation runs dozens of experiments simultaneously: retrieval, ranking, re-ranking, UI, ads. Giving each its own exclusive slice of users would leave too little traffic per test. Google's overlapping experiment infrastructure (Tang and colleagues, KDD 2010) organised experiments into layers: experiments in the same layer (changing the same component) are mutually exclusive, while experiments in different layers are randomised independently, so each user can be in one experiment per layer. Interactions between layers are assumed small and checked occasionally. Platform hygiene matters as much as design: A/A tests (both arms identical) confirm that the platform does not produce false differences, sample-ratio checks run on every test, and metric definitions are shared.

9. Experimenting on each stage of the funnel

Experiments on different funnel stages (rec1) need slightly different handling. A retrieval change alters which candidates the ranker sees; its effect depends on the ranker, so test it with the production ranker, and add funnel diagnostics to the experiment (share of shown items from the new source, recall against the ranker's choices). Interleaving at the retrieval level is awkward, because the two candidate sets feed one ranker; teams usually A/B test retrieval changes directly. A ranking change is the natural fit for interleaving followed by A/B. A re-ranking change (diversity, freshness, ads, rules) affects the page as a whole and its value often appears in session and long-term metrics, so it needs A/B tests with longer durations and holdouts; interleaving is unsuitable because re-ranking acts on the whole page. Changes to features or data pipelines should first be validated for training/serving parity (rec9), then tested like ranking changes.

10. Reading a result and deciding

The decision rule should be written before the test starts. A typical one: ship if the primary metric's 95% confidence interval excludes zero in the positive direction, no guardrail is breached beyond its non-inferiority margin, there is no sample ratio mismatch, and the cohort curve has stabilised. Results that are positive but inconclusive are common for ranking; the options are to extend the test (if the cohort curve is stable and power was the problem), to run a larger second test, or to judge the change on secondary evidence (interleaving, offline gains) with explicit acknowledgement of the risk. Results that are positive on the primary metric but mixed on secondary metrics deserve a look at what changed: a ranker that raises watch time by showing longer videos is different from one that raises it by finding better ones. And every decision, positive or negative, should be recorded with its stage-by-stage numbers, so the organisation learns which offline and interleaving signals predict A/B outcomes.

11. A staged programme, end to end

Put together, a healthy ranking experimentation programme has four stages, each cheaper and less conclusive than the next. Offline evaluation (rec8) with counterfactual estimates where propensities exist (rec10) screens dozens of ideas. Interleaving on a few percent of traffic for a few days prunes the survivors to the best two or three. A/B tests with a pre-registered OEC, guardrails, power analysis, variance reduction and cohort analysis measure absolute effects over weeks. Long-term holdouts measure the cumulative effect of everything over months and validate the surrogate metrics the A/B tests rely on. After each launch, record the effect at every stage; over time this calibrates how much each stage's results predict the next, which is the most valuable dataset an experimentation team owns.
deep:
Why interleaving is so sensitive

In an A/B test, the variance of the difference between arms includes the variance between users: a heavy user and a light user differ by orders of magnitude in engagement, and that difference has nothing to do with the rankers. Interleaving makes each user their own control: the outcome per user is a comparison between the two rankers' items shown to that same user at the same time, so user-level variation largely cancels. Only the within-user noise of which items they happened to engage with remains. That is the same principle as a paired design in statistics (ev7's paired bootstrap), applied inside a single page.

Credit assignment in interleaving

Team-draft interleaving credits each engagement to the team that contributed the item. Complications arise when both rankers would have contributed an item (it appears high in both lists): team-draft gives it to whichever picked it first, which is random by the coin flips, so it is fair in expectation. Engagements that are not per-item (session length, return visits) cannot be credited at all, which is another reason interleaving measures only immediate preference. Netflix's choice of "share of hours viewed within the interleaved row" is a sensible per-item, value-weighted credit for a video service.

The long-term methodology in Google's study

Hohnhold, O'Brien and Tang compare several designs for measuring learning effects. In the post-period method, after a long treatment period the treatment is switched off and both groups receive the same experience; any remaining difference in behaviour is what users learned during the treatment, isolated from the treatment's direct effect. The cookie-cookie-day design compares groups that entered the treatment at different times, measuring, on each day, users with different lengths of exposure, which separates learning from seasonal and system changes. The general lesson for recommender teams: to measure learning, you must separate "the treatment's effect while it is on" from "what users have learned from having had it", and that requires designs that switch treatments off or stagger them.

Sequential testing and peeking

Ranking teams watch dashboards daily, and stopping a test early when it looks significant inflates false positives (math7 showed peeking can raise a nominal 5% error rate several-fold). Sequential designs with always-valid confidence intervals or group-sequential boundaries allow monitoring and early stopping for clear harm or clear benefit without that inflation. For ranking, early stopping for harm (guardrail breaches) is especially valuable; early stopping for benefit should be rarer because of novelty effects: an early win may be curiosity.

Counterfactual estimates as a pre-test

Where the logging policy randomises and logs propensities (rec10), off-policy estimators can estimate a candidate ranker's performance before any live traffic, and some teams use them as a stage between offline metrics and interleaving. They are most reliable when the candidate stays close to production (most of its choices were plausible under the logging policy), which is also when online tests are least likely to show large effects. Their main value is ruling out clearly worse candidates cheaply and calibrating expectations; a positive counterfactual estimate is a reason to test, not to launch.

Heterogeneous effects and who a ranking change helps

An average effect of +0.3% can hide +2% for new users and −0.5% for heavy users. Ranking changes often have such heterogeneity, because they shift which content is shown to whom. Pre-registered segment analyses (new versus established users, heavy versus light, country, device) catch it; trawling dozens of segments after the fact finds spurious effects. Some teams estimate heterogeneous effects with causal machine-learning methods, but the practical minimum is a handful of pre-declared segments with multiple-comparison corrections.

Experiment duration and weekly cycles

Behaviour differs by day of week (weekend viewing, weekday commuting), so tests should cover whole weeks, usually at least two, even when power is reached sooner; a test that runs Monday to Thursday measures a different population of sessions than the product serves. Holidays and major events (a sports final, a product launch by a competitor) can swamp ranking effects for days; check whether the treatment effect is stable across them rather than discarding them silently, and avoid starting tests on unusual days.

Bandits versus experiments, revisited

rec11 noted that bandits allocate adaptively to maximise reward, which complicates inference. For ranking, a pragmatic split is: bandits for many short-lived variants (thumbnails, headlines, promotional modules), interleaving and A/B tests for rankers and policies. Adaptive experiments that shift traffic towards a winning arm during a test exist and can reduce the cost of testing bad variants, but their estimates need corrections for the adaptive allocation, and long-term effects still need a fixed holdout.
prod:
The public case: Netflix's two-stage experimentation with interleaving

In November 2017, Netflix engineers Joshua Parks, Juliette Aurisset and Michael Ramm described how Netflix accelerated testing of personalisation algorithms. The homepage of the service, then serving over 100 million members, is built from many rows, each ordered by a ranking algorithm. As those algorithms matured, the post explains, discerning wins in A/B metrics required increasingly large sample sizes and long durations, which limited how many ideas could be tested.

Their response was a two-stage process. The first stage, a fast pruning step, uses interleaving: a variant of team-draft interleaving in which a coin flip decides which ranker contributes the first title to a row and the rankers then alternate, each adding its highest-ranked title not already present. Member preference is measured by which ranker produced the greater share of hours viewed within the interleaved row, with viewing credited to the contributing ranker. The second stage is a traditional A/B test on the few best algorithms, powered with larger samples per cell to measure longer-term member behaviour such as retention.

They validated the first stage on two requirements. Sensitivity: running interleaving and an A/B test in parallel on the same pair of rankers and using bootstrap subsampling to compare the sample sizes needed, they found interleaving "can require >100× fewer subscribers to correctly determine ranker preference even compared to the most sensitive A/B metric". Alignment: across many rankers tested against production, the change in interleaving preference showed "a very strong correlation" with the change in their most sensitive A/B metric. They also stated the limits: interleaving is engineering-intensive, business logic can interfere and needs automated consistency checks, and it is a relative measure that cannot directly measure retention, which is why the A/B stage remains.

How ranking experiments go wrong in production

Sample ratio mismatch. A bug in the new ranker causes some treatment requests to time out and fall back to control's results, or logging drops some treatment events; arms end up 50.4/49.6 instead of 50/50 on millions of users, which is statistically impossible by chance. Every metric is now suspect. Check SRM automatically and stop the analysis until it is explained.

Shared caches. Recommendations cached per user leak between arms when a user's assignment changes, or a shared item-feature cache warmed by treatment traffic speeds up control. Key caches by experiment arm.

Interleaving bias from downstream logic. A diversity re-ranker applied after interleaving removes more of one ranker's items because that ranker tends to propose similar items; the comparison measures re-ranker interaction, not ranker quality. Apply consistency checks and, where possible, interleave after all logic.

Novelty misread as a win. A two-week test shows a lift that is entirely novelty; the launch's long-term effect is negative. Cohort plots and holdouts catch it.

Interference ignored. A marketplace ranking test shows +4% bookings in treatment, but total bookings across both arms did not change: treatment took bookings from control. Check total outcomes across arms and use cluster or switchback designs for supply-constrained products.

Culture and process

Experimentation programmes fail as often through process as through statistics. Common problems: launching on secondary metrics when the primary is flat ("but clicks went up"), re-running a test until it is significant, changing the primary metric after seeing results, and teams with revenue targets owning their own guardrails. The defences are boring and effective: pre-registration of metrics and decision rules, a central experimentation review that checks SRM, power and guardrails before launch, published results including failures, and a long-term holdout owned by a team without a stake in any individual launch.

What to monitor in an experimentation platform

Per experiment: SRM, exposure counts, pre-period balance on key metrics, primary and guardrail metrics with confidence intervals, cohort effect curves. Platform-wide: A/A false-positive rate, number of concurrent experiments per layer, launch decisions and their stage-by-stage effects (offline, interleaving, A/B, holdout). Long-term: holdout versus production on retention, engagement and ecosystem metrics, reviewed quarterly.
myths: A two-week A/B test tells you the effect of a ranking change.

It tells you the short-term effect on users who experienced the change for two weeks. Users adapt: a novel ranker attracts curiosity clicks that fade, while changes that improve quality or reduce annoyances (fewer bad ads) can take months to show their full effect. Google's long-term ads study found the short-term effect was not always predictive of the long-term one, which is why long-running holdouts exist.
Interleaving can replace A/B tests.

Interleaving measures which of two rankers users prefer when both contribute to the same list; it is extremely sensitive but relative and short-term. It cannot measure retention, revenue or long-term satisfaction, and business logic applied after ranking can distort it. Netflix uses it as a fast pruning stage before A/B tests, not as a replacement.
If the treatment group's metric is up, the treatment caused it.

Only if the groups are otherwise identical and do not affect each other. In marketplaces and social products they do: treatment users can book the hotel rooms control users would have booked, and creators respond to the attention they get from treatment users. Such interference can make an A/B test overstate or even reverse the true effect of launching to everyone.
Click-through rate is a fine primary metric for ranking tests.

CTR is easy to move and easy to game: clickbait, misleading thumbnails and position changes all raise it while lowering satisfaction. Ranking tests need primary metrics closer to value (successful sessions, watch time from satisfied sessions, purchases, return visits) and guardrails that catch the ways a ranker can cheat.
A bigger offline gain means a bigger online gain.

The relationship between offline and online changes is loose and differs by system and metric. Teams that track it over many launches typically find online effects much smaller than offline ones, and sometimes of the opposite sign. Offline metrics decide what to test; online experiments decide what ships.

Goal: simulate an A/B test and team-draft interleaving for two rankers, compare their sensitivity, and see a novelty effect. Python 3.12, standard library only.

  1. Create rec13_lab.py. Reproduce the sample-size calculation: 16 × p(1 − p) / δ² for p = 0.05 and relative lifts of 1%, 2% and 5%.
  2. Implement team_draft(list_a, list_b, k, rng) returning the interleaved list and each item's team. Check that with a fixed coin sequence (A, B, A) the lesson's lists give a, b, f, c, d, g with teams A, B, B, A, A, B.
  3. Simulate users: each user has an activity level drawn from a lognormal distribution (so some users engage 50 times more than others) and 200 items have true appeal values. Ranker B's ordering is slightly better than A's (B sorts by appeal plus small noise, A by appeal plus larger noise). A user engages with an item at position k with probability activity × appeal × 1/(1 + 0.5k), capped at 1.
  4. A/B test: assign N users to each arm, compute total engagements per user, and test the difference in means. Interleaving: give 2N users interleaved lists and count wins per user. For N in 100, 300, 1,000, 3,000, 10,000, repeat 200 times and record how often each method correctly identifies B as better (at the 5% level).
  5. Novelty: make treatment users' engagement multiplier 1.10 on day 1, decaying to 0.98 by day 28 (for example 0.98 + 0.12 × e−day/5). Simulate 28 days and print the cumulative measured lift after 7, 14 and 28 days and the effect by day.

What to look for. Interleaving should identify the better ranker reliably at far smaller N than the A/B test, because user activity differences cancel within each user. The A/B test should need much larger samples because of the lognormal activity spread; try removing that spread to see the gap shrink. In the novelty simulation, the cumulative lift should look positive at 7 and 14 days even though the steady-state effect is negative; the day-by-day curve reveals it.
recap: Ranking changes must be tested online because offline metrics are biased proxies; the A/B test randomises users and compares outcomes.
Ranking effects are small relative to noise, so A/B tests need many users: about 3 million per arm to detect a 1% relative lift on a 5% click rate with the 16σ²/δ² rule of thumb.

Interleaving shows each user one list mixing two rankers' results and credits engagement to the ranker that contributed each item; team-draft interleaving alternates picks after a coin flip so each position is equally likely to come from either ranker.

Netflix reported that interleaving needed over 100 times fewer subscribers than its most sensitive A/B metric to identify the better ranker, and that interleaving preference correlated strongly with A/B results.
Interleaving is relative and short-term, so it is used to prune candidates quickly before A/B tests measure absolute and longer-term effects.
Choose a primary metric close to user value, secondary metrics that explain it, and guardrails (latency, complaints, diversity, ecosystem) that block launches even when the primary metric improves.
Novelty and learning effects make short tests misleading; watching the treatment effect over time by cohort and running long-term holdouts reveal them.
Google's long-term ads study found that showing users low-quality ads taught them to ignore ads, and the methodology led to a 50% reduction in mobile search ad load.

Interference between users (marketplaces, social graphs, creators) violates the independence an A/B test assumes; cluster randomisation, switchback designs, two-sided randomisation and budget splitting reduce it.
glossary: A/A test
An experiment in which both arms receive the same experience, used to check that the platform's randomisation and metrics produce no false differences.
Cluster randomisation
Randomising groups of connected users (a city, a social cluster) rather than individuals, so interference stays within an arm.
Guardrail metric
A metric that must not get worse beyond a threshold, regardless of the primary metric's result.
Holdout
A small group of users kept on the old experience for a long time to measure the cumulative effect of many launches.
Interference
When one unit's treatment affects another unit's outcome, such as treatment users buying up inventory that control users would have bought.
Interleaving
An online comparison in which one list mixes results from two rankers and user engagement is credited to the ranker that contributed each item.
Learning effect
A change in user behaviour that develops over weeks or months as users adapt to a new experience.
Minimum detectable effect (MDE)
The smallest true effect an experiment is designed to detect with the chosen power and significance level.
Novelty effect
A temporary change in behaviour caused by something being new, which fades as users get used to it.
Overall evaluation criterion (OEC)
The single metric or combination agreed in advance to decide whether a change ships.
Primary metric
The metric an experiment is designed to move and judged on.
Surrogate metric
A short-term metric validated to predict a long-term outcome that cannot be measured within the experiment.
Switchback experiment
An experiment that alternates the whole market between treatment and control over time periods, used when users cannot be separated.
Team-draft interleaving
An interleaving method in which, after a coin flip, two rankers alternately contribute their highest-ranked item not yet in the list.
Two-sided randomisation
Randomising both sides of a marketplace (buyers and sellers) to measure and bound interference effects.
drill:
Design: testing a new ranker for a food-delivery app's home feed

A food-delivery app wants to test a new restaurant ranker on its home feed. Restaurants have limited kitchen capacity at peak times; couriers are shared across all orders in a city. Offline, the ranker is 5% better on nDCG@10 of orders. The team proposes a two-week user-level A/B test with orders per user as the primary metric. Critique the plan and propose a better one.

Answer

Problems. (1) Interference: treatment users who get better rankings will order from the best restaurants and use couriers, increasing wait times and sold-out items for control users in the same city; user-level comparison overstates the effect (treatment gains partly come from control losses). (2) Orders per user is a reasonable primary metric but misses satisfaction (late deliveries, cancellations) and supply effects (restaurant overload). (3) Two weeks may capture novelty but not learning (users discovering new favourite restaurants changes ordering over months). (4) No pruning stage: if several ranker variants exist, testing each this way is slow.

Better plan. Stage 1: interleaving on the home feed with a small share of users to compare variants quickly on order and click preference; interleaving shares supply within a user's list too, but a small traffic share limits supply effects, and it is only a pruning signal. Stage 2: a switchback or city-cluster experiment for the best variant: randomise cities (or city-hour slots in a switchback with discarded transition periods) so supply competition stays within an arm. Primary metric: completed orders per active user (or per city-hour), with guardrails on delivery time, cancellations, sold-out rate, restaurant acceptance rate and small-restaurant order share. Use CUPED with each city's pre-period orders to recover power lost to the small number of clusters. Run four weeks with cohort analysis, and keep a long-term holdout of a few cities for the quarter. Compare the cluster estimate with a parallel user-level estimate to measure how much interference bias the user-level design would have had.
qa: E
Why do ranking changes need online experiments at all?

Offline metrics are computed on data logged from the old system, are biased by position and selection, and are proxies for what the business cares about. Only an online experiment measures what actually happens when real users receive the new ranking: whether they engage more, are more satisfied, and return. Offline evaluation chooses what to test; online experiments decide what ships.
E
What is interleaving?

Instead of showing users either ranker A's list or ranker B's list, each user sees one list built by merging the two, with each item labelled by which ranker contributed it. User engagement (clicks, watch time) is credited to the contributing ranker, and the ranker that wins for more users is preferred. Because each user compares both rankers directly, it removes the large between-user variance that A/B tests must average out.
E
What is a guardrail metric? Give examples for a feed ranker.

A metric that must not get worse beyond a set threshold, whatever happens to the primary metric. For a feed ranker: p99 latency and error rate, rate of hides and reports, diversity of content shown, share of exposure to new creators, ad revenue (if the change should not affect it), and crash rate. A treatment that raises watch time but doubles hides should not ship.
M
How many users does an A/B test need to detect a 1% relative lift in a 5% click-through rate?

The absolute effect is 0.05 × 0.01 = 0.0005. With the rule of thumb n per arm ≈ 16 σ² / δ² for 80% power at a 5% two-sided significance level, and σ² = p(1 − p) = 0.0475, n ≈ 16 × 0.0475 / 0.0005² ≈ 3.0 million users per arm. In practice per-user metrics have their own variance (users differ in activity), which can raise or lower this, and variance reduction such as CUPED (math7) can cut it substantially.

Follow-up: How would you reduce it? — CUPED with pre-experiment activity as a covariate, a more sensitive metric, interleaving for the first-stage comparison, or accepting a larger minimum detectable effect.
M
Walk through team-draft interleaving for two short rankings.

Ranker A: a, b, c, d, e. Ranker B: b, f, a, g, c. Flip a coin; say A picks first: A adds a. B adds its highest item not yet chosen, b. Next round, flip again; say B first: B adds f, then A adds its highest remaining, c. Next round, A first: A adds d, B adds g. The list is a, b, f, c, d, g with owners A, B, B, A, A, B. If the user plays b and d, B gets one credit and A one; with more engagement the counts decide the user's preference, aggregated over many users with a sign test.
M
What are novelty and learning effects and how do you detect them?

A novelty effect is a temporary change because something is new: users click a redesigned row out of curiosity, and the lift fades. A learning effect is a gradual change as users adapt: they learn that recommendations have become more relevant and use them more, or learn to ignore a surface that annoys them. Detect both by plotting the treatment effect by day since a user first entered the experiment (cohort analysis) and by running longer tests or holdouts; a decaying curve suggests novelty, a growing one learning.
M
Why might interleaving and A/B results disagree?

Interleaving measures relative preference within a single list on the current visit; A/B measures absolute outcomes over time, including effects interleaving cannot see: changes in how often users return, long-term satisfaction, effects on content supply. A ranker that wins clicks by showing more clickbait can win interleaving and lose an A/B test on retention. Business logic applied after interleaving (deduplication, re-ranking) can also bias credit. Netflix reported strong alignment with its most sensitive A/B metric, but uses A/B tests as the second stage for exactly these reasons.
M
How do you choose the primary metric for a recommendation experiment?

It should reflect user value, be sensitive enough to detect realistic effects in a feasible test, and be hard to game. For a video service, total watch time is sensitive but gameable by autoplay; 'satisfied sessions' (sessions above a duration threshold) or return rate is closer to value. Validate candidates historically: which short-term metric best predicted long-term retention in past experiments? Pre-register it with secondary metrics and guardrails before the test starts.
M
What is a long-term holdout and why keep one?

A small share of users (often 1-5%) kept on an older version of the system, or without a class of features, for months. It measures the cumulative effect of many launches, each of which was tested only for a few weeks, and reveals slow effects such as ad blindness, satiation, or ecosystem changes. The cost is that those users get a worse product for the duration, so holdouts are small and periodically refreshed.
H
How does interference arise in a two-sided marketplace experiment, and how do you handle it?

Treatment and control users share inventory and suppliers. If a new ranker helps treatment users find the best listings, they book them, leaving control users worse listings: the treatment looks better partly because it took from control, and launching to everyone would show a smaller effect. Sellers also react to demand from both arms. Remedies: randomise by cluster (city or market) so competition stays within an arm; switchback designs that alternate a market between treatment and control over time slots; two-sided randomisation of both buyers and sellers to estimate the bias; and budget-split designs that give each arm its own share of supply.
Follow-up: What do cluster designs cost? — Far fewer independent units (cities instead of users), so much less statistical power; variance reduction and longer tests compensate.
H
Design the experimentation programme for a team that ships 30 ranking changes a year.

Stage 0: offline evaluation harness (rec8) filters candidates. Stage 1: interleaving against production on a few percent of traffic for days to prune to the best few. Stage 2: A/B tests with pre-registered primary metric (for example satisfied sessions per user), secondary metrics and guardrails, power analysis and CUPED, two to four weeks with cohort analysis for novelty. Overlapping experiments in orthogonal layers so many run at once. A permanent 2% long-term holdout refreshed twice a year, measuring retention and ecosystem metrics against all launches combined. A launch review comparing each change's offline, interleaving and A/B effects to keep calibrating which stage predicts what.
H
Your ranking A/B test shows +0.4% watch time after two weeks, but the effect was +1.2% in week one and +0.1% in week two. What do you conclude and do?

The decaying effect suggests a novelty effect: users explored the changed recommendations out of curiosity and then returned to old habits, so the steady-state effect may be near zero or even negative. Check by cohort (effect by days since exposure, not calendar days), check whether the decay is real or noise with confidence intervals per week, and extend the test or move it to a longer holdout. Also check guardrails and satisfaction metrics: novelty that raises short-term watching at the cost of satisfaction is worse than nothing. Do not ship on the two-week average.
refs: Innovating Faster on Personalization Algorithms at Netflix Using Interleaving (Netflix Tech Blog, November 2017)

The public case: team-draft interleaving as a fast first stage; over 100 times fewer subscribers than the most sensitive A/B metric to identify the better ranker; strong correlation with A/B results; limitations.
Focusing on the Long-term: It's Good for Users and Business (Hohnhold, O'Brien, Tang, KDD 2015)
Methodology for measuring long-term user learning (post-period and cookie-cookie-day designs), ads blindness driven by ad quality, and a 50% reduction in mobile search ad load.

The practitioner's reference on A/B testing: OEC, guardrails, variance reduction, novelty effects, interference and holdouts.
